dzungar-khanate.r: The [[e:dzungars|Dzungars]] combined nomadic herding with farming by [[e:uyghurs|Uyghur]] Taranchi settlers in the Ili valley and with metalworking, making firearms and [[e:field-artillery|cannon]] with the help of a captured Swedish officer, Johan Gustaf Renat. They followed [[e:tibetan-buddhism|Tibetan Buddhism]] and intervened in [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]], sacking Lhasa in 1717. Under Tsewang Rabtan they raided the [[s:kazakh-khanate|Kazakh Khanate]] in the 1720s, the 'Great Disaster'.
dzungar-khanate.e: After civil war over the succession, the [[e:qianlong-emperor|Qianlong Emperor]] sent Qing armies in 1755. Following the revolt of Amursana, Qing forces carried out a [[e:genocide|genocide]] of the [[e:dzungars|Dzungars]] between 1755 and 1758, and [[e:smallpox|smallpox]] killed many more. [[e:dzungaria|Dzungaria]] became part of Qing [[e:xinjiang|Xinjiang]].

duchy-of-poland.t: The first Polish state, created by the Piast dukes around Gniezno, which adopted Christianity in 966 and became a kingdom in 1025.
duchy-of-poland.o: Around 960 Mieszko I of the Piast dynasty ruled the Polans of [[s:duchy-of-greater-poland|Greater Poland]] from strongholds at Gniezno and Poznan. He married the Bohemian princess Dubrawka and was baptised in 966, bringing his realm into [[e:latin|Latin]] Christendom. By the 990s he had added [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]], [[s:duchy-of-silesia|Silesia]] and Lesser [[e:poland|Poland]].
duchy-of-poland.r: The Piast dukes ruled through a network of fortified centres and a mounted retinue, and supported themselves with tribute and the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]]. Around 991 Mieszko placed his lands under papal protection in the document known as Dagome iudex. His son Boleslaw I welcomed Otto III at the Congress of Gniezno in 1000, which created an archbishopric at Gniezno.
duchy-of-poland.e: Boleslaw I fought the emperor Henry II for years, gaining Lusatia at the Peace of Bautzen in 1018, and the same year briefly took Kiev. Shortly before his death in 1025 he was crowned king, and the duchy became the [[s:kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385|Kingdom of Poland]] (1025-1385).

duchy-of-znojmo.t: The southern Moravian appanage of the Přemyslid dynasty, centred on Znojmo, whose Romanesque rotunda preserves rare paintings of the Bohemian dukes.
duchy-of-znojmo.o: Znojmo in southern [[s:margraviate-of-moravia|Moravia]] was split off from the Brno [[e:appanage|appanage]] around 1092, when Conrad I of Brno became Duke of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] and his son Litold received Znojmo. It was one of three Moravian appanages, alongside Olomouc and Brno, held by junior Přemyslid princes.
duchy-of-znojmo.r: The princes ruled from the castle of Znojmo on a crag above the Dyje (Thaya) river, close to the Austrian border. The castle's Romanesque rotunda of Saint Catherine contains wall paintings of 1134 showing the legendary and historical Přemyslid rulers, an important source for the dynasty's self-image. Conrad II of Znojmo was a strong contender for the Bohemian throne.
duchy-of-znojmo.e: The [[e:appanage|appanage]] system ended in the late 12th century as [[s:margraviate-of-moravia|Moravia]] became a margraviate; around 1197 Vladislaus Henry united the Moravian lands. Znojmo became a royal town in the 13th century under Ottokar I.

duchy-of-mecklenburg-gustrow.t: North German duchy that briefly passed to Wallenstein during the Thirty Years' War, ruled from a fine Renaissance palace at Güstrow.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-gustrow.o: [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] had already been divided before, but the partition of 1621 between the brothers Adolf Frederick I and John Albert II created a lasting Mecklenburg-Güstrow in the east of the country, with [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg-Schwerin]] in the west. [[s:lordship-of-rostock|Rostock]] and the estates remained shared between the two duchies.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-gustrow.r: Both dukes were deposed in 1628 by Emperor Ferdinand II, who gave [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] to his general Albrecht von Wallenstein; Wallenstein governed from Güstrow until Swedish troops restored the dukes in 1631. Government was weakened by powerful noble estates, and the countryside suffered heavily from war and depopulation. The duchy was Lutheran.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-gustrow.e: Gustav Adolph, the last duke, died without male heirs in 1695. A long succession dispute followed until the Treaty of [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]] in 1701 divided [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] into the [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg-schwerin|Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin]] and the [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg-strelitz|Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz]].

duchy-of-prussia.t: The first officially Lutheran state, created in 1525 when the Teutonic Order's grand master turned duke and vassal of Poland.
duchy-of-prussia.o: After defeats by [[e:poland|Poland]], the [[s:state-of-the-teutonic-order|State of the Teutonic Order]] was reduced to East [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]]. In 1525 Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach, advised by Luther, secularised the order's state and, by the Treaty of Kraków, did homage to his uncle King Sigismund I of Poland as hereditary Duke of Prussia.
duchy-of-prussia.r: [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] was the first state to adopt [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] officially. Albert founded the University of Königsberg in 1544 and supported [[e:printing-press|printing]] in German, Polish and Lithuanian. The estates were strong, and the land exported grain through Königsberg. After Duke Albert Frederick fell mentally ill, the [[e:prince-elector|electors]] of [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] ruled as regents and in 1618 inherited the duchy, creating Brandenburg-Prussia.
duchy-of-prussia.e: Elector Frederick William, the Great Elector, won full [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] from [[e:poland|Poland]] by the Treaty of Wehlau in 1657. Because [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] lay outside the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]], his son Frederick crowned himself King in Prussia at Königsberg in 1701, founding the [[s:kingdom-of-prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]].

duchy-of-krnov.t: A Silesian duchy, known in German as Jägerndorf, held successively by Přemyslids, Hohenzollerns and the princes of Liechtenstein.
duchy-of-krnov.o: Krnov (Jägerndorf) emerged from the Přemyslid lands of the [[s:duchy-of-opava|Duchy of Opava]]. After Duke [[e:nicholas-ii|Nicholas II]] died in 1365 his sons divided his possessions, and by 1377 John I held Krnov together with Racibórz as his own duchy, a fief of the [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Kingdom of Bohemia]].
duchy-of-krnov.r: After several changes of ruler, Krnov was bought in 1523 by Margrave George of Brandenburg-Ansbach, who introduced [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] and rebuilt the castle. His Hohenzollern heirs held it until 1621, when Johann Georg lost it for supporting the Bohemian revolt. Emperor Ferdinand II then granted it to Karl of [[s:principality-of-liechtenstein|Liechtenstein]], whose family kept the ducal title thereafter.
duchy-of-krnov.e: [[e:frederick-ii|Frederick II]] of [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] cited the Hohenzollern claim to Krnov when he invaded [[s:duchy-of-silesia|Silesia]], and in 1742 Prussia annexed the northern part, while the town stayed in [[s:duchy-of-upper-and-lower-silesia|Austrian Silesia]]. The Liechtensteins kept the title until 1918, when Krnov became part of [[s:czechoslovakia|Czechoslovakia]].

duchy-of-carinthia.t: The oldest duchy of the Austrian lands, heir to Slavic Carantania, which kept its unique installation rite at the Prince's Stone until 1414.
duchy-of-carinthia.o: In 976 Emperor Otto II separated Carinthia from the [[s:duchy-of-bavaria|Duchy of Bavaria]] to weaken the rebellious Duke Henry the Quarrelsome, creating the first new duchy of the Empire. It included [[s:carantania|Carantania]] and huge marches extending to [[s:commune-of-verona|Verona]], Styria and Carniola, many of which later became separate.
duchy-of-carinthia.r: Dukes were installed at the Prince's Stone near Karnburg and the Duke's Chair on the Zollfeld, in a ceremony partly in Slovene. Ruling families included the Eppensteiners and the Sponheimers. The population was mixed German and Slovene. Mining of lead and iron, and the rebuilding of Klagenfurt as capital by the Carinthian estates, to whom Maximilian I gave the town in 1518, shaped later centuries.
duchy-of-carinthia.e: In 1335 the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] inherited Carinthia, which stayed in their hands as a crown land until 1918. The plebiscite of 1920 kept southern Carinthia in [[e:austria|Austria]], though some areas went to [[e:yugoslavia|Yugoslavia]] and [[e:italy|Italy]]. It is today an Austrian federal state.

duchy-of-glogow.t: Silesian Piast duchy on the Oder whose dukes claimed Greater Poland, later a Bohemian fief held briefly by the future King Sigismund I of Poland.
duchy-of-glogow.o: Konrad I, a son of Henry II the Pious, received Głogów and the lands around it in a division of the Silesian inheritance around 1251. Głogów, a fortified town on the Oder, became the capital of a duchy covering much of northern [[s:duchy-of-silesia|Silesia]].
duchy-of-glogow.r: Konrad's son Henry III of Głogów was one of the most powerful Silesian princes, holding [[s:duchy-of-greater-poland|Greater Poland]] for a time and claiming the [[e:kingdom-of-poland|Polish crown]]. After him the duchy was divided among branches, including Żagań and Oleśnica. Half of Głogów passed directly to the Bohemian crown in 1331, and the remaining dukes became [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Kingdom of Bohemia]]. German settlement and town law transformed the region.
duchy-of-glogow.e: After the Piast lines died out and disputes followed, Głogów was granted to the Jagiellonian Sigismund, who ruled it from 1499 until 1506 before becoming King of [[e:poland|Poland]]. It then returned to the Bohemian crown, passed to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1742, and to Poland in 1945.

duchy-of-saint-sava.t: Domain of the Kosača family whose ruler's title, herceg, gave the region of Herzegovina its name.
duchy-of-saint-sava.o: Stjepan Vukčić Kosača inherited the lands of Hum and the coast from his uncle Sandalj Hranić in 1435, becoming the mightiest noble of the [[s:kingdom-of-bosnia|Kingdom of Bosnia]]. In 1448 he styled himself Herceg of Saint Sava, after the relics of the Serbian saint kept at the monastery of Mileševa in his territory, asserting independence from the Bosnian king.
duchy-of-saint-sava.r: From his castle at Blagaj near Mostar, Stjepan controlled the [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] between the Adriatic and the interior, levying customs on trade with [[s:republic-of-ragusa|Ragusa]] and developing the port of Novi, today Herceg Novi. His lands mixed adherents of the Bosnian Church, [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] and Catholic Christians, and he quarrelled with Ragusa, [[e:venice|Venice]] and his own son Vladislav.
duchy-of-saint-sava.e: The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] conquered Bosnia in 1463 and most of Stjepan's lands by 1465; he died in 1466. His son Vlatko held a shrinking coastal remnant until Herceg Novi fell in 1482. Another son converted and became the Ottoman grand [[e:vizier|vizier]] Hersekzade Ahmed Pasha.

duchy-of-the-franks.t: The great Robertian principality between the Seine and the Loire whose dukes overshadowed the last Carolingian kings and became the Capetian dynasty.
duchy-of-the-franks.o: The Robertian family had led the defence of [[s:neustria|Neustria]] against the [[e:vikings|Vikings]] since Robert the Strong in the 860s, and two of its members, Odo and Robert I, had briefly been kings. In 936 Hugh the Great helped restore the Carolingian Louis IV and was recognised as 'duke of the [[e:frankish-kingdom|Franks]]', second only to the king.
duchy-of-the-franks.r: Hugh the Great held counties and lay abbacies around [[e:paris|Paris]], Orléans and Tours, including Saint-Martin of Tours and Saint-Denis, giving him more land and men than the king. He controlled royal successions and dealt as an equal with the dukes of [[s:duchy-of-normandy|Normandy]] and [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]]. His son Hugh Capet inherited the title in 956.
duchy-of-the-franks.e: When the last Carolingian king, Louis V, died in 987, the [[e:magnates|magnates]] elected Hugh Capet king. The duchy's lands became the royal domain of the new Capetian [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]], which his descendants ruled for eight centuries.

duchy-of-sabbioneta.t: The small Lombard duchy of Vespasiano Gonzaga, who built Sabbioneta from scratch as an ideal Renaissance city.
duchy-of-sabbioneta.o: Vespasiano Gonzaga, a soldier and courtier of [[e:philip-ii-of-spain|Philip II of Spain]] from a cadet branch of the Gonzaga, inherited Sabbioneta and the surrounding lands between [[s:duchy-of-mantua|Mantua]] and [[s:duchy-of-parma-and-piacenza|Parma]]. From the 1550s he rebuilt the village as a fortified ideal city, and Emperor Rudolf II made it a duchy in 1577.
duchy-of-sabbioneta.r: Sabbioneta was laid out on a regular plan with star-shaped walls, a ducal palace, a long gallery for Vespasiano's art and antiquities, and the Teatro all'Antica by Vincenzo Scamozzi, completed around 1590, one of the first purpose-built [[e:theatre|theatres]] in modern [[e:europe|Europe]]. The duke ran a small, tightly controlled court and drew craftsmen and Jewish printers to the town.
duchy-of-sabbioneta.e: Vespasiano died in 1591 without a surviving son, and the duchy passed through his daughter to the Carafa and then other heirs, losing its importance. It later passed to the Gonzaga of [[s:duchy-of-guastalla|Guastalla]] and was eventually absorbed into Austrian-ruled [[e:lombardy|Lombardy]] in the 18th century.

democratic-kampuchea.t: The Khmer Rouge state of Pol Pot, whose radical communist experiment killed some 1.5 to 2 million Cambodians between 1975 and 1979.
democratic-kampuchea.o: The Communist Party of [[s:kingdom-of-cambodia|Kampuchea]], known as the [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] Rouge, grew from a small insurgency in the 1960s to a large army during the civil war against the [[s:khmer-republic|Khmer Republic]]. It captured Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975 and proclaimed Democratic Kampuchea, with Sihanouk briefly as nominal head of state until 1976.
democratic-kampuchea.r: The regime, led by Pol Pot, emptied the cities, abolished money, markets, schools and religion, and forced the population into agricultural communes. Former officials, intellectuals, ethnic minorities such as the [[e:cham|Cham]] and Vietnamese, and party members accused of treachery were executed, many after torture at the Tuol Sleng prison. Starvation, overwork and disease caused most of the deaths.
democratic-kampuchea.e: Border attacks on [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]] provoked a Vietnamese invasion in December 1978, and Phnom Penh fell on 7 January 1979, when the [[s:peoples-republic-of-kampuchea|People's Republic of Kampuchea]] was established. The [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] Rouge fought on from the Thai border into the 1990s, and a UN-backed tribunal later convicted surviving leaders of [[e:genocide|genocide]].

da-changhe.t: The short-lived dynasty of the Zheng family that replaced Nanzhao in Yunnan in 902 and opened a period of rapid dynastic change around Lake Erhai.
da-changhe.o: [[s:zheng-wang-shichong|Zheng]] Maisi, a powerful minister descended from a [[s:later-tang|Tang]] official captured by [[s:nanzhao|Nanzhao]], killed the Meng royal family in 902 and proclaimed the kingdom of Da Changhe, keeping the capital at Yangjumie near modern Dali.
da-changhe.r: Little is known of its government, which seems to have continued [[s:nanzhao|Nanzhao]] institutions; sources are sparse. Three [[s:zheng-wang-shichong|Zheng]] rulers reigned, and the court was weakened by rivalry among the great families of the Erhai region.
da-changhe.e: In 928 the official Yang Ganzhen had [[s:zheng-wang-shichong|Zheng]] Longdan, the last ruler, killed and placed Zhao Shanzheng on the throne as ruler of [[s:da-tianxing|Da Tianxing]]. Within a decade the Duan family founded the more durable [[s:dali-kingdom|Dali Kingdom]].

dharampur-state.t: A Sisodia Rajput state in the hills of southern Gujarat, whose 20th-century ruler was a noted patron and scholar of Indian music.
dharampur-state.o: The ruling family claimed descent from the Sisodias of [[s:udaipur-state|Mewar]], and tradition dates their arrival in the hills inland from Valsad to 1262. The capital was moved to the new town of Dharampur in the 18th century.
dharampur-state.r: Dharampur was a largely forested state with many Kokna and Warli people. It paid [[e:chauth|chauth]] to the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]] and later came under British supervision through the [[e:surat|Surat]] Agency. Maharana Vijayadevji, who ruled in the first half of the 20th century, wrote on music and supported musicians.
dharampur-state.e: Dharampur merged into Bombay State in 1948 and is now in Valsad district, [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

danish-gold-coast.t: Denmark's forts on the coast of modern Ghana, centred on Christiansborg at Osu, a hub of the Danish slave trade until the colony was sold in 1850.
danish-gold-coast.o: Danish traders, led by Hendrik Carloff, arrived on the [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast]] in 1658 and seized the Swedish forts. [[e:denmark|Denmark]] built Fort Frederiksborg near Cape Coast and in 1661 bought the site of Christiansborg at Osu, near modern Accra, from the king of Accra.
danish-gold-coast.r: The Danish West [[e:india|India]] and [[e:guinea|Guinea]] Company and later the crown ran a string of forts east of Accra, exchanging textiles, guns and alcohol for gold and enslaved Africans, who were shipped to the [[s:danish-west-indies|Danish West Indies]]. In 1792 [[e:denmark|Denmark]] became the first European state to ban the transatlantic [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]], effective from 1803, after which the Danes tried plantation farming inland.
danish-gold-coast.e: Unprofitable after the end of the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]], the forts were sold to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 1850 and joined the [[s:gold-coast-colony|British Gold Coast]] colony. Christiansborg, also known as Osu Castle, later served as the seat of [[e:ghana|Ghana's]] government.
danish-gold-coast.re: Lutheran Christianity, Akan and Ga religion

dhar-state.t: A Maratha Puar state in Malwa centred on Dhar, the old Paramara capital of King Bhoja.
dhar-state.o: Udaji Rao and Anand Rao Puar were [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] commanders active in the conquest of [[e:malwa|Malwa]]. Around 1728–32 the [[e:peshwa|Peshwa]] [[e:baji-rao-i|Baji Rao I]] confirmed Anand Rao in Dhar, a city with a long royal past as the 11th-century capital of the Paramara king Bhoja. The Puars of Dhar were related to the Puars of [[s:dewas-senior|Dewas Senior]] and [[s:dewas-junior|Dewas Junior]].
dhar-state.r: Dhar was badly weakened by the wars of Scindia and Holkar around 1800 and recovered under British protection after the treaty of 1819. Its ruler was briefly deprived of the state after the revolt of 1857, which was restored in 1860 minus the Bairasia district. A Maharaja governed a mainly [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] population; the Bhoj Shala and the Dhar fort are its main monuments.
dhar-state.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]], Dhar merged into [[s:madhya-bharat|Madhya Bharat]] in 1948 and became part of Madhya Pradesh in 1956.

derg.t: The military committee that overthrew Haile Selassie in 1974 and ruled Ethiopia as a Marxist-Leninist dictatorship under Mengistu Haile Mariam.
derg.o: Amid famine, [[e:inflation|inflation]] and protest, a committee (derg) of junior officers formed in mid-1974 and gradually stripped Emperor [[e:haile-selassie|Haile Selassie]] of power, deposing him on 12 September 1974 and ending the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]]. In November it executed some 60 former officials. Leadership passed from Aman Andom and Tafari Benti to [[e:mengistu-haile-mariam|Mengistu Haile Mariam]] by 1977.
derg.r: The Derg nationalised all rural and urban land in 1975, abolished the monarchy and allied with the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]]. The Red Terror of 1977 to 1978 killed tens of thousands of suspected opponents. With Soviet and Cuban help it repelled [[e:somalia|Somalia's]] invasion of the [[e:ogaden|Ogaden]] in 1978, but fought long wars against Eritrean and Tigrayan rebels. The famine of 1983 to 1985 killed hundreds of thousands.
derg.e: In 1984 the Workers' Party of [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Ethiopia]] was founded, and a new constitution in 1987 turned the military government into the civilian-styled [[s:peoples-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia]], with Mengistu as president.

duchy-of-racha.t: A highland duchy in the upper Rioni valley of western Georgia whose hereditary dukes, or eristavis, held power for over seven centuries.
duchy-of-racha.o: Racha, the mountain basin of the upper Rioni, became a saeristavo, or duchy, of the united [[s:kingdom-of-georgia|Kingdom of Georgia]] in the 11th century. Its hereditary eristavis governed on behalf of the crown and guarded the passes to the North [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]], while the church of Nikortsminda, built under Bagrat III, marked royal interest in the region.
duchy-of-racha.r: The dukes ruled from Oni and mountain castles over villages of farmers, herders and vineyard owners. Under the Kakhaberidze family in the 12th and 13th centuries Racha was rich and influential at the royal court. After [[s:georgia|Georgia]] split in 1490, Racha became a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-imereti|Kingdom of Imereti]] under the Chkheidze family, whose dukes often rebelled.
duchy-of-racha.e: Repeated rebellions and intervention in Imereti's civil wars brought the dukes into conflict with their kings. The duchy was abolished in 1789 and incorporated directly into the [[s:kingdom-of-imereti|Kingdom of Imereti]], which [[e:russia|Russia]] annexed in 1810.

dutch-malabar.t: The Dutch East India Company's commandment on the Malabar Coast, centred on Fort Cochin and its pepper trade.
dutch-malabar.o: Seeking to break the Portuguese hold on [[e:pepper|pepper]], the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] ([[e:dutch-east-india-company|VOC]]) allied with the [[s:kingdom-of-calicut|Zamorins of Calicut]] and took Quilon in 1661 and Cochin in 1663 from [[s:portuguese-india|Portuguese India]]. The Malabar posts were organised as a commandment governed from Fort [[s:kingdom-of-cochin|Kochi]], with factories at Cannanore, Cranganore and Quilon.
dutch-malabar.r: The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] made treaties with the Raja of Cochin, making him effectively a dependent ally, and bought [[e:pepper|pepper]] under monopoly contracts. The commander Hendrik van Rheede sponsored the Hortus Malabaricus, a pioneering twelve-volume study of the plants of Malabar. Dutch power was checked when Marthanda Varma of [[s:travancore|Travancore]] defeated them at Colachel in 1741.
dutch-malabar.e: After Colachel the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] lost influence, selling Cannanore to the [[s:arakkal-kingdom|Arakkal kingdom]] and later posts to [[s:travancore|Travancore]]. British forces occupied Cochin in 1795 during the [[e:french-revolutionary-wars|French Revolutionary Wars]], and the territory was formally ceded in 1814.

duchy-of-mecklenburg-stargard.t: A junior Mecklenburg duchy around Neubrandenburg and Stargard that lasted just over a century before reuniting with the main line.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-stargard.o: In 1352 the brothers Albert II and John I, raised to dukes of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] in 1348, divided their lands. John received the Lordship of Stargard in the east, with Neubrandenburg and Strelitz, which Mecklenburg had acquired from [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] in the 13th century.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-stargard.r: The duchy was an agrarian land of [[e:knighthood|knightly]] estates and small towns such as Neubrandenburg, with its brick Gothic gates, Friedland and Woldegk. Its dukes remained junior partners of their cousins in the [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg|Duchy of Mecklenburg]] and joined in their wars with [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] and [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]]. Few details of its administration survive.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-stargard.e: When Duke Ulrich II died without sons in 1471, Stargard reverted to the main [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] line. The region re-emerged in 1701 as the core of the [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg-strelitz|Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz]].

duchy-of-croatia.t: Early medieval Croatian duchy on the Dalmatian coast, ruled by the Trpimirović line, which became the Kingdom of Croatia under Tomislav.
duchy-of-croatia.o: [[e:croats|Croats]] settled the Dalmatian hinterland in the 7th century. Around 800 a duchy emerged under Frankish overlordship, confirmed by the Peace of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-aachen|Aachen]] of 812 between the [[s:franks|Franks]] and [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]]. Duke Borna is the first well-attested ruler.
duchy-of-croatia.r: Dukes ruled from seats at Nin, Klis and Bijaći, with a Latin-influenced Christian elite and Byzantine Dalmatian towns such as Zadar and Split nearby. Trpimir I issued a charter in 852 calling himself duke of the [[e:croats|Croats]]. In 879 Branimir won papal recognition, and Croatia turned firmly to [[e:rome|Rome]]. Stone churches with interlace decoration and [[e:latin|Latin]] inscriptions survive.
duchy-of-croatia.e: Around 925 Tomislav united it with the [[s:duchy-of-pannonian-croatia|Duchy of Pannonian Croatia]] and is recognised as the first king, creating the [[s:kingdom-of-croatia-925-1102|Kingdom of Croatia]] (925-1102).

despotate-of-dobruja.t: Bulgarian principality on the Black Sea coast ruled from Kaliakra, a naval power that fought Byzantium and Genoa before falling to the Ottomans.
despotate-of-dobruja.o: In the breakup of the [[s:second-bulgarian-empire|Second Bulgarian Empire]]'s authority, a local realm emerged in the coastal region of Karvuna, later called Dobruja. Its first known ruler, Balik, appears in 1346 sending troops to aid the Byzantine empress Anna of [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]] in the civil war.
despotate-of-dobruja.r: Balik's brother Dobrotitsa (c. 1347–1386), styled despot by [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], ruled from Kaliakra and [[s:odessos|Varna]]. He built a fleet that fought Genoese traders and backed claimants to the [[s:empire-of-trebizond|Empire of Trebizond]]. The despotate controlled [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] ports and the grain trade, and remained [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] and broadly Bulgarian, while also dealing with the [[s:tsardom-of-vidin|Tsardom of Vidin]] and [[s:principality-of-wallachia|Wallachia]].
despotate-of-dobruja.e: Dobrotitsa's son Ivanko made peace with the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] and [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]], but the Ottomans conquered the despotate around 1388. Mircea the Elder of [[s:principality-of-wallachia|Wallachia]] held part of Dobruja briefly before it passed fully to the Ottomans.

duchy-of-zator.t: A tiny Silesian Piast duchy on the upper Vistula, sold to the Polish king in 1494.
duchy-of-zator.o: Zator, east of Oswiecim, was created in 1445 when the [[s:duchy-of-oswiecim|Duchy of Oswiecim]] was divided among the sons of Duke Casimir I, and Wenceslaus I took the Zator lands. Like Oswiecim, it was formally a fief of the [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Kingdom of Bohemia]].
duchy-of-zator.r: The duchy was a small agricultural land in the Vistula valley, known for its fish ponds, where the breeding of carp later became a local speciality. Its dukes were minor Piasts with limited resources, and the duchy was further divided among Wenceslaus's sons.
duchy-of-zator.e: In 1494 Duke Jan V sold Zator to King John I Albert of [[e:poland|Poland]]. It was incorporated, together with Oswiecim, into the [[s:kingdom-of-poland-1385-1569|Kingdom of Poland]] (1385-1569) in 1564.

dhrangadhra-state.t: The senior Jhala Rajput state of Kathiawar, which moved its capital from Halvad to Dhrangadhra in the 18th century.
dhrangadhra-state.o: The Jhala [[e:rajputs|Rajputs]] had ruled in the Jhalawad region of northern Saurashtra since medieval times, with their seat at Halvad. Around 1742 the ruler moved the capital to Dhrangadhra, giving the state its later name; [[s:wankaner-state|Wankaner]], [[s:limbdi-state|Limbdi]] and [[s:wadhwan-state|Wadhwan]] were branches of the same clan.
dhrangadhra-state.r: Dhrangadhra was a 13-gun salute state of the Kathiawar Agency ruled by a [[e:british-raj|Raj]] Saheb. Its economy relied on [[e:cotton|cotton]], salt from the Little Rann and the local sandstone, still sold as Dhrangadhra stone. The rulers were reformers in education and administration in the early 20th century.
dhrangadhra-state.e: Mayurdhwajsinhji Meghrajji III acceded to [[e:india|India]] and Dhrangadhra was merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948. He later sat in the Indian parliament; the town is in Surendranagar district of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

durotriges.t: Dorset confederation of hillfort dwellers whose resistance ended when Vespasian's legion stormed strongholds such as Maiden Castle and Hod Hill.
durotriges.o: The Durotriges took shape in the late Iron Age across Dorset and neighbouring parts of Somerset, Wiltshire and Hampshire, a landscape dominated by great multivallate hillforts. Their harbour at Hengistbury Head traded with Armorica in the 1st century BCE, bringing in Italian wine [[e:amphora|amphorae]] and Gaulish pottery in exchange for metals, grain and [[e:cattle|cattle]].
durotriges.r: Power seems to have been spread among several centres rather than held by one king, and no ruler's name appears on their coins, which became crude cast and debased [[e:silver|silver]] issues. Hillforts such as Maiden Castle were heavily refortified and stocked with [[e:sling|sling]] stones. The Durotriges buried their dead in crouched inhumations, unlike the cremation rites of the south-east, and Kimmeridge shale was worked into bracelets.
durotriges.e: In 43 and 44 the future emperor Vespasian, leading the legio II Augusta, took more than twenty strongholds in the south-west according to Suetonius; a Roman fort was built inside Hod Hill. The territory became the civitas of the Durotriges with its centre at Durnovaria, modern Dorchester, within [[s:roman-britain|Roman Britain]].

duchy-of-jawor.t: Lower Silesian Piast duchy at the foot of the Sudetes, later joined with Świdnica, which kept its independence from Bohemia longer than any other.
duchy-of-jawor.o: In 1274 the [[s:duchy-of-legnica|Duchy of Legnica]] was divided among the sons of Bolesław II the Bald, and Bolko I the Strict received Jawor with its lands. He soon added Świdnica and built a strong duchy on the Bohemian border, protected by castles such as Bolków and Grodziec.
duchy-of-jawor.r: Bolko I founded Krzeszów Abbey and fortified the mountain passes. After his death the lands were divided, with Henry I ruling Jawor until 1346. They were then reunited under Bolko II the Small, who resisted Bohemian overlordship, ruling as an independent Piast prince while other Silesian dukes became Bohemian [[e:vassal|vassals]]. German settlers and town law shaped the economy of farming and cloth.
duchy-of-jawor.e: Bolko II married his niece Anne to [[e:charles-iv|Charles IV]], so on the death of his widow Agnes in 1392 the duchy passed to the Bohemian crown. Jawor later passed to the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] and [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], and has been Polish since 1945; its Lutheran Peace Church is a World Heritage Site.

duchy-of-athens.t: Crusader state of Athens and Thebes ruled in turn by Burgundian, Catalan and Florentine lords for two and a half centuries.
duchy-of-athens.o: In 1205 Boniface of Montferrat granted [[s:athens|Athens]] and [[s:thebes|Thebes]] to the Burgundian knight Otho de la Roche, who took the title Lord of [[e:athens|Athens]]. His nephew Guy I was styled Duke of Athens by the mid-13th century. The duchy covered Attica, Boeotia and parts of Locris, and was nominally subject to the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]].
duchy-of-athens.r: Under the de la Roche family the duchy prospered, with its court at [[s:thebes|Thebes]], a [[e:silk|silk]] industry and a [[e:latin|Latin]] church that turned the Parthenon into a Catholic cathedral of Our Lady. Greek peasants remained [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]]. In 1311 the Catalan Company killed Duke Walter of Brienne at Halmyros and ruled the duchy for the [[s:crown-of-aragon|Crown of Aragon]] and [[e:sicily|Sicily]].
duchy-of-athens.e: Nerio I Acciaioli, a Florentine banker's son, took [[s:athens|Athens]] in 1388 and founded a new ducal line. The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]], who already exacted tribute, captured [[e:athens|Athens]] in 1456 and the Acropolis in 1458, annexing the duchy.
duchy-of-athens.la: Old French, Catalan, Italian, Medieval Greek

dal-riata.t: A Gaelic kingdom spanning north-east Ireland and Argyll whose kings, settling Scotland's west coast, helped make Gaelic the language of medieval Scotland.
dal-riata.o: Dal Riata originated in County Antrim, and by about 500 its rulers held lands across the North Channel in Argyll. Tradition credits Fergus Mor mac Eirc with moving the dynasty to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], though the story was shaped by later writers. The Scottish part grew into a federation of kindreds centred on the hillfort of Dunadd.
dal-riata.r: Power was shared among kindreds such as [[s:cenel-ngabrain|Cenel nGabrain]], [[s:cenel-loairn|Cenel Loairn]] and Cenel nOengusa, recorded in the Senchus fer nAlban, a [[e:census|census]] of houses and naval levies. Columba's monastery on Iona, founded in 563 with royal favour, made the kingdom a centre of Irish [[e:christianity|Christianity]], scholarship and missionary work reaching [[s:kingdom-of-northumbria|Northumbria]].
dal-riata.e: Defeat at Mag Rath in 637 weakened its hold on its Irish lands. In the 8th century it fell under the Picts, and [[e:vikings|Viking]] raids from the 790s shattered its sea power. By the mid 9th century its territory and Gaelic culture merged with [[s:kingdom-of-the-picts|Pictland]] into the kingdom later known as Alba, the [[s:kingdom-of-scotland|Kingdom of Scotland]].

duchy-of-florence.t: The first Medici duchy, created by Charles V in 1532, under which Cosimo I conquered Siena and turned Florence into a princely state.
duchy-of-florence.o: After the siege of 1529–1530 ended the last [[s:republic-of-florence|Republic of Florence]], Emperor [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]] made Alessandro de' Medici hereditary duke in 1532. Alessandro ruled with the support of imperial troops and built the Fortezza da Basso to control the city.
duchy-of-florence.r: Alessandro was murdered by his cousin Lorenzino in 1537, and the 17-year-old Cosimo I de' Medici was chosen to succeed him. Cosimo crushed the republican exiles at Montemurlo that year and built an efficient absolutist state. He founded the Uffizi offices, designed by Giorgio Vasari from 1560, created a navy and the Order of Saint Stephen, and conquered the [[s:republic-of-siena|Republic of Siena]] in 1555.
duchy-of-florence.e: In 1569 [[e:papacy|Pope]] Pius V raised Cosimo to Grand Duke of [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]], and the duchy became the Grand Duchy of Tuscany.

duchy-of-pomerania.t: A Baltic duchy ruled by the native Griffin dynasty for five centuries, from its Christianisation in the 1120s to its partition after the Thirty Years' War.
duchy-of-pomerania.o: Wartislaw I united Slavic tribes around the lower Oder and Szczecin in the early 12th century under Polish overlordship. In 1124 and 1128 [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Otto of Bamberg converted the Pomeranians to [[e:christianity|Christianity]]. In 1181 Bogislaw I became a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]], making [[e:pomerania|Pomerania]] part of the Empire.
duchy-of-pomerania.r: The Griffin dukes encouraged German settlement and founded towns, many of which joined the [[s:hanseatic-league|Hanseatic League]], including Stralsund, Greifswald and Szczecin. The duchy was frequently divided into Pomerania-Wolgast and Pomerania-Stettin. Bogislaw X reunited it in 1478, and Johannes Bugenhagen introduced the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] in 1534. [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] long claimed overlordship.
duchy-of-pomerania.e: The last duke, Bogislaw XIV, died in 1637 during the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]], with [[e:sweden|Sweden]] occupying the land. The [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 split the duchy: Sweden took western [[e:pomerania|Pomerania]] and [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] the east. Most of the region became Polish in 1945.

dhrol-state.t: A Jadeja Rajput state of Kathiawar founded by a kinsman of the Jams of Nawanagar, one of the salute states of the peninsula.
dhrol-state.o: Dhrol was founded in 1595 by Hardholji, a brother of Jam Sataji of Nawanagar, who took the town and its surrounding villages from earlier holders. It belonged to the wider family of Jadeja states that spread from [[s:cutch-state|Kutch]] into northern Kathiawar.
dhrol-state.r: The Thakor Sahib ruled a compact territory of [[e:cotton|cotton]] and grain villages in the [[s:nawanagar-state|Halar]] region. Like other Kathiawar states it paid tribute to the Mughal governors of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] and later to the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads]] of [[s:baroda-state|Baroda]], before coming under British protection after the settlement of 1807. It was a nine-gun salute state.
dhrol-state.e: Dhrol merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948, which became part of Bombay State in 1956 and of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960. The town now lies in [[s:nawanagar-state|Jamnagar]] district.

duchy-of-savoy.t: The Alpine duchy of the house of Savoy that straddled France and Italy and grew into the Kingdom of Sardinia, the core of united Italy.
duchy-of-savoy.o: In 1416 Emperor Sigismund raised Count Amadeus VIII of the [[s:county-of-savoy|County of Savoy]] to the rank of duke. Amadeus later retired and was elected antipope Felix V in 1439. The duchy then included Savoy, Piedmont, Nice, Bresse and the Vaud.
duchy-of-savoy.r: The dukes ruled an Alpine state of pass tolls, farming and soldiers. French occupation from 1536 ended when Emmanuel Philibert recovered his lands at Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559 and moved the capital from Chambéry to Turin in 1563. [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]] lost [[s:republic-of-geneva|Geneva]] and the Vaud but built a centralised military state. Victor Amadeus II gained [[e:sicily|Sicily]] in 1713, exchanged for [[e:sardinia|Sardinia]] in 1720.
duchy-of-savoy.e: From 1720 the dukes were kings of [[e:sardinia|Sardinia]]. [[e:france|France]] annexed [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]] in 1792–1815. In 1847 the 'perfect fusion' merged the mainland states with Sardinia, ending the duchy as a separate state; Savoy itself passed to France in 1860.

demetae.t: People of south-west Wales whose name survives in Dyfed, and who accepted Roman rule with little recorded fighting.
demetae.o: The Demetae lived in what is now Pembrokeshire and western Carmarthenshire, a region of small defended farmsteads, known as raths, and coastal promontory forts. Ptolemy recorded them in the 2nd century, but no earlier writer describes them, and they were probably a grouping of local communities with long roots in the Iron Age.
demetae.r: Unlike their neighbours the [[s:silures|Silures]] and [[s:ordovices|Ordovices]], the Demetae are not recorded as resisting [[e:rome|Rome]], and their territory needed few garrisons. Farming and [[e:cattle|cattle]]-rearing sustained a dispersed population, and the region looked west across the Irish Sea. The [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] mined gold at Dolaucothi on the eastern edge of their land.
demetae.e: After the conquest of Wales in the 70s the Demetae formed a civitas centred on Moridunum, modern Carmarthen, one of the westernmost towns of [[s:roman-britain|Roman Britain]]. The name passed to the post-[[s:roman-kingdom|Roman Kingdom]] of [[s:kingdom-of-dyfed|Dyfed]], ruled by a dynasty of Irish descent, and survives in the modern county of Dyfed.

darkoti-state.t: One of the tiniest princely states in India, a Rajput chiefship of a few villages in the Shimla hills.
darkoti-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500, but little is reliably known of its origins.
darkoti-state.r: Darkoti covered only a handful of villages east of Shimla and had a very small population and revenue. It was restored under British protection after the Anglo-Nepalese War as one of the Simla Hill States. Its history is poorly recorded.
darkoti-state.e: Darkoti merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now part of Shimla district.

danish-kingdom-of-east-anglia.t: The Viking kingdom founded by Guthrum in East Anglia after his defeat by Alfred, the first Danish state in England to accept Christianity.
danish-kingdom-of-east-anglia.o: After Alfred defeated Guthrum at Edington in 878, the Danish leader accepted baptism with the name Aethelstan. In 879 his army settled [[s:kingdom-of-east-anglia|East Anglia]], the former Kingdom of East Anglia, and a treaty with Alfred around 886 fixed the boundary along the Lea, the Ouse and Watling Street.
danish-kingdom-of-east-anglia.r: Guthrum ruled as a Christian king and minted coins under his baptismal name. Danish settlers took land across Norfolk and Suffolk, and soon after his death coins honouring the martyred King Edmund were issued, showing rapid integration. Later rulers, such as Eohric, are poorly documented.
danish-kingdom-of-east-anglia.e: The kingdom joined attacks on English territory, but Edward the Elder conquered it in 917 to 918, and the East Anglian Danes submitted. It became part of the [[s:kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons|Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons]] and later an earldom of [[e:england|England]].

dutch-formosa.t: The Dutch East India Company's colony in south-western Taiwan, which brought the first large-scale Chinese settlement to the island before Koxinga expelled it in 1662.
dutch-formosa.o: Seeking a base for the [[e:china|China]] trade, the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] failed to take [[e:macau|Macau]] in 1622 and occupied the Penghu islands, but a Ming fleet forced them out in 1624. By agreement they moved to Tayouan on the coast of [[s:republic-of-china|Taiwan]], where they built Fort Zeelandia, within the sphere of [[e:dutch-east-india-company|Dutch East India Company]] territories in [[e:asia|Asia]].
dutch-formosa.r: The Company ruled through a governor and council, subdued indigenous villages by force and treaty, and expelled the Spanish from the north in 1642. It recruited Chinese settlers to grow [[e:rice|rice]] and [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], taxing them heavily, and exported deer skins to [[e:japan|Japan]]. Reformed missionaries such as Georgius Candidius wrote the Siraya language in [[e:latin|Latin]] letters. Chinese discontent erupted in the Guo Huaiyi revolt of 1652.
dutch-formosa.e: In 1661 the Ming loyalist [[e:koxinga|Koxinga]] landed with a large fleet and besieged Fort Zeelandia for nine months. Governor Frederick Coyett surrendered in February 1662, and the colony became the [[s:kingdom-of-tungning|Kingdom of Tungning]].
dutch-formosa.re: Indigenous religions, Chinese folk religion, Reformed Christianity

duala-kingdoms.t: Trading chiefdoms of the Duala people on the Wouri estuary, whose kings Bell and Akwa controlled commerce with Europeans and signed the treaty that created German Kamerun.
duala-kingdoms.o: The Duala settled on the Wouri estuary, probably in the 17th century, and by the late 1600s were dealing with European ships that called at the river. Their settlements grew into rival lineage chiefdoms, chief among them Bell (Bonanjo) and Akwa, with Deido and Bonaberi as smaller units. Leaders styled themselves kings in dealings with European traders.
duala-kingdoms.r: Power rested on middleman trade: the Duala bought slaves, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and later [[e:palm-oil|palm oil]] and palm kernels from inland peoples and sold them to British, [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and German merchants, refusing outsiders direct access to the interior. Kings ruled with lineage heads and the ngondo assembly. British missionaries, notably Alfred Saker from 1845, introduced Baptist [[e:christianity|Christianity]] and a written Duala language.
duala-kingdoms.e: On 12 July 1884 King Bell and King Akwa signed a treaty with German agents, and the estuary became the core of [[s:kamerun|Kamerun]]. Douala grew into [[e:cameroon|Cameroon's]] main port, and Bell and Akwa families remained prominent; Rudolf Duala Manga Bell was executed by the Germans in 1914.

dynasty-of-e.t: The mixed series of Babylonian kings who ruled from about 979 to 732 BCE, through Aramean upheaval and growing Assyrian domination.
dynasty-of-e.o: The Dynasty of E is the conventional name for the kings who followed the Elamite ruler Mar-biti-apla-usur on the throne of [[e:babylon|Babylon]] from around 979 BCE; the king lists use an abbreviation of uncertain meaning. They were not a single family. The first, Nabu-mukin-apli, ruled at a time when Arameans cut Babylon off and the New Year festival could not be held.
dynasty-of-e.r: Nabu-apla-iddina restored the cult of Shamash at [[e:sippar|Sippar]], commemorated on the Sun-god Tablet. Marduk-zakir-shumi I relied on Shalmaneser III of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] to put down his brother's revolt, a sign of growing dependence. [[e:chaldean-tribes|Chaldean tribes]] such as [[s:bit-yakin|Bit-Yakin]] and [[s:bit-amukani|Bit-Amukani]] grew powerful in the south. Under Nabonassar (747 to 734 BCE) systematic astronomical observations and the [[e:babylonian-chronicles|Babylonian Chronicles]] began, later used by Ptolemy.
dynasty-of-e.e: After Nabonassar, Nabu-mukin-zeri of [[s:bit-amukani|Bit-Amukani]] seized the throne in 732 BCE, and Tiglath-Pileser III of [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] took [[e:babylon|Babylon]] in 729 BCE, beginning direct Assyrian kingship there.

dominion-of-ceylon.t: Sri Lanka's first independent state, a Commonwealth dominion that won freedom peacefully and later became a republic.
dominion-of-ceylon.o: [[s:british-ceylon|British Ceylon]] gained independence on 4 February 1948 under the [[e:ceylon|Ceylon]] Independence Act, with the British monarch remaining head of state and a Governor-General. D. S. Senanayake of the United National Party became the first prime minister, and the Soulbury Constitution provided a Westminster-style parliament.
dominion-of-ceylon.r: The new state disenfranchised most plantation Tamils of Indian origin through the citizenship laws of 1948 and 1949. S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike won the 1956 election and passed the Sinhala Only Act, deepening tension with Tamils. After his assassination in 1959, his widow Sirimavo Bandaranaike became the world's first woman prime minister in 1960. A youth insurrection by the JVP was suppressed in 1971.
dominion-of-ceylon.e: A new constitution adopted on 22 May 1972 ended dominion status and renamed the country [[s:sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], with William Gopallawa, the last Governor-General, becoming its first president and Sirimavo Bandaranaike remaining prime minister.

denkyira.t: Akan kingdom that dominated the gold-rich central forest in the 17th century before being overthrown by the rising Asante.
denkyira.o: Denkyira emerged in the early 17th century in the forest south-west of present-day [[e:kumasi|Kumasi]], among [[e:akan|Akan]] clans that had moved from the area of [[s:kingdom-of-adansi|Adansi]]. Controlling rich goldfields and routes to the coastal forts, it conquered neighbouring states, including Adansi, and grew into the leading power of the central Akan forest.
denkyira.r: Under Boa Amponsem in the late 17th century, Denkyira took tribute from many [[e:akan|Akan]] states, including the young [[e:ashanti-empire|Asante]] chiefdoms, and held the [[e:elmina|Elmina]] Note, a rent paid by the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] at Elmina. Its wealth came from gold mining and trade in gold and slaves with the [[s:dutch-gold-coast|Dutch Gold Coast]].
denkyira.e: Denkyira's demands provoked revolt. In 1701 [[e:osei-tutu-i|Osei Tutu]] of [[e:ashanti-empire|Asante]] defeated and killed King [[e:ntim-gyakari|Ntim Gyakari]] at Feyiase, and Denkyira became tributary to the [[s:ashanti-empire|Ashanti Empire]]. It survives as a traditional area in [[e:ghana|Ghana's]] Central Region.

dar-sila.t: A Daju sultanate in south-eastern Chad, heir to the old Daju kings of Darfur, that kept its autonomy between Wadai and Darfur until 1916.
dar-sila.o: The Daju had ruled in [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]] before the [[s:tunjur-kingdom|Tunjur]], as the [[s:daju-kingdom|Daju kingdom]]. Their royal line later moved south-west to the Sila region, in present-day south-eastern [[e:chad|Chad]], where by the mid-17th century they had established a sultanate, eventually based at Goz Beida.
dar-sila.r: Dar Sila's sultans ruled a farming population in a well-watered savanna region and controlled hunting and slave-raiding zones to the south. The sultanate paid tribute at times to the [[s:wadai-empire|Wadai Empire]] or the [[s:darfur-sultanate|Darfur Sultanate]] but retained its own dynasty. Few details of its government are recorded.
dar-sila.e: After the French conquest of [[e:wadai-empire|Wadai]], the sultan of Dar Sila resisted, and French forces occupied Goz Beida in 1916. The sultanate became part of [[s:chad-french-colony|Chad (French colony)]], and its sultans continued as traditional rulers.

duchy-of-franconia.t: The short-lived stem duchy of the Franks in central Germany whose duke Conrad I became king of East Francia in 911.
duchy-of-franconia.o: In the early 10th century the Conradine family won a bloody feud with the Babenbergs for dominance in Franconia, the Frankish heartland along the Main and the middle [[e:rhine|Rhine]]. After Adalbert of Babenberg was executed in 906, Conrad the Younger became the leading [[e:magnates|magnate]], recognised as duke of the [[s:franks|Franks]].
duchy-of-franconia.r: In 911 Conrad was elected king of [[s:east-francia|East Francia]] as Conrad I, the first non-Carolingian ruler, while his brother Eberhard governed Franconia. Conrad struggled against the [[e:saxons|Saxon]], Bavarian and Swabian dukes and the [[e:magyars|Magyars]]. Dying in 918, he reportedly sent the royal insignia to Henry the Fowler of Saxony, his former enemy.
duchy-of-franconia.e: Eberhard accepted Henry I's kingship but rebelled against [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] and was killed at the Battle of Andernach in 939. Otto did not appoint a new duke; Franconia passed directly to the crown and fragmented into bishoprics such as Würzburg and Bamberg and later secular lordships.

dutch-east-indies.t: The Dutch colonial state in the Indonesian archipelago from 1800 to 1949, forerunner of the borders of modern Indonesia.
dutch-east-indies.o: When the charter of the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] expired at the end of 1799, its Asian possessions passed to the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] state. Governor-General Herman Willem Daendels reorganised [[e:java|Java]] from 1808, and after the interlude of [[s:british-java|British Java]] the Dutch returned in 1816, then fought the Java War of 1825 to 1830 against Prince Diponegoro.
dutch-east-indies.r: Under the [[e:cultivation-system|Cultivation System]] introduced by [[e:johannes-van-den-bosch|Johannes van den Bosch]] in 1830, Javanese villages had to grow export crops such as [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]], [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] and [[e:indigo|indigo]], making the colony hugely profitable. Conquest of the outer islands followed, including the long Aceh War from 1873. The Ethical Policy after 1901 expanded schooling, and nationalist movements such as Sarekat [[e:islam|Islam]] and Sukarno's party grew.
dutch-east-indies.e: [[e:japan|Japan]] conquered the colony in 1942. [[s:indonesia|Indonesia]] proclaimed independence in August 1945, and after four years of war and diplomacy the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]] transferred [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] on 27 December 1949, keeping only [[s:netherlands-new-guinea|Netherlands New Guinea]] until 1962.

duchy-of-leczyca.t: A small Piast duchy of central Poland that changed hands among the Kuyavian and Masovian dukes before rejoining the Crown.
duchy-of-leczyca.o: Leczyca, an old stronghold where Polish church synods were held in the 12th century, became a separate duchy in the age of division. In 1229 Konrad I of Masovia took control of it, and after Konrad's death in 1247 it passed to his son Casimir I of Kuyavia, whose descendants ruled it in various combinations with [[s:duchy-of-sieradz|Sieradz]] and Kuyavia.
duchy-of-leczyca.r: Leczyca was a farming land in the middle of [[e:poland|Poland]] with a fortified castle and a collegiate church at Tum, one of the finest Romanesque churches in the country. Its dukes were minor Piasts, among them Wladyslaw I the Elbow-high, who held it in the 1290s while building his base for reuniting Poland. The duchy suffered raids by the Lithuanians and the Teutonic Order.
duchy-of-leczyca.e: After [[e:poland|Poland]] was reunited in 1320, Leczyca continued as a duchy under Wladyslaw of Dobrzyn, a nephew of the king. When he died in 1352 it was incorporated into the [[s:kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385|Kingdom of Poland]] (1025-1385) as a province, later the Leczyca Voivodeship.

duchy-of-teck.t: Swabian duchy of a Zähringen branch named after Teck castle near Kirchheim, a ducal title without a duchy that later passed to the British royal family's ancestors.
duchy-of-teck.o: Adalbert, a younger son of Duke Conrad of Zähringen, inherited lands around the castle of Teck on the edge of the Swabian Jura and called himself Duke of Teck from 1187. The ducal title came from his family's rank rather than any ancient duchy, and the lands were modest, centred on Kirchheim and Owen.
duchy-of-teck.r: The dukes ruled a small cluster of castles, towns and farmland and often served greater lords, including the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]]. The family split into lines and, under financial pressure, sold its holdings piece by piece. Most of the territory, including Kirchheim, was sold to the Counts of Württemberg in 1381 to 1386.
duchy-of-teck.e: The last duke, Ludwig, Patriarch of Aquileia, died in 1439. Württemberg later took the ducal title, and in 1871 it was revived for Francis of Teck, father of Queen Mary of [[s:kingdom-of-great-britain|Great Britain]]. Teck castle survives in part.

dominion-of-new-zealand.t: New Zealand's four decades as a British dominion, which built one of the world's first welfare states and fought in both world wars.
dominion-of-new-zealand.o: [[s:new-zealand|New Zealand]] declined to join the [[s:commonwealth-of-australia|Commonwealth of Australia]] in 1901. At the request of Prime Minister Joseph Ward, the [[s:colony-of-new-zealand|Colony of New Zealand]] was proclaimed a dominion on 26 September 1907, signalling self-governing status within the [[s:british-empire|British Empire]]. The change was largely symbolic, as the country already ran its own affairs.
dominion-of-new-zealand.r: William Massey's Reform government held office from 1912 to 1925 and sent the expeditionary force whose losses at Gallipoli in 1915 shaped national identity. Farm exports of wool, meat and butter to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] dominated the economy, and the Depression hit hard. The first Labour government under Michael Joseph Savage, from 1935, built state housing and the Social Security Act of 1938. Peter Fraser led the country through the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]].
dominion-of-new-zealand.e: [[s:new-zealand|New Zealand]] was cautious about formal independence and did not adopt the [[e:statute-of-westminster-1931|Statute of Westminster]] of 1931 until November 1947. With that act it became fully sovereign, and the term dominion fell out of use.

dvaravati.t: A Mon Buddhist civilisation of central Thailand from the 7th to 11th centuries, the earliest Theravada culture of the Chao Phraya basin.
dvaravati.o: Dvaravati takes its name from [[e:silver|silver]] coins found at Nakhon Pathom and other sites inscribed 'meritorious deeds of the king of Dvaravati', matching the Duoluobodi of Chinese pilgrims. Moated towns appear in the Chao Phraya valley from around the 6th and 7th centuries, built by Mon-speaking communities.
dvaravati.r: Whether Dvaravati was a single kingdom or a cultural network of city-states, including Nakhon Pathom, U Thong, Khu Bua, Si Thep and [[s:lavo-kingdom|Lopburi]], is debated. Its people were early adopters of [[e:theravada-buddhism|Theravada Buddhism]], using Pali and Old Mon in inscriptions, and produced distinctive Buddha images, stone Wheels of the Law and terracotta stupa decoration. Moats, canals and [[e:rice|rice]] farming supported the towns.
dvaravati.e: From the 10th and 11th centuries the region came under the influence of the [[s:khmer-empire|Khmer Empire]], and Lavo became a [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] centre. Dvaravati's Mon Buddhist traditions passed to [[s:hariphunchai|Hariphunchai]] in the north and fed into the later Thai kingdoms of [[s:sukhothai-kingdom|Sukhothai]] and [[s:ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya]].

domain-of-matthew-csak.t: Vast private domain of the magnate Matthew Csák in north-western Hungary, ruled like an independent state during the struggle for the crown.
domain-of-matthew-csak.o: Matthew III Csák, of a leading baronial clan, built up power in the Váh valley in the 1290s as royal authority collapsed. After the death of Andrew III in 1301 ended the Árpád line, he backed rival claimants and seized castles across north-western [[e:hungary|Hungary]], centred on Trencsén (Trenčín).
domain-of-matthew-csak.r: At its height he controlled some fourteen counties in modern Slovakia and northern [[e:hungary|Hungary]], with around 50 castles. He kept his own court, palatine and household officials, granted lands, made treaties with [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] and ran justice and taxation like a king. He refused to submit to Charles I, and the pope excommunicated him in 1311.
domain-of-matthew-csak.e: Charles I defeated his allies at Rozgony in 1312 but could not take his heartland. After Matthew died in 1321, royal armies quickly took his castles, and the domain returned to the [[s:kingdom-of-hungary-1301-1526|Kingdom of Hungary]] (1301-1526).

delaware-colony.t: The Lower Counties on the Delaware, a former Swedish and Dutch settlement area that shared Pennsylvania's governor but kept its own assembly and became the first state.
delaware-colony.o: The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] settlement of Zwaanendael near modern Lewes was destroyed in 1631, and in 1638 [[s:new-sweden|New Sweden]] built Fort Christina at what is now Wilmington. [[s:new-netherland|New Netherland]] conquered the Swedish colony in 1655, founding New Amstel, later New Castle. After the English conquest of 1664 the area was ruled from [[e:new-york|New York]] under James, Duke of York.
delaware-colony.r: In 1682 James granted the three counties of New Castle, Kent and [[s:kingdom-of-sussex|Sussex]] to William Penn, who governed them with the [[s:province-of-pennsylvania|Province of Pennsylvania]]. The Lower Counties resented domination by Philadelphia and from 1704 met in their own assembly at New Castle, while still sharing the Penn family's governor. Farmers of Swedish, Finnish, [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and English descent grew grain and tobacco, and enslaved Africans worked many farms in the south.
delaware-colony.e: On 15 June 1776 the assembly declared the Lower Counties separate from both [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and Pennsylvania, and Caesar Rodney's ride helped carry the vote for independence. As the state of Delaware, it was the first to ratify the [[s:united-states|United States]] Constitution in 1787.

duchy-of-bavaria.t: One of Germany's oldest territories, a duchy for more than a thousand years under the Agilolfings, Welfs and Wittelsbachs, and the core of modern Bavaria.
duchy-of-bavaria.o: The Bavarians (Baiuvarii) appear in the mid 6th century between the [[e:danube|Danube]], the Lech and the [[e:alps|Alps]], a people formed from Germanic groups and the Romanised population. Around 555 the Frankish kings recognised Garibald I of the Agilolfing family as duke. Bavaria later became a stem duchy of [[s:east-francia|East Francia]] and the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]].
duchy-of-bavaria.r: The Agilolfing dukes ruled almost as kings, with their own law code, the Lex Baiuvariorum, and bishoprics organised by Saint Boniface in 739 at Salzburg, [[s:free-imperial-city-of-regensburg|Regensburg]], Freising and Passau. Regensburg was the early capital. From 1180 the Wittelsbach family held the duchy, ruling from Munich, Landshut and Ingolstadt during long periods of division.
duchy-of-bavaria.e: [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]] deposed Duke Tassilo III in 788, but the duchy was revived. Albert IV reunited Bavaria in 1505 and imposed [[e:primogeniture|primogeniture]]. In 1623 Maximilian I received the electoral dignity during the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]], and the duchy became the [[s:electorate-of-bavaria|Electorate of Bavaria]], later the [[s:kingdom-of-bavaria|Kingdom of Bavaria]] in 1806.

duchy-of-bukovina.t: Habsburg crown land carved from northern Moldavia, a mosaic of Romanians, Ukrainians, Jews and Germans centred on Czernowitz.
duchy-of-bukovina.o: In 1774 Austrian troops occupied the north-western corner of [[s:principality-of-moldavia|Moldavia]], linking newly acquired [[s:kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria|Galicia]] with [[s:principality-of-transylvania|Transylvania]], and the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] ceded it in 1775. Named Bukovina, the beech land, it was ruled by the military until 1786, then attached to [[e:galicia|Galicia]]. In 1849 it became a separate crown land with the title of duchy.
duchy-of-bukovina.r: Bukovina had its own diet from 1861 and a governor at Czernowitz, which grew into a German-speaking university town after 1875. [[e:romanians|Romanians]], Ukrainians, [[e:jews|Jews]], Germans and [[e:poles|Poles]] lived side by side, and in 1910 the diet adopted a compromise sharing seats among national groups. The [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] metropolitan resided in Czernowitz, and the painted monasteries of Suceava were preserved.
duchy-of-bukovina.e: As [[e:austro-hungarian-empire|Austria-Hungary]] collapsed in 1918, a congress in Czernowitz voted for union with [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]]. In 1940 the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] annexed northern Bukovina, which is now part of [[e:ukraine|Ukraine]], while southern Bukovina remains in [[e:romania|Romania]]. Its Jewish community was largely destroyed in the Holocaust.
duchy-of-bukovina.re: Eastern Orthodox Christianity, Judaism, Catholic Christianity
