duchy-of-bourbon.t: The central French duchy of a Capetian branch whose last great duke betrayed Francis I and whose cousins later became kings of France.
duchy-of-bourbon.o: The lords of [[s:ile-bourbon|Bourbon]] had held the Bourbonnais since the 10th century. In 1272 the heiress Beatrice of [[e:house-of-bourbon|Bourbon]] married Robert of Clermont, son of Louis IX, and in 1327 [[e:charles-iv|Charles IV]] raised the barony to a duchy for their son Louis I, creating the Capetian house of Bourbon.
duchy-of-bourbon.r: The dukes ruled from Moulins and gathered [[s:county-of-forez|Forez]], [[s:lordship-of-beaujeu|Beaujolais]], [[s:county-of-auvergne|Auvergne]] and [[s:county-of-la-marche|La Marche]] through marriage and inheritance, making their lands one of [[e:france|France's]] largest princely blocs. Louis II, called the Good Duke, was a model crusading prince. Anne of France and her husband Peter II governed the kingdom during the minority of Charles VIII.
duchy-of-bourbon.e: Charles III, constable of [[e:france|France]], fell out with [[e:francis-i|Francis I]], who claimed his lands; he joined [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]] in 1523 and was killed leading the sack of [[e:rome|Rome]] in 1527. His lands were confiscated and joined to the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]], but a younger [[s:ile-bourbon|Bourbon]] line gave France Henry IV.

danube-sich.t: The refuge of Zaporozhian Cossacks in the Ottoman Danube Delta after Catherine the Great destroyed their Sich.
danube-sich.o: When the Russian army abolished the [[s:zaporozhian-sich|Zaporozhian Sich]] in 1775, several thousand [[e:cossacks|Cossacks]] fled to Ottoman territory. After moving between several sites, they settled in the [[e:danube|Danube]] Delta, where the sultan allowed them to found a new Sich in return for military service. Its main centre from 1814 was at Dunavets, in modern [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]].
danube-sich.r: The [[e:danube|Danube]] Sich kept the old Zaporozhian institutions of an elected kish otaman, a council and kurins. The [[e:cossacks|Cossacks]] fished, farmed and fought in Ottoman campaigns, including against Serbian and Greek rebels. They clashed repeatedly with the Nekrasov Cossacks, Russian Old Believers settled nearby, over fishing grounds and Ottoman favour.
danube-sich.e: During the [[e:russo-turkish-war-1877-1878|Russo-Turkish War]] of 1828, the kish otaman Osyp Hladky defected to [[e:russia|Russia]] with part of the Host. In response the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] destroyed the Sich. The defectors formed the Azov [[e:cossacks|Cossack]] Host in Russia, while the others dispersed within Ottoman lands.

duchy-of-finland.t: Short-lived Finnish duchy granted to the future John III of Sweden, whose independent policy led his brother Eric XIV to crush it in 1563.
duchy-of-finland.o: In 1556 Gustav Vasa granted his second son John the Duchy of [[s:grand-duchy-of-finland|Finland]], covering south-western [[e:finland|Finland]], as an [[e:appanage|appanage]]. John set up his court at Turku Castle, which he enlarged in [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] style, and governed with considerable independence.
duchy-of-finland.r: Duke John ran his own administration, collected taxes and pursued a foreign policy of his own, which brought him into conflict with his half-brother, King Eric XIV. In 1562 he married Catherine Jagiellon, sister of King [[e:sigismund-ii-augustus|Sigismund II Augustus]] of [[e:poland|Poland]], and lent money to Poland while [[e:sweden|Sweden]] and Poland competed for [[s:livonian-confederation|Livonia]].
duchy-of-finland.e: Eric XIV regarded this as treason. In 1563 his army besieged and took Turku Castle, and John and Catherine were imprisoned at Gripsholm. The duchy was abolished, and [[s:grand-duchy-of-finland|Finland]] returned to direct rule by the [[s:kingdom-of-sweden|Kingdom of Sweden]]. John deposed Eric in 1568 and reigned as John III.

duchy-of-magdeburg.t: The secularised Archbishopric of Magdeburg as a Brandenburg-Prussian duchy, rebuilt after the Thirty Years' War's worst massacre.
duchy-of-magdeburg.o: The [[s:archbishopric-of-magdeburg|Archbishopric of Magdeburg]] was devastated in the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]], when Tilly's army sacked the city in 1631. The [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 promised it to [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] on the death of its administrator, Augustus of Saxe-Weissenfels; when he died in 1680, it became the Duchy of Magdeburg.
duchy-of-magdeburg.r: [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] made Magdeburg one of its strongest fortresses and an administrative centre. The duchy was a rich grain region of the Magdeburg Börde, and Huguenot and Palatine refugees settled in the city. The University of Halle, founded in 1694 in the duchy, became a centre of Pietism and the early [[e:age-of-enlightenment|Enlightenment]] under August Hermann Francke and Christian Thomasius.
duchy-of-magdeburg.e: [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] lost the duchy to the [[s:kingdom-of-westphalia|Kingdom of Westphalia]] in 1807. In 1815 it returned to Prussia and formed the core of the Province of Saxony, with Magdeburg as provincial capital, a role it now holds in Saxony-Anhalt.

daura-emirate.t: The emirate established in Daura, the legendary mother city of the Hausa, after the Fulani jihad, while the old Hausa dynasty survived in exile.
daura-emirate.o: [[s:kingdom-of-daura|Daura]] is honoured in the Bayajidda legend as the oldest of the [[e:hausa|Hausa states]]. In the [[e:jihad|jihad]] of [[e:usman-dan-fodio|Usman dan Fodio]], [[e:fula|Fulani]] forces under Mallam Ishaku took the town around 1806, and the Hausa ruler fled north. Ishaku became the first Fulani emir, under the overall authority of [[e:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto]], while the exiled Hausa line set up rival courts at Zango and Baure.
daura-emirate.r: The [[e:fula|Fulani]] [[e:emirate|emirate]] was small and exposed, lying on the frontier between the [[s:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto Caliphate]] and the unconquered [[e:hausa|Hausa states]] of [[s:sultanate-of-maradi|Maradi]] and [[s:sultanate-of-damagaram|Damagaram]] to the north. It ruled through titled officials on the [[e:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto]] pattern, collected Islamic taxes and joined in the wars of the frontier. [[s:kingdom-of-daura|Daura]] remained a place of symbolic prestige for all Hausa.
daura-emirate.e: After British occupation in 1903 the old dynasty was restored: the British installed the head of the Zango line as emir, and his descendants still reign. The Anglo-French boundary split the old [[s:kingdom-of-daura|Daura]] country between [[e:nigeria|Nigeria]] and [[e:niger-river|Niger]].

da-yining.t: The short dynasty of Yang Ganzhen in western Yunnan, overthrown in 937 by Duan Siping, founder of the Dali Kingdom.
da-yining.o: Yang Ganzhen, a leading official of the Erhai region who had brought down [[s:da-changhe|Da Changhe]] in 928 and installed [[s:da-tianxing|Da Tianxing]], deposed his own puppet Zhao Shanzheng in 929 and proclaimed the kingdom of Da Yining at Yangjumie.
da-yining.r: Sources are scanty. Later accounts describe Yang Ganzhen's rule as oppressive and his government as unstable, alienating both the Bai nobility and the many tribal peoples of eastern Yunnan.
da-yining.e: In 937 Duan Siping, a military commander of the Tonghai region, allied with eastern tribes, marched on the capital and overthrew Yang Ganzhen. He founded the [[s:dali-kingdom|Dali Kingdom]], which lasted until the Mongol conquest.

dutch-republic.t: The federal republic born of the revolt against Spain, which became the world's leading trading power and a centre of art, science and toleration.
dutch-republic.o: The northern provinces of the [[s:habsburg-netherlands|Habsburg Netherlands]] rose against Philip II from 1568 under William the Silent. They allied in the Union of [[s:lordship-of-utrecht|Utrecht]] in 1579 and renounced Philip by the [[e:act-of-abjuration|Act of Abjuration]] in 1581. After failing to find a new sovereign, the provinces governed themselves as a republic, recognised by [[e:spain|Spain]] in the Peace of Münster in 1648.
dutch-republic.r: Each province was sovereign, sending delegates to the States General at The Hague, while Holland's Grand Pensionary and the Orange-Nassau stadtholders competed for leadership. Founded in 1602, the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] built an Asian trading empire. [[e:amsterdam|Amsterdam]] became [[e:europe|Europe's]] financial centre, and Rembrandt, Vermeer, Spinoza and Huygens worked in relative freedom, though the Reformed church was official.
dutch-republic.e: After the disaster year of 1672, William III led resistance to [[e:france|France]] and became king of [[e:england|England]] in 1689. The 18th century brought decline and clashes between Orangists and Patriots. In 1795 French armies and [[e:dutch|Dutch]] revolutionaries founded the [[s:batavian-republic|Batavian Republic]].

dilmun.t: The island trading power of Bahrain that linked Mesopotamia with Magan and the Indus, remembered in Sumerian myth as a pure land.
dilmun.o: Dilmun appears in Sumerian texts by the late 3rd millennium BCE as a trading partner of Ur. From around 2200 BCE the settlement at Qal'at al-[[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Bahrain]] grew into a walled town, and the Barbar culture built temples at Barbar and Saar and tens of thousands of burial mounds across northern [[e:bahrain|Bahrain]], with influence reaching Failaka in [[s:sheikhdom-of-kuwait|Kuwait]] and the coast of eastern [[e:arabia|Arabia]].
dilmun.r: Dilmun was a merchant state, handling [[e:copper|copper]] from [[s:magan|Magan]], carnelian and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] from the [[e:indus|Indus]] and grain and textiles from [[e:mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], and it set its own weight standard and stamp seals. Its gods Inzak and Enki were worshipped at freshwater springs. Around 1500 BCE [[s:kassite-babylonia|Kassite Babylonia]] ruled the island through governors at Qal'at al-[[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Bahrain]], and its date trade flourished.
dilmun.e: Later kings of Dilmun paid tribute to the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]]: Uperi sent gifts to [[e:sargon-ii|Sargon II]] in 709 BCE. Dilmun passed under Neo-Babylonian control and vanishes as a political entity in the 6th century BCE, the island later reappearing as Tylos in Greek sources. Its burial mounds are a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

dauphine-of-viennois.t: The Alpine principality around Grenoble whose last ruler sold it to France on condition that the heir to the throne bear the title Dauphin.
dauphine-of-viennois.o: Around 1029 Guigues the Old, count of Albon, began gathering lands in the Viennois and the Grésivaudan as royal power in the [[s:kingdom-of-arles|Kingdom of Arles]] weakened. His descendants made Grenoble their centre, and Guigues IV, nicknamed 'Dauphin', gave the family its distinctive title in the 12th century.
dauphine-of-viennois.r: The dauphins governed a mountain land of pastures, mines and passes towards [[e:italy|Italy]], and later added the Briançonnais and Gapençais. In 1339 Humbert II founded a university at Grenoble. The principality had its own council and courts, and its lords balanced between [[s:county-of-savoy|Savoy]], [[s:county-of-provence|Provence]] and the French crown.
dauphine-of-viennois.e: Humbert II, childless and deep in debt, sold the Dauphiné to Philip VI under the Treaty of [[e:roman-empire|Romans]], completed in 1349. It went to the king's grandson Charles, and from then on the eldest son of the French king held the title Dauphin, while the province joined the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].

duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia-1918.t: German client state proclaimed by Courland's Baltic German nobles in 1918, which offered its ducal crown to Kaiser Wilhelm II.
duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia-1918.o: Under German occupation, the Courland Landesrat, a council dominated by Baltic German nobles, proclaimed on 8 March 1918 the restoration of the [[s:duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia|Duchy of Courland and Semigallia]], covering the former [[s:governorate-of-courland|Governorate of Courland]]. It offered the ducal crown to [[e:wilhelm-ii|Wilhelm II]], and [[e:germany|Germany]] recognised the duchy on 15 March.
duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia-1918.r: The duchy had no real government of its own and depended on the German military administration that had replaced [[s:ober-ost|Ober Ost]]. Its leaders planned German settlement and close union with the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]]. Latvians, the great majority of the population, were excluded from its councils and rejected it.
duchy-of-courland-and-semigallia-1918.e: In autumn 1918 the duchy was to join the [[s:united-baltic-duchy|United Baltic Duchy]], but [[e:germany|Germany's]] defeat in November ended the scheme. The [[s:republic-of-latvia|Republic of Latvia]], proclaimed on 18 November 1918, took over its territory after the War of Independence.

demerara-essequibo.t: A British-ruled sugar colony on the Guiana coast, formed from two Dutch colonies and shaken by the great slave rebellion of 1823.
demerara-essequibo.o: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] had occupied the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] colonies of [[s:demerara|Demerara]] and [[s:essequibo|Essequibo]] since 1796. In 1812 the British administration united them as Demerara-Essequibo, renaming the capital Stabroek as Georgetown, after George III. The Convention of [[e:london|London]] in 1814 formally ceded the territory to [[e:britain|Britain]].
demerara-essequibo.r: The colony kept [[e:dutch|Dutch]] laws and its Court of Policy, in which planters held most power. [[e:sugar-plantation|Sugar]] dominated the economy, worked by tens of thousands of enslaved Africans. In August 1823 the [[s:demerara|Demerara]] rebellion involved some 10,000 or more enslaved people, who demanded rights they believed had been granted in [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]]. It was crushed with many executions. The missionary John Smith, accused of encouraging it, died in prison, inspiring abolitionists in [[e:britain|Britain]].
demerara-essequibo.e: In 1831 Demerara-Essequibo was merged with [[s:berbice|Berbice]] to form [[s:british-guiana|British Guiana]]. [[e:slavery|Slavery]] was abolished across the [[s:british-empire|British Empire]] in 1834. Georgetown remained the capital and is today the capital of [[s:co-operative-republic-of-guyana|Guyana]], and the rebellion of 1823 is remembered as a milestone on the road to emancipation.

cr.a: Original: Acts of Union 1800 Vector: Yaddah

dir-state.t: A Pashtun principality of the mountainous north-west frontier, ruled by its Nawabs until absorption into Pakistan in 1969.
dir-state.o: The ruling family of Dir, of the Yusufzai Pashtun Painda Khel, traced their power to a religious leader, Mulla Ilyas, known as Akhund Baba, in the 17th century. His descendants became khans and later Nawabs of the Panjkora valley.
dir-state.r: The Nawabs ruled a rugged valley of tribal Pashtun farmers through personal authority and levies, receiving British [[e:subsidy|subsidies]] to keep the route to [[s:chitral-state|Chitral]] open after 1895. Rule was autocratic and modern education and services were very limited.
dir-state.e: Dir acceded to [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]] in 1948. In 1960 Nawab Shah Jahan Khan was deposed, and in 1969 the state was abolished and became a district of the North-West Frontier Province, later divided into Upper and Lower Dir.

duchy-of-aragvi.t: A powerful Georgian duchy in the Aragvi valley, centred on the fortress of Ananuri, that controlled the main road across the Caucasus.
duchy-of-aragvi.o: The upper Aragvi valley lay on the route that later became the Georgian Military Road through the Darial Pass. From the late 14th century the eristavis of Aragvi held the region hereditarily, first under the [[s:kingdom-of-georgia|Kingdom of Georgia]] and after 1490 as [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-kartli|Kingdom of Kartli]].
duchy-of-aragvi.r: The dukes commanded the mountaineers of Mtiuleti, Gudamakari and the Pshav and Khevsur communities and could field large armies. Their fortress of Ananuri, with its 17th-century churches, overlooked the road. Ambitious dukes such as Nugzar and Zurab played major roles in Kartli's politics; Zurab helped defeat Persian forces in 1625 before being killed on the king's orders in 1629.
duchy-of-aragvi.e: Feuds with the dukes of [[s:duchy-of-ksani|Ksani]], who stormed Ananuri in 1739, and rebellions against the crown weakened the house. In 1743 King Teimuraz II abolished the duchy and annexed it to the [[s:kingdom-of-kartli|Kingdom of Kartli]].

duchy-of-alamannia.t: The Frankish duchy that ruled the Alemanni of south-west Germany and Switzerland for two centuries, until the Carolingians abolished it at Cannstatt.
duchy-of-alamannia.o: After [[e:clovis-i|Clovis]]' victories over the [[s:alemanni|Alemanni]] around 496 and 506, the southern Alemanni stayed under Ostrogothic protection until 536, when the Ostrogoth king Witigis ceded them to the [[s:franks|Franks]]. The Merovingian kings then placed the Alemanni under dukes, a region covering modern Baden-Württemberg, Alsace, eastern [[s:swiss-confederation|Switzerland]] and Bavarian Swabia.
duchy-of-alamannia.r: The dukes governed under Frankish overlordship but often acted independently, especially as Merovingian power weakened. Law was codified in the Pactus and the Lex Alamannorum of the early 8th century. [[e:christianity|Christianity]] spread through bishoprics at Constance and [[s:canton-of-basel|Basel]] and monasteries such as St Gall, founded on the hermitage of Gallus, and Reichenau, founded in 724.
duchy-of-alamannia.e: Duke Lantfrid and his successor Theudebald resisted the rising Carolingian mayors of the palace. In 746 Carloman summoned the Alemannic nobility to Cannstatt and executed many of them, ending the ducal office. Alamannia was then ruled by Frankish counts until the [[s:duchy-of-swabia|Duchy of Swabia]] emerged in the early 10th century.

duchy-of-arenberg.t: Small Eifel territory of the Arenberg family, great nobles of the Habsburg Netherlands who held ducal rank in the Empire.
duchy-of-arenberg.o: The lordship of Arenberg, named after a castle in the Eifel, passed through heiresses to the Ligne family in the 16th century, which took the Arenberg name. It became a princely county in 1576, and in 1644 Emperor [[e:ferdinand-iii-of-castile|Ferdinand III]] raised it to a duchy under Philippe-Charles d'Arenberg.
duchy-of-arenberg.r: The Eifel territory was tiny; the dukes' wealth and influence lay in vast estates in the Spanish and later [[s:austrian-netherlands|Austrian Netherlands]], where they served as governors, generals and courtiers in Brussels. The family was Catholic. After losing the left-bank lands to [[e:france|France]], the duke received the former Münster district of Meppen and the [[s:free-imperial-city-of-cologne|Cologne]] enclave of Recklinghausen in 1803.
duchy-of-arenberg.e: Arenberg joined the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]] in 1806, but [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] annexed its northern lands to [[e:france|France]] in 1810. In 1815 Meppen came under the [[s:kingdom-of-hanover|Kingdom of Hanover]] and Recklinghausen under [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], with the dukes as mediatised lords.

duchy-of-inowroclaw.t: A Kuyavian Piast duchy on the Teutonic border, ruled by Ziemomysl and his sons until Casimir the Great absorbed it.
duchy-of-inowroclaw.o: In the division of the [[s:duchy-of-kuyavia|Duchy of Kuyavia]] after Casimir I's death in 1267, the northern lands around Inowroclaw went to his son Ziemomysl. He relied on support from the Teutonic Order and the dukes of Pomerelia, which caused revolts among his own nobles.
duchy-of-inowroclaw.r: Inowroclaw was a salt-producing land near the Vistula, and its towns grew under German law. After Ziemomysl died in 1287 his sons Leszek, Przemysl and Casimir shared and exchanged its parts, including Gniewkowo. The duchy was devastated during the war between [[e:poland|Poland]] and the Teutonic Knights in the 1320s and 1330s.
duchy-of-inowroclaw.e: Casimir III the Great gradually bought out the local dukes. The last claimant, Wladyslaw the White of Gniewkowo, gave up his rights and became a monk in the 1360s, and around 1364 Inowroclaw was incorporated into the [[s:kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385|Kingdom of Poland]] (1025-1385).

duchy-of-wurttemberg.t: The south-west German duchy, raised in 1495, that combined strong estates, a model Lutheran church and a constitution dating from 1514.
duchy-of-wurttemberg.o: The [[s:county-of-wurttemberg|County of Württemberg]], reunited by Count Eberhard im Bart in 1482, was raised to a duchy at the Diet of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-worms|Worms]] in 1495; Eberhard had founded the University of Tübingen in 1477. His successor Ulrich proved a violent ruler, and the peasant revolt of the Poor Conrad in 1514 forced him to accept the Treaty of Tübingen, guaranteeing the estates' rights.
duchy-of-wurttemberg.r: Expelled by the Swabian League in 1519, Ulrich lost the duchy to the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]] until 1534, when he returned and introduced [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]]. Duke Christoph built a model Lutheran church order and school system. The Landtag, dominated by town notables because the nobility had left the duchy, controlled taxation. Stuttgart was the capital, and Ludwigsburg was built as a Baroque residence from 1704.
duchy-of-wurttemberg.e: Duke [[e:frederick-ii|Frederick II]] gained the rank of elector in 1803 and, allied with [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]], became king in 1806, doubling his lands; the duchy became the [[s:electorate-of-wurttemberg|Electorate of Württemberg]] and then the [[s:kingdom-of-wurttemberg|Kingdom of Württemberg]]. Its territory is now part of Baden-Württemberg.

dhurwai-state.t: A tiny Bundela chiefship of the Bundelkhand Agency in central India.
dhurwai-state.o: Dhurwai was recognised by the British as a separate holding in the early 19th century, one of the small Bundela estates confirmed after the British gained control of [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]].
dhurwai-state.r: It consisted of a few villages under a hereditary Bundela chief. Little else is recorded of its history.
dhurwai-state.e: After independence Dhurwai was merged into [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] with the other [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] states and absorbed by 1950.

duchy-of-split.t: Short-lived Dalmatian duchy granted to the Bosnian magnate Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić, uniting Split and the central Dalmatian islands under one lord.
duchy-of-split.o: In the struggle for the Hungarian crown between Sigismund of [[s:county-of-luxembourg|Luxembourg]] and Ladislaus of Naples, the powerful Bosnian noble Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić backed Ladislaus. In 1403 Ladislaus rewarded him with the title of Duke of Split, together with the islands of Brač, Hvar and Korčula, carving a duchy out of royal [[e:dalmatia|Dalmatia]].
duchy-of-split.r: Hrvoje ruled from Split while remaining Grand Duke of Bosnia, so the duchy linked the inland Bosnian lands with the Adriatic trade of the city. Split kept its communal statutes and council. Hrvoje's court produced the richly illuminated Glagolitic Missal of Hrvoje, made in Split around 1404, one of the finest Croatian medieval [[e:manuscript|manuscripts]].
duchy-of-split.e: Hrvoje later reconciled with Sigismund, but fell from favour and was declared a traitor in 1413; Split threw off his rule and returned to the Hungarian crown. Hrvoje died in 1416, and in 1420 Split passed to [[e:venice|Venice]], which held it for nearly four centuries.

daju-kingdom.t: The earliest remembered kingdom of Darfur, centred on the Jebel Marra mountains of western Sudan.
daju-kingdom.o: The Daju kingdom is known mainly from oral tradition, a few Arabic references and archaeology, so its history is very uncertain. [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]] traditions name the Daju as the first dynasty to rule the region, from around the 12th century, based in the fertile valleys and slopes of the Jebel Marra massif.
daju-kingdom.r: The Daju were a Nilo-Saharan-speaking people who farmed [[e:millet|millet]] and [[e:sorghum|sorghum]] and kept [[e:cattle|cattle]], ruling over neighbouring peoples through a [[e:sacred-kingship|sacred kingship]]. Stone-built sites on Jebel Marra may date from their era. The state probably took part in trade routes linking the [[e:nile|Nile]] valley and Christian [[e:nubia|Nubia]] with the [[e:lake-chad|Lake Chad]] region.
daju-kingdom.e: Traditions say the Daju were displaced by the [[s:tunjur-kingdom|Tunjur]] around the 14th or 15th century, and Daju groups moved south and west, where Daju-speaking communities still live in [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]], [[e:kordofan|Kordofan]] and [[e:chad|Chad]]. The later [[s:darfur-sultanate|Darfur Sultanate]] looked back on them as its forerunners.

decapolis-levant.t: The Decapolis, a group of Greek cities east of the Jordan freed by Pompey, famous for the colonnaded streets of Gerasa.
decapolis-levant.o: The [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]] cities, among them Gerasa, Gadara, [[s:pella|Pella]], Philadelphia, Scythopolis and Hippos, had grown as Greek-style towns under the [[s:ptolemaic-empire|Ptolemaic Empire]] and the [[s:seleucid-empire|Seleucid Empire]]. The [[s:hasmonean-kingdom|Hasmonean Kingdom]] conquered many of them, and in 63 BCE [[e:pompey|Pompey]] freed them and attached them to Roman [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]].
decapolis-levant.r: Each city governed itself, minted coins and dated years from [[e:pompey|Pompey's]] liberation. They were less a formal league than a regional group with shared Greek culture, temples to Zeus and Artemis, and trade with the [[s:nabataean-kingdom|Nabataean Kingdom]]. The Gospels mention the [[s:decapolis|Decapolis]] as the setting of Jesus' ministry.
decapolis-levant.e: In 106 CE [[e:trajan|Trajan]] created the province of [[e:arabia|Arabia]], dividing the cities between it and [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]]. Gerasa, modern Jerash, preserves one of the best-preserved Roman cityscapes.

dholpur-state.t: A Jat-ruled state on the Chambal, created in 1806 when the British gave Dholpur to the Rana of Gohad.
dholpur-state.o: The Jat Ranas of Gohad had held lands near [[s:gwalior-state|Gwalior]] in the 18th century. In 1806 the British returned Gohad and Gwalior to the [[e:scindias|Scindias]] and compensated Rana Kirat Singh with Dholpur, [[s:principality-of-bari|Bari]] and Rajakhera on the Chambal river.
dholpur-state.r: Dholpur was a 15-gun salute state of the Rajputana Agency, ruled by a Maharaj Rana over a population of farmers in the ravine country of the Chambal. Its red sandstone quarries supplied building stone across northern [[e:india|India]]. Udaybhan Singh, who ruled from 1911, was the last Maharaj Rana.
dholpur-state.e: Udaybhan Singh acceded to [[e:india|India]], and in 1948 Dholpur joined the [[s:matsya-union|Matsya Union]], which merged into the [[s:united-state-of-rajasthan|United State of Rajasthan]] in 1949. It is now a district of Rajasthan.

duchy-of-saxe-coburg-and-gotha.t: Twin Ernestine duchy whose dynasty placed rulers on the thrones of Belgium, Britain, Portugal and Bulgaria.
duchy-of-saxe-coburg-and-gotha.o: In the Ernestine redistribution of 1826, Duke Ernest I of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld gave up Saalfeld and received Gotha, forming Saxe-Coburg and Gotha. The two duchies remained legally separate, joined only in the person of the duke, with separate parliaments.
duchy-of-saxe-coburg-and-gotha.r: Ernest I's brother Leopold became King of the Belgians in 1831, and his son Albert married Queen [[s:colony-of-victoria|Victoria]] in 1840. Ernest II was a liberal patron of the German national movement and of music. Gotha was a centre of [[e:cartography|cartography]] with the Justus Perthes firm and of insurance, while Coburg was a court town. Victoria's son Alfred and grandson Charles Edward later succeeded as dukes.
duchy-of-saxe-coburg-and-gotha.e: Charles Edward abdicated in November 1918. The [[s:free-state-of-coburg|Free State of Coburg]] voted to join Bavaria in 1920, while Gotha joined the [[s:free-state-of-thuringia|Free State of Thuringia]].

duchy-of-swabia.t: The stem duchy of south-west Germany, home of the Hohenstaufen emperors, which collapsed with the execution of the last Staufer in 1268.
duchy-of-swabia.o: After the death of the Alemannic dukes in 746, Alamannia was governed by counts. In 915 Count Erchanger defeated King Conrad I's forces at Wahlwies and was proclaimed duke; Conrad executed him in 917, but Burchard II established the duchy, recognised by Henry the Fowler in 919. Swabia covered south-west [[e:germany|Germany]], Alsace and eastern [[s:swiss-confederation|Switzerland]].
duchy-of-swabia.r: Dukes were often royal relatives, and from 1079 the office went to the Staufer family, who became emperors with Conrad III and [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]]. Swabia was rich in monasteries, imperial cities such as Ulm and [[s:free-imperial-city-of-augsburg|Augsburg]], and lesser nobles. Its [[e:knighthood|knightly]] culture produced Minnesang poets.
duchy-of-swabia.e: After the fall of the Staufer, the last duke, Conradin, was beheaded at Naples in 1268. The duchy dissolved into many territories, including the [[s:county-of-wurttemberg|County of Württemberg]], the [[s:margraviate-of-baden|Margraviate of Baden]], [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] lands and [[e:free-imperial-city|free imperial cities]], which later formed the Swabian League and the Swabian Circle.

duchy-of-sandomierz.t: A Piast duchy of eastern Lesser Poland around the Vistula town of Sandomierz, usually joined to Krakow in the age of division.
duchy-of-sandomierz.o: Boleslaw III's testament of 1138 assigned Sandomierz and its land to his young son Henry, who took control in 1146. Henry went on [[e:crusade|crusade]] to the Holy Land in 1154 and was killed fighting the pagan Prussians in 1166, after which the duchy passed to his brother Casimir II the Just.
duchy-of-sandomierz.r: Sandomierz was a prosperous trading town on the Vistula, on the route between Krakow and Rus'. For most of the period it was ruled by the same dukes as Krakow, so the two duchies formed Lesser [[e:poland|Poland]]. The [[e:mongols|Mongols]] sacked the town in 1241 and again in 1260, killing many of its inhabitants and the [[e:dominican-order|Dominican friars]] of Saint James.
duchy-of-sandomierz.e: Its rulers included Leszek the White, Boleslaw V the Chaste and Leszek the Black. Wladyslaw I the Elbow-high gained Sandomierz in the early 14th century, and in 1320 it became part of the reunited [[s:kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385|Kingdom of Poland]] (1025-1385).

djibouti.t: A small republic at the mouth of the Red Sea whose port serves as Ethiopia's gateway to the sea and hosts military bases of several world powers.
djibouti.o: The [[s:french-territory-of-the-afars-and-the-issas|French Territory of the Afars and the Issas]] became independent on 27 June 1977 as the Republic of Djibouti, after a referendum in which voters overwhelmingly chose independence. Hassan Gouled Aptidon, an Issa [[e:somalis|Somali]] politician, became its first president.
djibouti.r: Gouled made his party, the People's Rally for Progress, the only legal party in 1981. [[e:afar|Afar]] grievances led to the FRUD rebellion of 1991 to 1994, ended by power-sharing agreements. Ismail Omar Guelleh succeeded Gouled in 1999 and has held office since. The economy rests on the port, which handles most of [[e:ethiopia|Ethiopia's]] foreign trade, and on rents from foreign bases, including French, American and Chinese.
djibouti.e: Djibouti has remained politically stable but tightly controlled, with limited opposition. New ports and the electrified railway to [[e:addis-ababa|Addis Ababa]], opened in 2016 to 2018, have strengthened its role as a regional trade hub.

daspalla-state.t: A small princely state in the hills south of the Mahanadi in Odisha, ruled from Kunjabangarh until 1948.
daspalla-state.o: Tradition holds that the ruling family was a branch of the Bhanja rulers of [[s:baudh-state|Baudh State]], founding Daspalla around 1498. Its early history is not well documented.
daspalla-state.r: Daspalla was a hilly, forested state with a large Kondh population. It was tributary to the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]] and, from 1803, one of the Orissa Tributary Mahals under British supervision. Little else of its history is recorded.
daspalla-state.e: Daspalla merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948 and is now in [[s:nayagarh-state|Nayagarh]] district.

duchy-of-austria.t: The Babenberg and Habsburg duchy on the Danube, created by the Privilegium Minus in 1156, which became the core of the Habsburg monarchy.
duchy-of-austria.o: In 1156 [[e:frederick-barbarossa|Frederick Barbarossa]] issued the Privilegium Minus, raising the [[s:margraviate-of-austria|Margraviate of Austria]] to a duchy for Henry II Jasomirgott, in compensation for giving up Bavaria. The new duchy received special privileges, including inheritance through female lines. [[e:vienna|Vienna]] became the ducal capital.
duchy-of-austria.r: The Babenbergs acquired Styria in 1192 and made [[e:vienna|Vienna]] a centre of Minnesang. After the line died out in 1246, Ottokar II of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] took [[e:austria|Austria]], but in 1278 Rudolf I of [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] defeated him at the Marchfeld. Rudolf IV founded the University of Vienna in 1365 and forged the Privilegium Maius to claim higher rank.
duchy-of-austria.e: In 1453 Emperor Frederick III, himself a [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]], confirmed the Privilegium Maius, raising [[e:austria|Austria]] to an archduchy. The [[s:archduchy-of-austria|Archduchy of Austria]] became the core of the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburg]] monarchy, the [[s:austrian-empire|Austrian Empire]] and, ultimately, the modern [[s:first-austrian-republic|Republic of Austria]].

delos.t: The sacred island of Apollo, independent from 314 to 167 BCE, when its sanctuary became a meeting place of kings and a hub of Aegean commerce.
delos.o: Delos, birthplace of Apollo and Artemis in Greek myth, had long been under Athenian control. In 314 BCE, with [[e:antigonus-i-monophthalmus|Antigonus]] I extending his power into the [[e:aegean|Aegean]], the Athenians were ousted and the Delians governed their island as an independent city, also hosting the [[s:nesiotic-league|Nesiotic League]].
delos.r: Independent Delos was run by an archon, council and assembly, while elected hieropoioi managed the sanctuary's lands, loans and treasures; their yearly inscribed accounts are among the richest economic records from antiquity. Kings of [[e:kingdom-of-macedon|Macedon]], [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and [[e:pergamon|Pergamon]] built porticoes and dedications. Banking and trade grew, drawing merchants from [[e:italy|Italy]] and the East.
delos.e: In 167 BCE [[e:rome|Rome]] handed Delos to [[s:athens|Athens]] and made it a free port to damage [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]]; the Delians were expelled to Achaea. Delos then boomed as a slave and grain market until sacked in 88 BCE by the forces of Mithridates VI and again by [[e:piracy|pirates]] in 69 BCE. It is now a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

da-chu.t: A puppet state set up by the Jurchen at Kaifeng in 1127 under the former Song chancellor Zhang Bangchang, which lasted only about a month.
da-chu.o: After the [[s:jin-dynasty-1115-1234|Jin dynasty]] (1115-1234) captured [[e:kaifeng|Kaifeng]] and deported the [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] emperors [[e:emperor-huizong|Huizong]] and Qinzong in the [[e:jingkang-incident|Jingkang incident]] of 1127, the [[e:jurchens|Jurchen]] wished to leave a friendly regime behind. They forced Zhang Bangchang, a Song chief minister, to accept the throne as emperor of Chu.
da-chu.r: Zhang Bangchang accepted reluctantly and did not behave as a full emperor, avoiding the throne hall and imperial forms of address. His regime existed only as long as [[e:jurchens|Jurchen]] troops remained in [[e:kaifeng|Kaifeng]].
da-chu.e: When the [[e:jurchens|Jurchen]] withdrew north, Zhang stepped down after about thirty-three days, invited the deposed Empress Meng to act as regent and supported Zhao Gou, who became the first emperor of [[s:southern-song|Southern Song]]. Zhang was soon ordered to commit suicide for having accepted the throne.

duchy-of-saxe-eisenberg.t: Tiny Ernestine duchy in eastern Thuringia whose single duke built a celebrated baroque palace chapel.
duchy-of-saxe-eisenberg.o: In the 1680 division of the inheritance of Ernest the Pious, his fifth son Christian received Eisenberg and its district, between Gera and Jena, founding the Duchy of Saxe-Eisenberg.
duchy-of-saxe-eisenberg.r: Christian rebuilt Christiansburg Palace in Eisenberg and added a richly decorated baroque chapel, still one of the finest in Thuringia. He was interested in alchemy and kept a small Lutheran court. The duchy was largely rural, with no independent policy of note.
duchy-of-saxe-eisenberg.e: Christian died in 1707 without a male heir. After a dispute among his relatives, Saxe-Eisenberg passed to [[s:duchy-of-saxe-gotha|Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg]]; in 1826 it went with Altenburg to the new [[s:duchy-of-saxe-altenburg|Duchy of Saxe-Altenburg]].

duchy-of-bavaria-straubing.t: A Wittelsbach inheritance that joined a Lower Bavarian duchy with the rich Low Country counties of Holland, Zeeland and Hainaut.
duchy-of-bavaria-straubing.o: After the death of Emperor Louis the Bavarian his sons divided their lands, and in 1353 a further partition created Bavaria-Straubing for William I and Albert I, together with the counties of [[s:county-of-hainaut|Hainaut]], Holland and [[s:county-of-zeeland|Zeeland]] inherited through their mother Margaret. Albert governed the whole inheritance from 1358, after his brother became insane.
duchy-of-bavaria-straubing.r: The dukes lived mostly in The Hague and governed Straubing through deputies, while in the [[s:county-of-holland|County of Holland]] they were drawn into the Hook and Cod factional wars. In Bavaria they built the ducal castle at Straubing from 1356. The [[e:danube|Danube]] plain of the Gäuboden around the town was among the most fertile farmland in Bavaria.
duchy-of-bavaria-straubing.e: After William VI died in 1417 his daughter Jacqueline of [[s:county-of-hainaut|Hainaut]] fought her uncle John III for the inheritance. John died in 1425, the [[e:low-countries|Low Countries]] passed to Philip the Good of [[s:duchy-of-burgundy|Burgundy]], and in 1429 the Straubing lands were divided among the [[s:duchy-of-bavaria-munich|Duchy of Bavaria-Munich]], the [[s:duchy-of-bavaria-ingolstadt|Duchy of Bavaria-Ingolstadt]] and the [[s:duchy-of-bavaria-landshut|Duchy of Bavaria-Landshut]].

despotate-of-serres.t: Realm of the despot Jovan Uglješa around Serres in eastern Macedonia, a successor of the Serbian Empire destroyed at the Maritsa in 1371.
despotate-of-serres.o: After Stefan Dušan's death in 1355, his widow, Empress Jelena, ruled Serres, the city he had taken from [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] in 1345. Around 1365 she handed power to the despot Jovan Uglješa, brother of Vukašin Mrnjavčević, who ruled eastern Macedonia from Serres.
despotate-of-serres.r: Uglješa governed a largely Greek population and was close to the monasteries of [[s:monastic-community-of-mount-athos|Mount Athos]], to which he made many grants. In 1368 he reconciled his church with the Patriarch of [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]], ending the schism caused by Dušan's patriarchate. Alarmed by the Ottoman conquest of Thrace, he sought allies against them.
despotate-of-serres.e: In 1371 Uglješa and his brother Vukašin led a large army against the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] and were killed at the Maritsa. [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] under Manuel II then retook Serres, which fell to the Ottomans in 1383.

dutch-gold-coast.t: Dutch forts on the coast of present-day Ghana, run from Elmina for nearly three centuries as a base for the gold and slave trades.
dutch-gold-coast.o: [[e:dutch|Dutch]] merchants began trading on the [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast]] in the 1590s, challenging the Portuguese monopoly. In 1612, at the invitation of the [[s:kingdom-of-asebu|Kingdom of Asebu]], they built Fort [[s:county-of-nassau|Nassau]] at Moree. The [[e:dutch-west-india-company|Dutch West India Company]] captured [[e:elmina|Elmina]] from the [[s:portuguese-gold-coast|Portuguese Gold Coast]] in 1637 and Axim in 1642, making Elmina its headquarters.
dutch-gold-coast.r: A director-general at [[e:elmina|Elmina]] governed a chain of forts and lodges along the coast, trading cloth, guns and metal goods for gold and, from the late 17th century, enslaved Africans shipped to [[e:dutch|Dutch]] colonies in the [[e:americas|Americas]]. Relations with inland powers such as [[s:denkyira|Denkyira]] and the [[s:ashanti-empire|Ashanti Empire]] were vital; [[e:ashanti-empire|Ashanti]] held the Elmina Note, a rent paid by the Dutch. In the 1830s and 1840s the Dutch recruited soldiers there for the [[e:east-indies|East Indies]] army.
dutch-gold-coast.e: In 1868 the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and British exchanged forts to consolidate their zones, and in 1872 the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]] handed its remaining posts to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]]. They became part of the [[s:gold-coast-colony|Gold Coast Colony]], and [[e:elmina|Elmina Castle]] is now a World Heritage Site.

duchy-of-ziebice.t: A Lower Silesian duchy, known in German as Münsterberg, that passed from the Piasts to the Poděbrady and Auersperg families before being sold to Prussia.
duchy-of-ziebice.o: In 1322 the sons of Duke Bolko I of Świdnica divided his lands, and Bolko II received Ziębice (Münsterberg), south of Wrocław, as a separate duchy split from the [[s:duchy-of-swidnica|Duchy of Świdnica]]. Bolko II resisted Bohemian overlordship longer than most Silesian dukes but did homage to King John of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] in 1336.
duchy-of-ziebice.r: The duchy was a modest agrarian territory of small towns and villages. The Piast line ended in 1428, and in 1456 the duchy passed to George of Poděbrady, later king of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]], whose sons held it as dukes of Münsterberg and introduced the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]]. In 1654 the emperor granted it to the Auersperg family, who seldom lived there.
duchy-of-ziebice.e: [[s:duchy-of-silesia|Silesia]] came under [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1742, though the Auerspergs kept the ducal title and estates. In 1791 they sold their remaining Silesian holdings to the Prussian crown, ending the duchy. The town, now Ziębice, became part of [[e:poland|Poland]] in 1945.

dardanian-kingdom.t: Kingdom of the Dardani in Kosovo and the upper Vardar, a persistent threat to Macedon that allied with Rome before being absorbed into Moesia.
dardanian-kingdom.o: The Dardani lived in the plains of Kosovo and around Scupi (Skopje) from at least the 4th century BCE. A Dardanian monarchy appears by the mid-4th century, and some historians count Bardylis, the Illyrian king who fought Philip II, as Dardanian.
dardanian-kingdom.r: Dardanian kings led a mixed Illyrian and Thracian population of farmers and herders. They raided Macedonia repeatedly and took advantage of the Celtic invasions of 279 BCE. King Longarus fought [[e:kingdom-of-macedon|Macedon]] in the 230s BCE, and his son Bato allied with [[e:rome|Rome]] against Philip V in 200 BCE, and King Monunius minted coins at Dyrrhachium. Roman writers described the Dardani as rough but musical.
dardanian-kingdom.e: [[e:rome|Rome]] fought the Dardani during the 1st century BCE, and [[e:marcus-licinius-crassus|Marcus Licinius Crassus]] brought them under control in 28 BCE. Their land became part of the province of Moesia and later the late Roman province of Dardania, birthplace of the emperor Justinian.

danish-india.t: Denmark's trading posts in India, led by Tranquebar on the Coromandel Coast, where the first Protestant missionaries in India began work in 1706.
danish-india.o: A Danish expedition under Ove Gjedde reached south [[e:india|India]], and in 1620 Raghunatha Nayak of Thanjavur granted the Danish [[e:east-india-company|East India Company]] the village of Tranquebar (Tharangambadi). The Danes built Fort Dansborg there, which became the centre of their Asian trade.
danish-india.r: Danish [[e:india|India]] was governed by the company and later the crown, trading in textiles, [[e:pepper|pepper]] and [[e:tea|tea]]. In 1706 the German missionaries Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau, sent by the Danish king, founded the Tranquebar Mission and translated the New Testament into Tamil. Serampore near Calcutta, acquired in 1755, became a centre of [[e:printing-press|printing]] and of Serampore College, founded by English Baptists. [[e:denmark|Denmark]] also claimed the Nicobar Islands.
danish-india.e: Overshadowed by [[s:british-raj|British India]] and loss-making, [[e:denmark|Denmark]] sold Tranquebar and Serampore to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 1845 and gave up its claim to the Nicobar Islands in 1868-1869. Fort Dansborg and Tranquebar's churches still stand.

daegaya.t: The leading Gaya kingdom of the 5th and 6th centuries, based at Goryeong, whose court produced the gayageum zither.
daegaya.o: Daegaya grew from Banpa-guk, a [[s:byeonhan|Byeonhan]] statelet in the Goryeong valley. Its founding legend names Ijinashi as first king, brother of Suro of [[s:geumgwan-gaya|Geumgwan Gaya]]. It rose to lead the northern Gaya states after Goguryeo's campaign of 400 weakened Gimhae.
daegaya.r: Daegaya's kings drew wealth from iron mines and controlled routes to the Seomjin river and the sea. In 479 King Haji sent an envoy to the [[s:southern-qi|Southern Qi]] court and received a title. Its royal cemetery at Jisan-dong includes tombs with dozens of sacrificed attendants. Under King Gasil the musician Ureuk composed twelve pieces for the newly devised gayageum.
daegaya.e: A marriage alliance with [[s:silla|Silla]] in 522 broke down, and in 562 Silla's general Isabu, with the young hwarang Sadaham, conquered Daegaya, ending the last Gaya state. Ureuk had already fled to Silla, preserving its music.

dongdan.t: The 'Eastern Khitan Kingdom' that the Liao set up in conquered Balhae, at first a semi-independent realm under the crown prince Yelü Bei.
dongdan.o: In 926 Abaoji, founder of the [[s:liao-dynasty|Liao dynasty]], destroyed [[s:balhae|Balhae]] after a short campaign and took its capital Huhan (Holhan). He renamed the country Dongdan and made his eldest son Yelü Bei its king, with his own court, officials and reign title, retaining many Balhae institutions.
dongdan.r: Dongdan was intended as a separate kingdom for the former [[s:balhae|Balhae]] population, partly governed by Balhae nobles. After Abaoji's death the throne of [[e:liao-dynasty|Liao]] went to Yelü Bei's brother Yelü Deguang, who distrusted him. Around 929 much of the population and the capital were moved west to Liaoyang, and in 930 Yelü Bei fled to the [[s:later-tang|Later Tang]].
dongdan.e: Thereafter Dongdan was little more than an administrative unit within [[e:liao-dynasty|Liao]], governed by Khitan appointees. It was formally abolished around 982 under Emperor Shengzong. Many [[s:balhae|Balhae]] refugees had meanwhile fled to [[s:goryeo|Goryeo]] or founded short-lived successor states such as [[s:dingan|Dingan]].

dutch-coromandel.t: The Dutch East India Company's trading posts on India's south-east coast, centred on Pulicat, a hub of the Asian textile trade.
dutch-coromandel.o: The [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] ([[e:dutch-east-india-company|VOC]]) arrived on the [[e:coromandel-coast|Coromandel Coast]] in the early 17th century and in 1610 obtained permission from the [[s:vijayanagara-empire|Vijayanagara]] rulers to build Fort Geldria at Pulicat. Further factories followed at Masulipatnam, Negapatnam, Sadras and Bimlipatnam, forming the governorate of Coromandel.
dutch-coromandel.r: [[e:coromandel-coast|Coromandel]] [[e:cotton|cotton]] textiles, printed and painted chintz above all, were the [[e:dutch-east-india-company|VOC's]] key goods for buying [[e:spice-trade|spices]] in [[s:indonesia|Indonesia]]. The company bought cloth from weavers through Indian merchants and also traded slaves during famines. Pulicat housed the governor and a mint. In 1690 the capital moved to Negapatnam, then back to Pulicat in 1781.
dutch-coromandel.e: British competition from Madras eroded [[e:dutch|Dutch]] trade, and the British occupied the posts during the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars. Under the [[e:anglo-dutch-treaty-of-1824|Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824]] the remaining settlements were transferred to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 1825.

duchy-of-nysa.t: Silesian duchy ruled by the bishops of Wrocław from Nysa, the Silesian Rome, a Catholic stronghold for over five centuries.
duchy-of-nysa.o: The [[e:bishop|bishops]] of Wrocław held the castellany of Nysa and Otmuchów from the 12th century. In 1290 Duke Henry IV Probus granted Bishop Thomas II full princely rights there, making the territory an episcopal duchy. Its bishops took the title Prince of Nysa and in 1342 accepted the overlordship of the [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Kingdom of Bohemia]].
duchy-of-nysa.r: The [[e:bishop|bishop]]-dukes ruled from Nysa and Otmuchów through officials and the estates. Nysa became a wealthy town of churches and convents, called the Silesian [[e:rome|Rome]]. After the [[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] spread in [[s:duchy-of-silesia|Silesia]], the bishops led the Counter-Reformation, and Archduke Charles of [[e:austria|Austria]], bishop from 1608, founded the [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] college Carolinum. The population was largely German-speaking.
duchy-of-nysa.e: In 1742 most of the duchy passed to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], which secularised it in 1810, while the southern part around Jeseník remained Austrian under the [[e:bishop|bishops]] until 1850. Nysa has been Polish since 1945.

democratic-republic-of-vietnam.t: The communist-led Vietnamese state proclaimed by Ho Chi Minh in 1945, which defeated France, fought the Vietnam War and reunified the country in 1976.
democratic-republic-of-vietnam.o: During the August Revolution of 1945 the [[e:viet-minh|Viet Minh]], a front led by the Indochinese Communist Party, seized power across much of [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]]. On 2 September 1945 Ho Chi Minh read the declaration of independence in Ba Dinh Square in [[e:hanoi|Hanoi]], proclaiming the Democratic [[s:republic-of-vietnam|Republic of Vietnam]].
democratic-republic-of-vietnam.r: The DRV fought [[e:france|France]] in the First [[e:indochina|Indochina]] War from 1946, winning at [[e:battle-of-dien-bien-phu|Dien Bien Phu]] in 1954. The [[s:republic-of-geneva|Geneva]] Accords left it in control of the north above the 17th parallel. It built a one-party socialist state with collectivised agriculture after a harsh land reform, backed by the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] and [[e:china|China]], and supported the southern insurgency through the Ho Chi Minh Trail against the [[s:republic-of-vietnam|Republic of Vietnam]] and the [[s:united-states|United States]].
democratic-republic-of-vietnam.e: After the [[e:paris|Paris]] Peace Accords of 1973 and the fall of Saigon in April 1975, the DRV merged with the [[s:republic-of-south-vietnam|Republic of South Vietnam]]. On 2 July 1976 the united country was proclaimed the [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Socialist Republic of Vietnam]].

dal-fiatach.t: Ruling dynasty of east County Down, centred on Downpatrick, which claimed to be the true Ulaid and held the Ulster kingship until 1177.
dal-fiatach.o: The Dál Fiatach were a dynasty of the [[s:kingdom-of-ulaid|Ulaid]] in what is now east County Down. They claimed descent from the ancient Ulaid royal line, and after the Ulaid were pushed east of the River Bann they became one of the two main powers in the Kingdom of Ulaid, with their stronghold at Dún Lethglaise, Downpatrick, associated with St Patrick's burial.
dal-fiatach.r: Dál Fiatach kings alternated the over-kingship of the [[s:kingdom-of-ulaid|Ulaid]] with the [[s:dal-naraidi|Dal nAraidi]]. Báetán mac Cairill, who died in 581, is said to have claimed authority as far as the [[s:isle-of-man|Isle of Man]] and [[e:scotland|Scotland]]. Fiachnae mac Demmáin fought for the kingship in the early 7th century. Their wealth lay in the fertile lands of Lecale and the Ards, and the monasteries of Bangor and Movilla lay nearby.
dal-fiatach.e: From the 11th century their kings were the Mac Duinn Sléibe, MacDunleavy. In 1177 the Anglo-Norman John de Courcy seized Downpatrick and defeated Ruaidrí Mac Duinn Sléibe, establishing the Anglo-Norman lordship of [[s:northern-ireland|Ulster]], later an earldom, and ending Dál Fiatach rule.

dungarpur-state.t: The senior Guhila Rajput state of the Vagad region in southern Rajasthan, from which Banswara split in the 16th century, ruled by Maharawals until 1948.
dungarpur-state.o: The Maharawals of Dungarpur claimed descent from the elder line of the Guhila dynasty of [[s:udaipur-state|Mewar]], said to have moved south into the Vagad hills in the late 12th century. The town of Dungarpur was founded in the 14th century and named after a local Bhil chief, Dungaria.
dungarpur-state.r: Vagad was a hilly, forested country with a large Bhil population. Rawal Udai Singh was killed fighting [[e:babur|Babur]] at Khanwa in 1527, after which his lands were divided between two sons, creating [[s:banswara-state|Banswara State]]. Dungarpur accepted Mughal and then [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] overlordship, and signed a treaty with the British in 1818. Its palaces are known for blue-grey stone and mirror work.
dungarpur-state.e: Maharawal Lakshman Singh joined the [[s:united-state-of-rajasthan|United State of Rajasthan]] in 1948, and Dungarpur is now a district of Rajasthan.

dulkadirids.t: A Turkmen beylik around Elbistan and Marash that served as the buffer, and the battleground, between the Mamluks and the Ottomans.
dulkadirids.o: In 1337 the [[e:mamluk|Mamluks]] recognised the [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] chief Zayn al-Din Karaja Bey as ruler of Elbistan and the surrounding uplands of the eastern [[e:taurus-mountains|Taurus]], creating a [[e:vassal|vassal]] state on their northern frontier.
dulkadirids.r: The Dulkadirids led pastoral [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] tribes, raised horses and controlled the passes between [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] and [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]]. Both [[e:mamluk|Mamluks]] and [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] tried to control them through marriage and by backing rival claimants. Shah Suwar rebelled against the Mamluks with Ottoman encouragement and was executed in [[e:cairo|Cairo]] in 1472. Ala al-Dawla Bozkurt, a long-reigning ruler, built in Marash and resisted the rising [[e:safavid-empire|Safavids]].
dulkadirids.e: When Ala al-Dawla failed to support the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] against the [[e:safavid-empire|Safavids]], [[e:selim-i|Selim I's]] army defeated and killed him in 1515. His nephew Ali Bey ruled as an Ottoman [[e:vassal|vassal]] until he was executed in 1522 and the [[e:beylik|beylik]] was annexed.

derdeship-of-tibesti.t: The office of the derde, paramount chief of the Teda people of the Tibesti mountains, an elected leader of a fiercely independent Saharan society.
derdeship-of-tibesti.o: The Teda, a branch of the Tubu peoples, have lived in the Tibesti mountains of northern [[e:chad|Chad]] and southern [[e:libya|Libya]] for centuries. By around 1700 they recognised a derde, a paramount chief chosen in rotation from leading families of the Tomaghra clan.
derdeship-of-tibesti.r: The derde acted mainly as judge and arbitrator among largely autonomous clans of [[e:camel|camel]] herders and oasis farmers, settling feuds through compensation. His power was moral rather than coercive. Teda raids reached across the [[e:sahara|Sahara]], and in the 19th century the [[s:senussi-order|Senussi Order]] gained influence through its lodges.
derdeship-of-tibesti.e: French troops occupied Tibesti in 1914, withdrew in 1916 and returned in 1929 to 1930, ending its independence. The derdeship survived as a traditional office in [[e:chad|Chad]]; the derde Oueddei Kichidemi's son Goukouni Oueddei became president of Chad in 1979.

duchy-of-brittany.t: The Celtic-speaking peninsula of western France, an independent-minded duchy for six centuries until its heiress Anne married two French kings.
duchy-of-brittany.o: After [[e:vikings|Viking]] occupation in the early 10th century, Alan Twisted Beard returned from exile in [[e:england|England]] and drove the Norse out, completing the reconquest with the victory at Trans in 939. He took the title of duke and made Nantes his base. The duchy's frontier with [[s:county-of-anjou|Anjou]] and [[s:duchy-of-normandy|Normandy]] remained contested for generations.
duchy-of-brittany.r: Brittany kept its own customs, coinage, Estates and courts, with Breton spoken in the west and Gallo and French in the east. The [[s:county-of-montfort|Montfort]] and [[s:county-of-blois|Blois]] families fought the War of the Breton Succession (1341–1364), won by John IV at Auray. Under the Montfort dukes the duchy prospered from salt, linen and shipping and was nearly sovereign.
duchy-of-brittany.e: [[e:francis-ii|Francis II's]] defeat at Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier in 1488 sealed French dominance. His daughter Anne of Brittany married Charles VIII and then Louis XII, and the Edict of Union of 1532 joined the duchy to the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]]. When the Dauphin, its last duke, became Henry II in 1547, the title merged with the crown.

duchy-of-eastern-zhou.t: A breakaway duchy east of Luoyang, created in a family quarrel in 367 BCE, which outlasted the Zhou kings by seven years before falling to Qin.
duchy-of-eastern-zhou.o: After the death of Duke Wei of the [[s:duchy-of-western-zhou|Duchy of Western Zhou]], his younger son Gen, backed by the [[s:state-of-zhao|State of Zhao]] and the [[s:state-of-han|State of Han]], set himself up at Gong (modern Gongyi, Henan) in 367 BCE as Duke Hui of [[s:eastern-zhou|Eastern Zhou]], splitting the remaining royal domain in two.
duchy-of-eastern-zhou.r: The duchy was a cluster of towns along the Luo River whose rulers competed with [[s:western-zhou|Western Zhou]] for influence over the king and survived by diplomacy with the great powers. Little is known of its internal life.
duchy-of-eastern-zhou.e: After the fall of [[s:western-zhou|Western Zhou]] in 256 BCE, the [[s:eastern-zhou|Eastern Zhou]] ruler continued to plot with other states against the [[s:state-of-qin|State of Qin]]. In 249 BCE [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin's]] chancellor Lü Buwei led an army that annexed the duchy, extinguishing the last political remnant of the Zhou royal house.

datia-state.t: A Bundela Rajput state of Bundelkhand, famed for the seven-storey palace built by Bir Singh Deo of Orchha.
datia-state.o: Datia was granted in 1626 to Bhagwan Rao, a son of Bir Singh Deo of [[s:orchha-state|Orchha]], making it a branch of the Orchha State. Bir Singh Deo had already built the great palace at Datia, completed around 1614.
datia-state.r: The Maharajas served the [[e:mughal-empire|Mughals]] as mansabdars and later contended with the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]]. In 1804 Datia made a treaty with the [[e:east-india-company|East India Company]] and became a salute state of the [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] Agency. Its economy rested on agriculture, and the town grew around the palace and the Pitambara Peeth temple.
datia-state.e: Datia joined [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] in 1948 and Madhya Pradesh in 1956. The Datia Palace, a landmark of Bundela architecture, survives in the town.

duchy-of-lower-lorraine.t: The northern half of old Lotharingia, a duchy over the Low Countries whose title was carried by Godfrey of Bouillon and survived in Brabant.
duchy-of-lower-lorraine.o: In 959 Archbishop Bruno of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-cologne|Cologne]] divided the [[s:duchy-of-lotharingia|Duchy of Lotharingia]], creating a separate duchy for the lands of the lower Meuse, Scheldt and [[e:rhine|Rhine]]. The German kings appointed its dukes, including the Carolingian Charles, brother of the West Frankish king [[e:lothair-i|Lothair]], from 977 to 991.
duchy-of-lower-lorraine.r: Ducal power was always limited, since counts such as those of Louvain, [[s:county-of-hainaut|Hainaut]], [[s:county-of-namur|Namur]], Holland and [[s:duchy-of-limburg|Limburg]] and the prince-[[e:bishop|bishops]] of [[s:prince-bishopric-of-liege|Liège]] and [[s:lordship-of-utrecht|Utrecht]] built their own principalities. The emperors used the office to reward loyal families: Godfrey the Bearded's house held it, and Godfrey of [[s:duchy-of-bouillon|Bouillon]] was duke before leading the [[e:first-crusade|First Crusade]] in 1096.
duchy-of-lower-lorraine.e: From 1106 the title was disputed between the counts of Louvain and [[s:duchy-of-limburg|Limburg]]. At the Diet of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-hall|Schwäbisch Hall]] in 1190 Emperor Henry VI limited the duke's authority to his own lands, and the Louvain dukes thereafter ruled as dukes of [[s:duchy-of-brabant|Brabant]], keeping the title duke of Lothier.

duchy-of-saxe-lauenburg.t: A small north German duchy on the lower Elbe that kept the Saxon ducal title for centuries but lost the electoral vote to its Wittenberg cousins.
duchy-of-saxe-lauenburg.o: When the Ascanian dukes of Saxony divided their lands, the younger line received the scattered northern territories around Lauenburg on the Elbe and Ratzeburg, formally separated from the [[s:duchy-of-saxe-wittenberg|Duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg]] in 1296. The [[e:golden-bull-of-1356|Golden Bull of 1356]] gave the [[e:saxons|Saxon]] electoral vote to Wittenberg rather than Lauenburg, leaving Lauenburg a minor duchy.
duchy-of-saxe-lauenburg.r: The dukes were often in debt and pledged lands, including the Vierlande and Bergedorf, to [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck|Lübeck]] and [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]]. The estates of the duchy held real power, and the old salt road from Lüneburg to [[e:lubeck|Lübeck]] crossed its territory. The duchy turned Lutheran in the 16th century. When the Ascanian line died out in 1689, the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg seized it.
duchy-of-saxe-lauenburg.e: Lauenburg passed with the [[s:electorate-of-hanover|Electorate of Hanover]] and in 1815 to [[e:denmark|Denmark]]. After the war of 1864 it went to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], whose king ruled it in personal union until it was incorporated into the [[s:kingdom-of-prussia|Kingdom of Prussia]] in 1876. [[e:otto-von-bismarck|Bismarck]] later received the honorary title Duke of Lauenburg in 1890.

duchy-of-benevento.t: Southern Lombard duchy and later principality that outlived the Lombard Kingdom by three centuries, a centre of southern Italian culture.
duchy-of-benevento.o: [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] warriors under Zotto established themselves at Beneventum in Campania around 571, perhaps first as soldiers in Byzantine pay. Under Arechis I the duchy expanded across most of southern [[e:italy|Italy]], apart from the Byzantine coastal cities, Calabria and Apulia's heel.
duchy-of-benevento.r: Benevento was effectively independent of [[s:commune-of-pavia|Pavia]]; Duke Grimoald I even became [[e:king-of-the-lombards|King of the Lombards]] in 662. When [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]] took the north in 774, Arechis II took the title of prince and claimed the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] heritage, building the church of Santa Sofia. The duchy developed the Beneventan script and was a cultural centre linked to Monte Cassino. Civil war in 849 split it into Benevento and [[s:principality-of-salerno|Salerno]], and [[s:principality-of-capua|Capua]] later broke away.
duchy-of-benevento.e: Weakened by Arab raids, [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]] and Normans, the principality shrank. In 1051 the city placed itself under [[e:papacy|Pope]] Leo IX, and when the last prince, Landulf VI, died in 1077, Benevento became a papal enclave, while its lands passed to the Normans.

daunians.t: Iapygian people of northern Apulia, known for their carved stone stelae and painted pottery, who allied with Rome against the Samnites.
daunians.o: The Daunians were the northernmost of the Iapygian peoples of Apulia, settled in the Tavoliere plain and the Gargano from the early 1st millennium BCE. Greek legend made the hero Diomedes, returning from Troy, the founder of Arpi and other towns, a story the Daunians themselves seem to have adopted.
daunians.r: Daunian society was organised in large settlements such as Arpi, Canusium, Salapia and Sipontum, with chieftains whose wealth appears in their tombs. Between the 7th and 6th centuries BCE they set up hundreds of anthropomorphic stone stelae near Sipontum, carved with weapons, ornaments and scenes of daily life. Their matt-painted pottery is distinctive. They farmed the plain, raised horses and traded across the Adriatic.
daunians.e: During the Samnite Wars the Daunian towns sided with [[e:rome|Rome]]; Livy records alliances in 318 BCE, and Rome founded Luceria in 314 BCE. Arpi went over to [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]] after [[e:battle-of-cannae|Cannae]] in 216 BCE and was punished when retaken. The towns became Roman municipia after the Social War, and Daunian identity faded into Roman Apulia.

dian-kingdom.t: A bronze-working kingdom around Lake Dian in Yunnan, whose tombs at Shizhaishan show lively scenes of ritual, war and daily life cast on cowrie containers.
dian-kingdom.o: Dian grew among the farming and fishing peoples around Lake Dian, near Kunming. Tradition holds that the Chu general Zhuang Qiao reached the lake around 279 BCE and, cut off by the [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] conquest of Chu's western lands, made himself king of Dian, but the kingdom's culture was overwhelmingly local.
dian-kingdom.r: Dian's elite were buried at Shizhaishan and Lijiashan with bronze drums, weapons and [[e:cowrie-shell|cowrie]]-shell containers topped with miniature figures showing sacrifices, weaving, markets and battles. These reveal a stratified society of farmers, herders and craftsmen, with women prominent in ritual. Dian controlled routes south towards South-East [[e:asia|Asia]] and west to [[s:myanmar|Burma]].
dian-kingdom.e: In 109 BCE the [[s:han-dynasty|Han Dynasty]] sent an army, and the king of Dian surrendered. Han created Yizhou [[e:commandery|Commandery]] but let the king keep his title, granting him a gold seal that was found at Shizhaishan in 1956. Dian culture faded into Han provincial life during the 1st century CE.

dinh-dynasty.t: The dynasty that reunited Vietnam after the anarchy of the Twelve Warlords and named the country Dai Co Viet, with its capital at Hoa Lu.
dinh-dynasty.o: Dinh Bo Linh, a local leader from Hoa Lu in present-day Ninh Binh, defeated the rival warlords one by one and in 968 proclaimed himself emperor, Dinh Tien Hoang. He named the state [[s:early-le-dynasty|Dai Co Viet]] and built a fortified capital among the limestone hills at Hoa Lu.
dinh-dynasty.r: Dinh Tien Hoang ruled with harsh punishments to restore order, organised the army into units, and gave Buddhist monks official ranks. He sent tribute to the [[e:song-dynasty|Song dynasty]], which recognised him as a [[e:vassal|vassal]] king in 973, while using the title of emperor at home. Coins called Thai Binh were issued, among the first Vietnamese coinage.
dinh-dynasty.e: In 979 Dinh Tien Hoang and his eldest son were assassinated, leaving the child Dinh Phe De on the throne. With a [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] invasion looming, the commander Le Hoan took power in 980 with the support of the queen mother, founding the [[s:early-le-dynasty|Early Le dynasty]]. Temples to the Dinh kings stand at Hoa Lu.

duchy-of-kozle.t: A minor Upper Silesian Piast duchy around the Oder town of Koźle, carved from the lands of the dukes of Bytom in the early 14th century.
duchy-of-kozle.o: Koźle belonged to the Upper Silesian lands of the [[s:duchy-of-bytom|Duchy of Bytom]], ruled by a branch of the Silesian Piasts. Around 1303 it was set apart for a junior member of the dynasty, beginning a short history as a separate duchy, though for much of the period it was held together with Bytom itself.
duchy-of-kozle.r: Like other small Silesian duchies, Koźle was a fortified market town on the Oder with surrounding villages, settled partly by German colonists under German town law. In 1327 its duke did homage to King John of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]], making the duchy a fief of the Kingdom of [[e:bohemia|Bohemia]]. Little else is recorded of its government.
duchy-of-kozle.e: The Bytom-Koźle line ended in 1355, and after a dispute Koźle passed to the dukes of the [[s:duchy-of-olesnica|Duchy of Oleśnica]], who held it until the late 15th century. It later reverted to the Bohemian crown, followed [[s:duchy-of-silesia|Silesia]] to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1742 and became part of [[e:poland|Poland]] in 1945.

duchy-of-lucca.t: A small Tuscan duchy created in 1815 for the former queen of Etruria, Maria Luisa of Bourbon, and absorbed by Tuscany in 1847.
duchy-of-lucca.o: The [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] gave [[s:republic-of-lucca|Lucca]] to Maria Luisa of [[e:spain|Spain]], former regent of the [[s:kingdom-of-etruria|Kingdom of Etruria]], as compensation for losing [[s:duchy-of-parma-and-piacenza|Parma]], which went to [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] widow Marie Louise. Maria Luisa took possession in 1817 and ruled until her death in 1824.
duchy-of-lucca.r: Maria Luisa revived court life, built roads and the aqueduct of [[s:republic-of-lucca|Lucca]] and encouraged the arts. Her son Charles Louis, Duke Charles I, ruled from 1824, an extravagant and unpredictable prince who spent much time abroad and left government to ministers. The duchy was small, conservative and dependent on [[e:austria|Austria]].
duchy-of-lucca.e: Under the [[e:vienna|Vienna]] settlement, the [[e:house-of-bourbon|Bourbons]] were to return to [[s:duchy-of-parma-and-piacenza|Parma]] when Marie Louise died. In October 1847, shortly before her death, Charles Louis handed [[s:republic-of-lucca|Lucca]] to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Grand Duchy of Tuscany]] and later became Duke of Parma.

dhami-state.t: A small Rajput hill state near Shimla, remembered for the Dhami firing of 1939, when its ruler's forces fired on protesters of the Praja Mandal.
dhami-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to around 1500, but little is reliably known of its origins. Its seat was at Halog.
dhami-state.r: Dhami was a small hill state, occupied by the Gurkhas in the early 19th century and restored under British protection after 1815. In July 1939 a march by the Dhami Prem Pracharini Sabha and Praja Mandal activists demanding reforms was fired on near Halog, killing protesters, an event remembered in the movement for democratic rule in the hill states.
dhami-state.e: Dhami merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now part of Shimla district.

dompu-sultanate.t: A small sultanate in eastern Sumbawa, conquered by Majapahit in the 14th century and lasting into independent Indonesia.
dompu-sultanate.o: Dompo is listed in the Javanese Nagarakretagama among the dependencies of [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit]], and an expedition to it is recorded in the mid-14th century. The register dates the sultanate from 1545, when its rulers are said to have adopted [[e:islam|Islam]], influenced by [[s:gowa-sultanate|Makassar]] and Bima.
dompu-sultanate.r: Dompu was an agricultural state of [[e:rice|rice]] and horses, whose people spoke the Bima language. It lived in the shadow of its larger neighbour Bima and of Gowa, and from the 17th century of the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]], which made treaties with the Sumbawa rulers. The eruption of Mount [[s:kingdom-of-tambora|Tambora]] in 1815 devastated the region, destroying the neighbouring kingdoms of Tambora and Pekat.
dompu-sultanate.e: Dompu remained a self-governing state under [[e:dutch|Dutch]] rule into the 20th century. After [[e:indonesian-independence|Indonesian independence]] the sultanates of Sumbawa were dissolved, Dompu becoming a regency of West Nusa Tenggara in 1958.

duklja.t: Medieval Serbian principality and kingdom on the Montenegrin coast, the first South Slav state whose ruler received a crown from the pope.
duklja.o: Duklja, named after the Roman town of Doclea, emerged among [[e:serbs|Serbs]] of the southern Adriatic hinterland. It appears in the 10th century under Byzantine overlordship; Prince Jovan Vladimir ruled it until his murder in 1016, and is venerated as a saint.
duklja.r: Around 1040 Stefan Vojislav threw off Byzantine control and defeated a Byzantine army near Bar in 1042. His son Mihailo I extended rule over [[s:grand-principality-of-serbia|Raška]], [[s:travunia|Travunia]] and [[s:zachlumia|Zachlumia]] and received a royal crown from [[e:papacy|Pope]] Gregory VII in 1077. His son Constantine Bodin briefly ruled a wide realm, and under him Bar became an archbishopric in 1089. The state lay on the Catholic-[[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] divide, with [[e:latin|Latin]] coastal towns such as [[s:commune-of-kotor|Kotor]] and Bar.
duklja.e: Dynastic strife after Bodin's death around 1101 let [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] and [[s:grand-principality-of-serbia|Raška]] intervene. Stefan Nemanja of the Grand [[s:principality-of-serbia|Principality of Serbia]] annexed it around 1186, and the region, later called Zeta, became a Nemanjić [[e:appanage|appanage]].

dyme.t: Westernmost city of Achaea and one of the four cities that refounded the Achaean League in 280 BCE.
dyme.o: Dyme lay on the coastal plain of western Achaea, near Cape Araxos, facing the Ionian Sea. It was one of the twelve cities of Achaea, formed in the early Iron Age from local villages.
dyme.r: Little is known of its government before the Hellenistic age. In 280 BCE Dyme, [[s:patrae|Patrae]], Tritaea and Pharae revived the [[s:achaean-league|Achaean League]], which grew into a major power. Exposed to the west, Dyme was sacked in 208 BCE by a Roman force during the First Macedonian War, its people enslaved and later ransomed by Philip V of the [[s:antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia|Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia]].
dyme.e: Dyme passed under Roman control in 146 BCE. In 67 BCE [[e:pompey|Pompey]] resettled defeated Cilician [[e:piracy|pirates]] there, and it received a Roman colony c. 44 BCE before Augustus placed it under [[s:patrae|Patrae]].

despotate-of-the-morea.t: Late Byzantine principality based at Mistras in the Peloponnese, a last flowering of Byzantine culture and the home of the philosopher Plethon.
despotate-of-the-morea.o: [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] regained Mistras, Monemvasia and the [[e:mani|Mani]] in 1262 from the [[s:principality-of-achaea|Principality of Achaea]] and slowly expanded from there. In 1349 John VI Kantakouzenos made his son Manuel Kantakouzenos despot of the province, giving it a permanent ruler. From 1383 it passed to members of the Palaiologos family, beginning with Theodore I.
despotate-of-the-morea.r: Despots, usually younger sons of the emperor, ruled from Mistras, whose churches with their frescoes survive. They gradually conquered the Frankish principality, completing it in 1432. Greek, Albanian and Slavic farmers formed the population. The philosopher Gemistos Plethon proposed radical reforms there. The Hexamilion wall across the Isthmus was rebuilt in 1415 against the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]].
despotate-of-the-morea.e: After the fall of [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] in 1453, the despots Thomas and Demetrios Palaiologos quarrelled and faced Albanian revolts. [[e:mehmed-ii|Mehmed II]] conquered the Morea in 1460, the last Greek fortresses falling in 1461.

despotate-of-melnik.t: Rhodope principality of Alexius Slav, a relative of the Asen tsars, who ruled from Melnik as an ally of the Latin crusaders.
despotate-of-melnik.o: After the death of [[e:tsar|Tsar]] Kaloyan in 1207, his relative Alexius Slav refused to recognise the new tsar Boril and seized the Rhodope region. He made Melnik, in the Struma valley, his capital and held Tsepina and other fortresses.
despotate-of-melnik.r: Alexius Slav allied with the [[s:latin-empire|Latin Empire of Constantinople]], marrying a daughter of Emperor Henry of [[s:county-of-flanders|Flanders]], and bore the title of despot. He built churches and a residence at Melnik, whose monastery of the Mother of God Spileotissa has a charter from him, and he fought Boril and the Epirotes.
despotate-of-melnik.e: After 1228 he disappears from the record. The Bulgarian tsar Ivan Asen II absorbed his lands around 1230, after defeating Epirus at Klokotnitsa, into the [[s:second-bulgarian-empire|Second Bulgarian Empire]].

datarpur-state.t: A small Rajput hill principality in the Shivalik foothills of the Punjab, swallowed by Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire in 1818.
datarpur-state.o: Datarpur was one of the petty [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] states of the outer Himalayan hills between the [[e:beas|Beas]] and [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]], in what is now Hoshiarpur district. Its ruling family belonged to the Dadwal clan and traced kinship to neighbouring hill houses such as those of [[s:kangra-state|Kangra]] and [[s:guler-state|Guler]].
datarpur-state.r: Little is recorded of its internal history. Like its neighbours it was a small chieftaincy of hill villages and forts, paying tribute in turn to the [[e:mughal-empire|Mughals]], to Raja Sansar Chand of [[s:kangra-state|Kangra]] and then to the [[e:sikhism|Sikhs]] as their power grew in the late 18th century.
datarpur-state.e: In 1818 [[e:ranjit-singh|Maharaja Ranjit Singh]] annexed Datarpur to the [[s:sikh-empire|Sikh Empire]], leaving the family a [[e:jagir|jagir]]. The area passed to the British with the Jalandhar Doab in 1846.
