duchy-of-neopatras.t: Catalan duchy in southern Thessaly, created on the ruins of the Greek Principality of Thessaly and ruled with Athens by the kings of Sicily and Aragon.
duchy-of-neopatras.o: After the Catalan Company conquered the [[s:duchy-of-athens|Duchy of Athens]] in 1311, it pushed north into Thessaly. When John II Doukas of the [[s:principality-of-thessaly|Principality of Thessaly]] died without heirs in 1318, the Catalans occupied the south of the region with its capital Neopatras (modern Ypati) and organised it as a duchy in 1319.
duchy-of-neopatras.r: Neopatras was held together with [[s:athens|Athens]] by the Aragonese kings of [[e:sicily|Sicily]], who appointed vicars-general such as Alfonso Fadrique to govern it. A small Catalan military class ruled over [[e:greeks|Greeks]] and Vlachs, following the customs of Barcelona. In 1379-1380 the duchies passed to Peter IV of [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]], who called the Acropolis the most beautiful jewel in the world.
duchy-of-neopatras.e: Attacks by the Navarrese Company, the Florentine Nerio Acciaioli and the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] broke the Catalan hold. Neopatras fell around 1390, and the Ottomans took Thessaly in the 1390s.

duchy-of-niemodlin.t: A small Upper Silesian Piast duchy around the castle of Niemodlin, split from the Duchy of Opole in 1313 and reabsorbed in 1382.
duchy-of-niemodlin.o: On the death of Duke Bolko I of Opole in 1313, his lands were divided among his sons. Bolesław the Elder received Niemodlin (Falkenberg), a castle town west of Opole, as his own duchy. He was close to the Bohemian court and in 1327 did homage to King John of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]].
duchy-of-niemodlin.r: The duchy consisted of Niemodlin and its surrounding villages, settled partly under German law, with the castle as the ducal residence. Its dukes depended on Bohemian patronage and on their cousins in the [[s:duchy-of-opole|Duchy of Opole]]. Little is recorded of its internal government.
duchy-of-niemodlin.e: The Niemodlin line died out with Duke Henry in 1382, and the duchy returned to the [[s:duchy-of-opole|Duchy of Opole]]. Niemodlin later passed through various Silesian lords, went to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1742 and became part of [[e:poland|Poland]] in 1945.

diocese-of-hispania.t: The late Roman administrative unit that grouped the provinces of Iberia and north-west Africa under a single vicar based at Mérida.
diocese-of-hispania.o: The diocese was created in [[e:diocletian|Diocletian's]] reforms around 297 to 314, grouping the provinces of [[s:hispania-baetica|Baetica]], [[s:lusitania|Lusitania]], [[s:carthaginiensis|Carthaginiensis]], [[s:gallaecia|Gallaecia]] and [[s:hispania-tarraconensis|Tarraconensis]] with [[s:mauretania-tingitana|Mauretania Tingitana]] across the Strait. The [[s:balearica|Balearica]] province was added around 369. It formed part of the Praetorian Prefecture of the [[e:gauls|Gauls]].
diocese-of-hispania.r: A vicarius at Emerita Augusta oversaw the provincial governors, mainly in justice and taxation, while separate officers commanded the army. Hispania was largely peaceful in the 4th century, a land of rich villas and cities. [[e:christianity|Christianity]] grew strong, as the Council of Elvira shows, and the emperor [[e:theodosius-i|Theodosius I]] came from Cauca in the north.
diocese-of-hispania.e: In 409 [[e:vandals|Vandals]], [[s:alans|Alans]] and [[s:suebi|Suebi]] crossed the [[e:pyrenees|Pyrenees]] during the usurpation of Constantine III and his general Gerontius. [[e:rome|Rome]] partly restored control with Visigothic help, but the diocese effectively broke up as barbarian kingdoms took over.

duchy-of-brno.t: One of the Moravian appanage duchies held by junior Přemyslid princes, centred on Brno, until Moravia was reunited as a margraviate.
duchy-of-brno.o: Duke Bretislaus I of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] arranged [[s:margraviate-of-moravia|Moravia]] as a domain for junior members of the Přemyslid dynasty. After his death in 1055, his sons divided it; Conrad I received the Brno portion, centred on the castle of Brno (Brünn) in southern [[e:moravia|Moravia]], while Olomouc and later Znojmo formed separate [[e:appanage|appanages]].
duchy-of-brno.r: The princes of Brno owed allegiance to the senior duke in [[e:prague|Prague]] but frequently joined in the dynasty's feuds; Conrad I himself briefly became Duke of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] in 1092. Brno grew as a castle and market centre. Little is known in detail of its administration, which followed the Bohemian castle system.
duchy-of-brno.e: In the late 12th century the Moravian [[e:appanage|appanages]] were absorbed. Around 1182 [[s:margraviate-of-moravia|Moravia]] was declared a margraviate directly subject to the emperor, and by about 1197 Vladislaus Henry united the Moravian lands under his rule. Brno later became the capital of the Margraviate of [[e:moravia|Moravia]].

dara-sultanate.t: One of the seven Muslim states of medieval Abyssinia named by Arab writers, a small principality tributary to the Ethiopian emperors.
dara-sultanate.o: Dara is known only from brief mentions, chiefly by the 14th-century Arab writer [[e:al-umari|al-Umari]], who listed it among the seven Muslim kingdoms of Abyssinia alongside [[e:ifat-sultanate|Ifat]], [[s:sultanate-of-dawaro|Dawaro]], [[s:arababni|Arababni]], [[s:hadiya-sultanate|Hadiya]], [[s:sharkha-sultanate|Sharkha]] and [[e:bale|Bale]]. It lay in the south-eastern [[e:ethiopian-highlands|Ethiopian highlands]], probably near Bale.
dara-sultanate.r: [[e:al-umari|Al-Umari]] describes it as the smallest and poorest of the seven states, with a modest army and an economy of farming and herding. Like its neighbours it paid tribute to the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]] after the campaigns of [[e:amda-seyon-i|Amda Seyon]] in the 1330s.
dara-sultanate.e: Dara disappears from the record in the 15th century, absorbed into neighbouring provinces and later overrun during the wars of Adal and the [[e:oromo-migrations|Oromo migrations]].

duchy-of-glad.t: Duchy in the Banat described in the Gesta Hungarorum as resisting the conquering Hungarians around 900; its existence is debated.
duchy-of-glad.o: The main source is the Gesta Hungarorum, written by an anonymous notary around 1200. It says Glad, who came from Vidin, ruled the land between the Mureș, the Tisza and the [[e:danube|Danube]], with Cumans, Bulgarians and Vlachs, from the fortress of Keve (Kovin).
duchy-of-glad.r: Nothing is known of its government beyond the Gesta, which claims Glad fought the Hungarians with Cuman, Bulgarian and Vlach forces before being defeated and submitting. Historians disagree on whether he was a real ruler, perhaps a Bulgarian governor, or a figure invented from later place-names.
duchy-of-glad.e: The Gesta says the Hungarians took his lands, which then passed to the [[s:principality-of-hungary|Principality of Hungary]]. The same source makes Ahtum, of the [[s:duchy-of-ahtum|Duchy of Ahtum]], his descendant.

duchy-of-slutsk.t: A Ruthenian duchy in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, ruled by the Olelkovich princes and famous for resisting Tatar raids.
duchy-of-slutsk.o: In 1395 Vytautas removed Volodymyr Olgerdovich from the [[s:principality-of-kiev|Principality of Kiev]] and gave him Slutsk and Kapyl in compensation. Volodymyr's descendants, the Olelkovich princes, held Slutsk as a hereditary duchy within the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]] for two centuries.
duchy-of-slutsk.r: The Olelkovich princes were among the greatest [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] [[e:magnates|magnates]] of the grand duchy, with their own court, troops and towns. In 1506 the regent Anastasia of Slutsk defended the town against a [[e:tatars|Tatar]] siege. The princes built churches and monasteries, and Slutsk became a centre of Orthodox learning and crafts.
duchy-of-slutsk.e: The male line of the Olelkovich princes died out in 1592. Through the marriage of the heiress Sophia Olelkovich to Janusz Radziwill, the duchy passed to the Radziwill family, who held it as a private estate. Slutsk later became famous for its woven [[e:silk|silk]] sashes.

donetsk-krivoy-rog-soviet-republic.t: A Bolshevik republic of the Donbas and Kryvyi Rih industrial regions, proclaimed in 1918 as part of Soviet Russia rather than Ukraine.
donetsk-krivoy-rog-soviet-republic.o: In February 1918 a regional congress of soviets in Kharkiv proclaimed the Donetsk-Krivoy Rog Soviet Republic over the [[e:coal|coal]] and iron districts of eastern and southern [[e:ukraine|Ukraine]]. Its leader, Fyodor Sergeyev, known as Artyom, argued that the industrial region belonged economically with [[e:russia|Russia]] rather than with the [[s:ukrainian-peoples-republic|Ukrainian People's Republic]].
donetsk-krivoy-rog-soviet-republic.r: The republic had a council of people's commissars in Kharkiv and tried to nationalise mines and factories, but it existed for only a few weeks. Its separate status was opposed by Bolsheviks who backed a single [[s:ukrainian-peoples-republic-of-soviets|Soviet Ukraine]], and [[e:moscow|Moscow]] did not formally recognise it as distinct from [[e:ukraine|Ukraine]].
donetsk-krivoy-rog-soviet-republic.e: After the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, German and Austro-Hungarian forces advanced into the [[e:donbas|Donbas]]. The government retreated to Luhansk and beyond, and by spring 1918 the republic was dissolved into [[s:ukrainian-peoples-republic-of-soviets|Soviet Ukraine]]'s structures, with its territory occupied by the [[e:central-powers|Central Powers]].

dal-naraidi.t: Leading kingdom of the Cruthin in south Antrim, whose king Congal Cáech fought for the high kingship and fell at Mag Rath in 637.
dal-naraidi.o: The Dál nAraidi were the leading dynasty of the Cruthin, a people of east [[s:northern-ireland|Ulster]] distinguished in early Irish sources from the [[s:kingdom-of-ulaid|Ulaid]] proper. By the 6th century they held south and central County Antrim, with their royal centre in Mag Line near the town of Antrim, and they competed with the [[s:dal-fiatach|Dal Fiatach]] for the kingship of the Kingdom of Ulaid.
dal-naraidi.r: Fiachnae mac Báetáin, who died in 626, became king of the [[s:kingdom-of-ulaid|Ulaid]] and is said to have campaigned in [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]]. Congal Cáech, king of the Ulaid and briefly claimant to the kingship of Tara, allied with [[s:dal-riata|Dál Riata]] but was defeated and killed by Domnall mac Áedo at Mag Rath in 637. St Comgall, founder of the monastery of Bangor, belonged to this people.
dal-naraidi.e: After Mag Rath their power declined, though their kings still held the [[s:kingdom-of-ulaid|Ulaid]] kingship at times until the 10th century. Pressure from [[e:vikings|Viking]] raiders, the Uí Néill and the [[s:dal-fiatach|Dal Fiatach]] reduced them, and by the 12th century their lands passed under Anglo-Norman and Ua Néill rule.

danish-greenland.t: Greenland as a Danish colony, from the missionary Hans Egede's arrival in 1721 to its integration into the Danish realm in 1953.
danish-greenland.o: Hoping to find the lost Norse colonists, the Norwegian priest Hans Egede sailed to Greenland in 1721 with the support of [[s:denmark-norway|Denmark-Norway]] and founded a mission and trading post, moving it to Godthåb (Nuuk) in 1728. Danish trading stations then spread along the west coast.
danish-greenland.r: From 1776 the Royal Greenland Trade [[e:departement|Department]] held a monopoly on trade, keeping the island closed to outsiders. The Inuit population lived by seal hunting, while the Danes bought skins, blubber and later cod. Lutheran and Moravian missions converted most Greenlanders. When [[e:norway|Norway]] was ceded to [[e:sweden|Sweden]] in 1814, Greenland stayed Danish, and in 1933 the Permanent Court of International Justice rejected Norway's claim to East Greenland.
danish-greenland.e: During the German occupation of [[e:denmark|Denmark]] the [[s:united-states|United States]] protected Greenland and built bases there. In 1953 a new Danish constitution ended colonial status and made Greenland an integral part of the [[s:kingdom-of-denmark|Kingdom of Denmark]]. Home rule followed in 1979 and self-government in 2009.

duchy-of-tuscia.t: Lombard duchy of Tuscany, centred on Lucca, whose duke Desiderius rose to become the last king of the Lombards.
duchy-of-tuscia.o: After the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombards]] occupied most of [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]] in the 570s, the region was organised under dukes, with [[s:republic-of-lucca|Lucca]] as the chief seat. Smaller duchies existed at [[s:clusium|Chiusi]] and elsewhere, but Lucca, on the route to [[e:rome|Rome]] later called the Via Francigena, emerged as the dominant centre.
duchy-of-tuscia.r: Little is known of the early dukes. Documents from [[s:republic-of-lucca|Lucca]], unusually rich for the 8th century, show a society of [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] landowners, churches and notaries, and Duke Walpert appears in the early 8th century. The Lombard nobleman [[e:desiderius|Desiderius]] held authority in [[s:march-of-tuscany|Tuscia]] before becoming king in 756. Lucca minted gold coins and was the main town of Lombard [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]].
duchy-of-tuscia.e: After [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne's]] conquest of 774, [[s:march-of-tuscany|Tuscia]] passed to Frankish counts and dukes based at [[s:republic-of-lucca|Lucca]]. By the 9th century these governors were styled margraves, and the region became the March of [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]].

duchy-of-gelou.t: Transylvanian duchy of Gelou, called a Vlach by the Gesta Hungarorum, whose defeat opened Transylvania to the Hungarians; its existence is debated.
duchy-of-gelou.o: The Gesta Hungarorum, written around 1200, is the only source. It describes Gelou as a Vlach ruling Vlachs and [[e:slavs|Slavs]] in the Someș valley of [[s:principality-of-transylvania|Transylvania]] at the time of the Hungarian conquest, with his centre usually placed at Dăbâca.
duchy-of-gelou.r: Nothing is known of the duchy beyond the chronicle, which praises the land for its salt and gold-bearing rivers and says its people were poorly armed and suffered Cuman and Pecheneg raids. An early medieval fortification at Dăbâca has been excavated, but its dating is disputed.
duchy-of-gelou.e: The Gesta says Tuhutum, a Hungarian chief, defeated Gelou's army at the river Almaș and had him killed by the Căpuș as he fled, and the inhabitants accepted him as lord; his descendants are linked to the [[s:realm-of-the-gyulas|Realm of the Gyulas]]. The episode is central to debates over the early history of [[e:romanians|Romanians]] in [[s:principality-of-transylvania|Transylvania]].

duchy-of-gaeta.t: Small coastal state between Rome and Naples that broke free of Byzantium in the 9th century and lasted until the Normans absorbed it in 1140.
duchy-of-gaeta.o: Gaeta, a fortified promontory on the Tyrrhenian coast, was part of Byzantine territory loosely tied to the [[s:duchy-of-naples|Duchy of Naples]]. In the 9th century, amid Arab raids and [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] pressure, it gained autonomy under local rulers styled hypatoi (consuls). Around 867 Docibilis I founded the dynasty that made it a hereditary state.
duchy-of-gaeta.r: The rulers of Gaeta, who later took the title of duke, controlled a small territory around the Gulf of Gaeta and grew rich from sea trade. They sometimes allied with Arab raiders settled at the Garigliano, then joined the Christian coalition that destroyed that base in 915. The duchy minted its own [[e:copper|copper]] coins, and its charters, the Codex Caietanus, document its society.
duchy-of-gaeta.e: From 1032 Gaeta fell under the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] princes of [[s:principality-of-capua|Capua]] and then under Norman lords. In 1140 it submitted to Roger II and joined the [[s:kingdom-of-sicily|Kingdom of Sicily]], keeping a degree of municipal autonomy.

deli-sultanate.t: East Sumatran Malay sultanate whose land concessions created the famous Deli tobacco industry and the city of Medan.
deli-sultanate.o: Deli was founded in 1632 by Tuanku Gocah Pahlawan, a commander sent by the [[s:aceh-sultanate|Aceh Sultanate]] under Iskandar Muda to secure the coast of eastern [[e:sumatra|Sumatra]]. His descendants ruled as [[e:vassal|vassals]] of Aceh and later of the [[s:siak-sultanate|Siak Sultanate]], before Deli declared itself an independent sultanate in the 19th century.
deli-sultanate.r: The sultans governed Malay coastal communities and held authority over neighbouring Karo Batak lands. After the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] took control in 1862, the court leased vast tracts to planters such as Jacob Nienhuys, whose wrapper tobacco became world famous. Chinese and Javanese contract labourers were brought in, and [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Mahmud Al Rasyid built the Maimun Palace in Medan in 1888.
deli-sultanate.e: Deli became the wealthiest of the self-governing states of the [[s:dutch-east-indies|Dutch East Indies]], and Medan grew into a major city. The social revolution of March 1946 ended the sultanate as a political power, though the sultan remains a ceremonial figure in Medan today.

duchy-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.t: The larger Mecklenburg state on the Baltic, ruled by one of Europe's oldest dynasties and known for its archaic feudal constitution.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.o: After the extinction of the Güstrow line in 1695, a succession dispute in the House of [[s:lordship-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg]] was settled by the Treaty of [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-hamburg|Hamburg]] in 1701. Frederick William received the larger western share as the Duchy of [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg-Schwerin]], with [[s:county-of-schwerin|Schwerin]], [[s:lordship-of-rostock|Rostock]] and [[e:wismar|Wismar's]] hinterland, while a smaller share became Mecklenburg-Strelitz.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.r: The dynasty descended from the Obotrite prince Niklot of the 12th century. Under the 1755 settlement with the estates, power was shared with the knighthood, preserving large noble estates and [[e:serfdom|serfdom]] until 1820. The economy rested on grain and [[e:cattle|cattle]]. Frederick [[e:francis-i|Francis I]] joined the [[s:confederation-of-the-rhine|Confederation of the Rhine]] and became grand duke in 1815. A liberal constitution of 1849 was annulled in 1850, and the old estates constitution remained in force until 1918.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-schwerin.e: [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg-Schwerin]] joined the [[s:north-german-confederation|North German Confederation]] and in 1871 the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]]. Grand Duke Frederick Francis IV abdicated in November 1918, and the state continued as the [[s:free-state-of-mecklenburg-schwerin|Free State of Mecklenburg-Schwerin]].

duchy-of-estonia-1561-1721.t: Northern Estonia under the Swedish crown, Sweden's first Baltic conquest, held from 1561 until Peter the Great took it in the Great Northern War.
duchy-of-estonia-1561-1721.o: As [[s:terra-mariana|Terra Mariana]] collapsed under Russian attack, the city of [[s:reval|Reval]] and the knighthoods of Harrien, [[s:virumaa|Wierland]] and Jerwen submitted to Eric XIV of [[e:sweden|Sweden]] in 1561. Sweden held on through the long [[e:livonian-war|Livonian War]], and the Treaty of Teusina in 1595 confirmed its possession of northern [[s:republic-of-estonia|Estonia]].
duchy-of-estonia-1561-1721.r: The duchy was ruled by a Swedish governor at [[s:reval|Reval]], but the Baltic German nobility kept wide self-government, their Lutheran church and control of their serfs. Swedish rule founded schools, including a [[e:gymnasium|gymnasium]] at Reval in 1631, and promoted [[e:printing-press|printing]] in Estonian; [[e:charles-xi-of-sweden|Charles XI's]] reduction of noble estates in the 1680s angered the nobles. Reval and Narva were key ports for Baltic trade.
duchy-of-estonia-1561-1721.e: In the [[e:great-northern-war|Great Northern War]] Russian forces took [[s:reval|Reval]] in 1710, and the [[e:treaty-of-nystad|Treaty of Nystad]] in 1721 confirmed the loss. The region became the [[s:governorate-of-estonia|Governorate of Estonia]] within the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]], its nobles' privileges guaranteed by [[e:peter-the-great|Peter the Great]].

dutch-bengal.t: The Dutch East India Company's directorate in Bengal, based at Chinsurah on the Hooghly, a major source of silk, opium and saltpetre.
dutch-bengal.o: The [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] ([[e:dutch-east-india-company|VOC]]) began trading in [[e:bengal|Bengal]] in the 1620s, opening a factory at Pipli and then establishing its main base at Chinsurah on the Hooghly river around 1635. In 1656 it built Fort Gustavus there, and Bengal became a separate directorate with posts at Kasimbazar, [[e:patna|Patna]] and Dhaka.
dutch-bengal.r: [[e:bengal|Bengal]] supplied raw [[e:silk|silk]], [[e:cotton|cotton]] cloth, saltpetre for [[e:gunpowder|gunpowder]] and opium for the Indonesian trade, and by the late 17th century was among the [[e:dutch-east-india-company|VOC's]] most profitable regions. The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] operated under the [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]] and later the [[s:nawabate-of-bengal|Nawabate of Bengal]], paying duties and seeking privileges by negotiation.
dutch-bengal.e: The British [[e:east-india-company|East India Company's]] victory at Chinsurah in 1759 ended [[e:dutch|Dutch]] ambitions in [[e:bengal|Bengal]]. The British occupied the posts during the Napoleonic Wars, and Chinsurah was ceded to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 1825 under the [[e:anglo-dutch-treaty-of-1824|Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824]].

deva-dynasty-of-bengal.t: A Hindu dynasty of south-eastern Bengal that ruled from the Dhaka region in the 13th century, after the Sena dynasty withdrew from the west.
deva-dynasty-of-bengal.o: The Deva dynasty is known almost entirely from a few [[e:copper|copper]]-plate inscriptions. It arose in the early 13th century in eastern [[e:bengal|Bengal]], around Vikrampur and the later Suvarnagrama (Sonargaon), as Sena power collapsed in western Bengal after Bakhtiyar Khalji's conquest of Nadia.
deva-dynasty-of-bengal.r: Dasharathadeva, the best-known king, styled himself supreme ruler and held the Dhaka and Comilla region; his inscriptions mention the capital at Suvarnagrama. The kings were Vaishnava [[e:hinduism|Hindus]] who made land grants to [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]] in [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]]. Little else is known of their administration or economy.
deva-dynasty-of-bengal.e: The dynasty disappears from the record in the late 13th century, when Sonargaon came under the control of Muslim governors of Lakhnauti and eventually the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]]. Sonargaon later became the capital of the [[s:sonargaon-sultanate|Sonargaon Sultanate]].

duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg.t: Duchy created in 1235 for Otto the Child, grandson of Henry the Lion, which reconciled the Guelphs with the Hohenstaufen and founded the house of Brunswick.
duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg.o: After Henry the Lion's fall in 1180, his family kept their allodial lands around Brunswick and Lüneburg. At the Diet of [[e:mainz|Mainz]] in 1235 his grandson Otto the Child surrendered these lands to Emperor [[e:frederick-ii|Frederick II]] and received them back as a new imperial duchy, ending the long feud between the Guelphs and the Hohenstaufen.
duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg.r: Otto ruled from Brunswick, where Henry the Lion's castle of Dankwarderode and the bronze lion stood, and from Lüneburg, whose salt works were the duchy's main source of wealth. The duchy lay between the Weser and the Elbe and included Hanover, Celle and Göttingen. After Otto's death in 1252 his sons Albert I the Tall and John ruled jointly.
duchy-of-brunswick-luneburg.e: In 1269 Albert and John divided the duchy, creating the [[s:principality-of-wolfenbuttel|Principality of Wolfenbüttel]] and the [[s:principality-of-luneburg|Principality of Lüneburg]]. The ducal title stayed common to all Guelph lines, from which the [[s:electorate-of-hanover|Electorate of Hanover]] and the British royal house of Hanover later descended.

despotate-of-angelokastron-and-lepanto.t: Albanian principality in Aetolia under the Shpata family, holding Angelokastron and the port of Lepanto after the Serbian conquest of Epirus.
despotate-of-angelokastron-and-lepanto.o: After Nikephoros II Orsini of Epirus was killed by Albanian clans in 1359, Albanian leaders divided southern Epirus. Gjin Bua Shpata took Angelokastron and Lepanto (Naupaktos) in Aetolia, while Peter Losha held the [[s:despotate-of-arta|Despotate of Arta]]. Both received the title of despot from the Serbian ruler Simeon Uroš.
despotate-of-angelokastron-and-lepanto.r: The Shpata ruled Albanian clans who had migrated south as herders and soldiers, alongside a Greek population. They fought the Angevins, the Tocco of Kefalonia, the Navarrese Company and the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]]. In 1374 Gjin Bua Shpata also took Arta, joining the two Albanian despotates.
despotate-of-angelokastron-and-lepanto.e: After Gjin's death in 1399 his family held on briefly: Lepanto was sold to [[e:venice|Venice]] in 1407, and Angelokastron fell to Carlo I Tocco around 1408.

dervish-state.t: A Somali religious and military state led by Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, which fought Britain, Italy and Ethiopia for two decades.
dervish-state.o: Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, a scholar of the Salihiyya [[e:sufism|Sufi]] order, returned from [[e:arabia|Arabia]] in the mid-1890s and began preaching in Berbera against British rule and Christian missions. Rejected by local elites, he moved inland, won over clans in the Nugaal and [[e:ogaden|Ogaden]], and in 1899 declared a holy war, building a movement of followers called Dervishes (Darawiish).
dervish-state.r: The Dervish State was a militant religious community under the sayyid's authority, with a council of leaders, armed horsemen and riflemen. Hassan was also a celebrated poet. It defeated several British expeditions, including at Dul Madoba in 1913, and built stone forts at Taleh. Its raids devastated rival clans, and famine and war killed many [[e:somalis|Somalis]].
dervish-state.e: In 1920 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] combined aircraft, the [[e:camel|Camel]] Corps and local levies to destroy the forts at Taleh. Hassan fled to the [[e:ogaden|Ogaden]] and died there later that year. Many [[e:somalis|Somalis]] remember the Dervishes as early fighters for independence.

duchy-of-burgundy.t: The wine-rich duchy around Dijon, home of Cluny and Cîteaux, that under its Valois dukes became the seed of a great European power.
duchy-of-burgundy.o: Richard the Justiciar, count of Autun, gathered the counties of western [[e:burgundy|Burgundy]] and was recognised as duke by around 918. After a century of disputes the duchy went in 1032 to Robert, younger brother of King Henry I, founding a Capetian line that ruled from Dijon for over 300 years.
duchy-of-burgundy.r: The dukes were great [[e:vassal|vassals]] of [[e:france|France]], governing through their council and the Estates of [[e:burgundy|Burgundy]]. The duchy was a heartland of monastic reform: Cluny lay on its borders, and Cîteaux, founded in 1098, launched the Cistercian order. Its vineyards in the Côte d'Or were already famous in the Middle Ages.
duchy-of-burgundy.e: When Philip of Rouvres died in 1361, John II of [[e:france|France]] took the duchy and in 1363 gave it to his son Philip the Bold, founding the [[s:burgundian-state|Burgundian State]]. After Charles the Bold fell at Nancy in 1477, Louis XI annexed the duchy to the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].

decapole.t: A league of ten imperial cities of Alsace, founded in 1354 for mutual defence, which survived until Louis XIV absorbed it.
decapole.o: In 1354 [[e:charles-iv|Emperor Charles IV]] joined ten [[e:free-imperial-city|free imperial cities]] of Alsace in an alliance: [[s:free-imperial-city-of-haguenau|Haguenau]], [[s:free-imperial-city-of-colmar|Colmar]], [[s:free-imperial-city-of-wissembourg|Wissembourg]], [[s:free-imperial-city-of-turckheim|Turckheim]], [[s:free-imperial-city-of-obernai|Obernai]], [[s:free-imperial-city-of-kaysersberg|Kaysersberg]], [[s:free-imperial-city-of-rosheim|Rosheim]], [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Munster]], [[s:free-imperial-city-of-selestat|Sélestat]] and [[s:republic-of-mulhouse|Mulhouse]]. They were placed under the imperial bailiff at Haguenau to defend their rights against local lords.
decapole.r: The cities governed themselves but pledged mutual aid, shared costs and met in diets. [[s:republic-of-mulhouse|Mulhouse]] left in 1515 to ally with the Swiss and Landau joined in 1521. Members were wine and market towns, and some, like [[s:free-imperial-city-of-colmar|Colmar]], adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] while others stayed Catholic. The league had no army or capital of its own.
decapole.e: The [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 transferred imperial rights in Alsace to [[e:france|France]] ambiguously, and [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]] occupied the cities in 1673. The Treaty of Nijmegen of 1679 confirmed French control, ending the league.

duchy-of-warsaw.t: Napoleon's Polish client state, which revived a Polish government and army after the partitions and introduced the Napoleonic Code.
duchy-of-warsaw.o: After defeating [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1806 and 1807, [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] created the Duchy of [[e:warsaw|Warsaw]] by the Treaty of Tilsit out of the lands Prussia had taken in the Second and [[e:third-partition-of-poland|Third Partitions]] of [[e:poland|Poland]]. He made Frederick Augustus I, King of Saxony, its duke, linking it to the [[s:kingdom-of-saxony|Kingdom of Saxony]].
duchy-of-warsaw.r: The constitution of 1807 abolished personal [[e:serfdom|serfdom]], declared equality before the law and introduced the [[e:napoleonic-code|Napoleonic Code]], though nobles kept their land. Real power lay with French officials and the needs of [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] wars. Prince Jozef Poniatowski built a Polish army that defeated [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1809, after which the duchy gained Krakow and [[e:lublin|Lublin]].
duchy-of-warsaw.e: About 100,000 soldiers from the duchy joined the invasion of [[e:russia|Russia]] in 1812, and Poniatowski died at Leipzig in 1813. Russia occupied the duchy, and the [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] divided it in 1815 into [[s:congress-poland|Congress Poland]], the [[s:grand-duchy-of-posen|Grand Duchy of Posen]] and the [[s:free-city-of-krakow|Free City of Krakow]].

duchy-of-saxe-altenburg.t: Ernestine duchy in eastern Thuringia, home of the card game Skat and of the dukes who exchanged Hildburghausen for Altenburg.
duchy-of-saxe-altenburg.o: When [[s:duchy-of-saxe-gotha|Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg]] died out in 1825, the Ernestine lands were rearranged in 1826. Duke Frederick of Saxe-Hildburghausen gave up his old duchy and received Altenburg, founding the new Duchy of Saxe-Altenburg.
duchy-of-saxe-altenburg.r: The duchy was Lutheran and agriculturally rich, with prosperous peasant farms and later lignite mining. The card game Skat was developed in Altenburg around 1810-1820, and the town remains its centre, with a Skat court. A constitution was granted in 1831, and in 1848 unrest forced Duke Joseph to abdicate. Ernest I ruled from 1853 to 1908.
duchy-of-saxe-altenburg.e: Saxe-Altenburg joined the [[s:north-german-confederation|North German Confederation]] and the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]]. Duke Ernest II abdicated in November 1918, and in 1920 the state merged into the [[s:free-state-of-thuringia|Free State of Thuringia]]. Altenburg Castle now houses a museum of playing cards.

duchy-of-saxe-hildburghausen.t: Small Ernestine duchy in southern Thuringia whose princess's 1810 wedding in Munich gave rise to the Oktoberfest.
duchy-of-saxe-hildburghausen.o: Ernest, the sixth son of Ernest the Pious, received Hildburghausen in the 1680 partition of the Saxe-Gotha inheritance. He made the small town his residence and was given full ducal [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]], later adding Eisfeld and Königsberg in Franconia.
duchy-of-saxe-hildburghausen.r: The dukes built a palace and attracted Huguenot refugees to a new town quarter. Extravagance led to bankruptcy, and in 1769 an imperial debt commission took over the finances. Duke Frederick's daughter Therese married Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria in Munich in October 1810, and the horse race held in her honour became the Oktoberfest; the Theresienwiese still bears her name.
duchy-of-saxe-hildburghausen.e: After [[s:duchy-of-saxe-gotha|Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg]] died out, the Ernestine lands were redistributed in 1826. Duke Frederick exchanged Hildburghausen for Altenburg, becoming Duke of Saxe-Altenburg, and Hildburghausen went to Saxe-Meiningen.

date-clan-domain.t: The domain of the Date of southern Mutsu, which under the one-eyed Date Masamune briefly dominated northeastern Japan.
date-clan-domain.o: The Date had long held lands in southern Mutsu. Date Tanemune issued the detailed Jinkai-shu law code in 1536, and from 1542 a war with his son Harumune split the clan; Harumune won and in 1548 moved the family seat to Yonezawa.
date-clan-domain.r: The Date built power through marriage alliances with neighbouring families across the Tohoku. Date Masamune, who lost an eye to [[e:smallpox|smallpox]] as a child, became head in 1584 and expanded aggressively, defeating the [[e:ashina-clan|Ashina]] at Suriagehara in 1589 to take Aizu, briefly controlling much of southern Tohoku.
date-clan-domain.e: Masamune submitted late to [[e:toyotomi-hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] in 1590, lost Aizu and in 1591 was moved to Iwadeyama. Siding with [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] in 1600, he founded the [[s:sendai-domain|Sendai Domain]], which the Date ruled until 1871.

duchy-of-mantua.t: The Gonzaga state of Mantua, whose court commissioned Mantegna, Giulio Romano and Monteverdi before war and plague ruined it.
duchy-of-mantua.o: In 1328 Luigi Gonzaga overthrew the Bonacolsi lords of Mantua and became captain of the people. The Gonzaga ruled as imperial vicars, became marquises in 1433 under Gianfrancesco Gonzaga and dukes in 1530 under Federico II, who also acquired Montferrat, later the [[s:duchy-of-montferrat|Duchy of Montferrat]].
duchy-of-mantua.r: Mantua's court was among the most brilliant in [[e:italy|Italy]]. Andrea Mantegna painted the Camera degli Sposi for Ludovico III; Isabella d'Este collected art; Giulio Romano built the Palazzo Te for Federico II. Under Vincenzo I, Monteverdi's Orfeo was staged in 1607. The duchy lived from farming, textiles and the condottiere service of its lords.
duchy-of-mantua.e: The main line died out in 1627, and the War of the Mantuan Succession brought an imperial sack in 1630. The Gonzaga-Nevers line ruled until Ferdinando Carlo sided with [[e:france|France]] and was deposed in 1708, when [[e:austria|Austria]] annexed Mantua.

cr.a: Coat_of_arms_of_the_House_of_Gonzaga_(1575).svg: F l a n k e r derivative work: Amber and Black (talk)

duchy-of-opava.t: Duchy carved out of northern Moravia for a son of King Ottokar II, later ruled by the Liechtensteins and capital of Austrian Silesia until 1918.
duchy-of-opava.o: Around 1269 King Ottokar II of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] gave the Opava region of northern [[s:margraviate-of-moravia|Moravia]] to his illegitimate son Nicholas I. Nicholas's descendants ruled it as a separate duchy, and it gradually came to be counted among the Silesian duchies rather than [[e:moravia|Moravia]], under the Kingdom of [[e:bohemia|Bohemia]].
duchy-of-opava.r: The Opava Přemyslids ruled until the 15th century, after which the duchy passed to the Poděbrady family, the Hungarian king Matthias Corvinus and the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburgs]]. In 1614 it was granted to [[e:karl-i|Karl I]] of [[s:principality-of-liechtenstein|Liechtenstein]], whose family kept the ducal title. Opava was a town of German and Czech speakers, cloth and trade, and the Counter-[[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] restored [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] after 1620.
duchy-of-opava.e: In 1742 [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] took the northern part; the rest became the core of [[s:duchy-of-upper-and-lower-silesia|Austrian Silesia]], with Opava as capital, and hosted the Congress of Troppau in 1820. In 1918 it joined [[s:czechoslovakia|Czechoslovakia]] and is now in the Czech Republic.

dulafid-dynasty.t: An Arab family of governors who ruled the Jibal region of western Iran for most of the 9th century from their own city, Karaj.
dulafid-dynasty.o: Abu Dulaf al-Qasim ibn Isa, of the Arab Banu Ijl, was a general and poet in the service of [[e:harun-al-rashid|Harun al-Rashid]] and [[e:al-mamun|al-Ma'mun]]. Around 825 he founded or developed the town of Karaj (Karaj Abi Dulaf, near modern Arak, not the city near Tehran) and governed much of the Jibal as an Abbasid official.
dulafid-dynasty.r: The Dulafids ruled hereditarily but in the name of the [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]], collecting taxes in a rich agricultural and horse-raising region on the route from [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] to Khurasan. Abu Dulaf was celebrated as a patron and poet and appears in Arabic literature for his generosity. His descendants, notably Ahmad ibn Abd [[e:al-aziz|al-Aziz]], fought the [[s:saffarid-dynasty|Saffarids]] and sometimes defied Baghdad.
dulafid-dynasty.e: After internal disputes, the [[e:caliphate|caliph]] al-Mu'tadid ended Dulafid rule in 897, reabsorbing the Jibal into direct caliphal administration.

deisi-muman.t: Kingdom of the Déisi in Waterford and south Tipperary, whose legendary migrations reached Wales and whose name survives in the Decies.
deisi-muman.o: The Déisi were a population group whose name means '[[e:vassal|vassals]]'. The early Irish tale The Expulsion of the Déisi tells how they were driven from [[s:kingdom-of-brega|Brega]] near Tara and wandered south, some settling in [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Munster]] and others crossing to [[s:kingdom-of-dyfed|Dyfed]] in Wales, where the Kingdom of Dyfed's kings later claimed Déisi descent. In Munster they settled in what is now County Waterford and south Tipperary.
deisi-muman.r: The Déisi Muman were a subject kingdom within the [[s:kingdom-of-munster|Kingdom of Munster]], paying tribute to the Eóganachta of Cashel. The monastery of Lismore, founded by St Mochuda in the 7th century, was one of the great schools of early Ireland and lay in their territory. A northern branch, the Déis Tuaiscirt, later grew into the Dál Cais, the dynasty of Brian Bóruma.
deisi-muman.e: The Ua Fáeláin, O'Phelan, kings ruled the Déisi in the 11th and 12th centuries. After the Anglo-Normans took Waterford in 1170 their lands were granted to settlers, and the kingdom faded around 1200. The name survives in the baronies of Decies in Waterford.

damnonii.t: People of the Clyde valley recorded by Ptolemy, whose territory was crossed by the Antonine Wall and later formed the heart of Strathclyde.
damnonii.o: The Damnonii appear in Ptolemy's 2nd-century Geography in the region of the Clyde, Ayrshire and parts of Stirlingshire, with places such as Vanduara and Alauna listed among their settlements. They derived from the Iron Age communities of west central [[e:scotland|Scotland]], who lived in hillforts, crannogs and enclosed farms.
damnonii.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions. Their land lay on the line of the Antonine Wall, built across the Forth and Clyde isthmus from 142, and was occupied by Roman forts during the periods of Roman advance into [[e:scotland|Scotland]]. Their society was otherwise rural and [[e:cattle|cattle]]-based, much like their neighbours.
damnonii.e: After the Roman withdrawal to Hadrian's Wall the Damnonii lived beyond the frontier. They are generally regarded as ancestors of the British people of the Clyde, whose [[s:kingdom-of-strathclyde|Kingdom of Strathclyde]] was centred on Alt Clut, Dumbarton Rock.

derbent-khanate.t: A short-lived khanate based in the ancient fortress city of Derbent, the Caspian gateway between the North Caucasus and Transcaucasia.
derbent-khanate.o: After [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah's]] death in 1747, the Persian governor of Derbent, Muhammad Husayn Khan, ruled the walled city and its hinterland as an independent khan. Derbent's Sasanian walls and citadel of Naryn-Kala still controlled the narrow coastal passage between the mountains and the [[e:caspian-sea|Caspian Sea]].
derbent-khanate.r: The khanate was small but strategically vital, drawing income from customs on the coastal route and from the trade of its port. Its population was mixed, including Azerbaijani, Persian, Tat-speaking Jewish and Lezgin communities. Rivalry with neighbouring [[s:kaitag-utsmiyate|Kaitag]] and Quba weakened it, and in 1765 Fatali Khan of the [[s:quba-khanate|Quba Khanate]] seized the city.
derbent-khanate.e: Derbent remained under Quba's rulers until Russian troops took it in 1796, briefly, and again in 1806, when the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] annexed it permanently. The city's walls and citadel are now a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

duchy-of-oldenburg.t: North German duchy, later grand duchy, created by a Danish-Russian exchange and ruled by a branch of the house that also held the Russian throne.
duchy-of-oldenburg.o: The [[s:county-of-oldenburg|County of Oldenburg]] had been ruled by the Danish kings since 1667. In the Treaty of Tsarskoye Selo of 1773, [[e:denmark|Denmark]] exchanged it with [[e:russia|Russia]] for the [[s:duchy-of-holstein-gottorp|Gottorp]] share of [[s:county-of-holstein|Holstein]], and Grand Duke Paul passed it to his relative Frederick Augustus, prince-[[e:bishop|bishop]] of [[s:free-and-hanseatic-city-of-lubeck|Lübeck]]. In 1774 the emperor raised Oldenburg to a duchy.
duchy-of-oldenburg.r: The dukes of the [[s:duchy-of-holstein-gottorp|Holstein-Gottorp]] line governed a Lutheran land of marshes, moors and [[e:cattle|cattle]] farming, with the secularised [[s:prince-bishopric-of-lubeck|Principality of Lübeck]] at Eutin and, from 1817, the [[s:principality-of-birkenfeld|Principality of Birkenfeld]]. Peter Frederick Louis was a careful administrator. [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]] annexed [[s:county-of-oldenburg|Oldenburg]] to [[e:france|France]] in 1811, but it was restored in 1813 and became a grand duchy, adopting a constitution in 1849.
duchy-of-oldenburg.e: [[s:county-of-oldenburg|Oldenburg]] joined the [[s:north-german-confederation|North German Confederation]] and the [[s:german-empire|German Empire]]. Grand Duke Frederick [[e:augustus-ii-the-strong|Augustus II]] abdicated in November 1918, and the state became the [[s:free-state-of-oldenburg|Free State of Oldenburg]].

drevlians.t: Forest-dwelling East Slavs west of Kiev who killed Prince Igor in 945 and suffered the ferocious revenge of his widow Olga.
drevlians.o: The Drevlians, the people of the trees, lived in the forests between the Pripyat and the middle [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]], west of the Polans. They appear in the Primary Chronicle as an old tribe with their own princes and their chief town at Iskorosten, modern Korosten in [[e:ukraine|Ukraine]].
drevlians.r: They were farmers, hunters and beekeepers, and the Kievan chronicler, hostile to them, describes them as living in a bestial way. After Oleg subdued them, in 883 according to the chronicle, they paid tribute to Kiev. In 945 Prince Igor tried to collect a second tribute, and the Drevlians under their prince Mal killed him.
drevlians.e: Igor's widow Olga took vengeance in 946, burying and burning Drevlian envoys and setting Iskorosten alight with birds carrying burning tinder. The Drevlian land was then ruled directly from Kiev, and in 970 [[e:sviatoslav-i-of-kiev|Sviatoslav I]] gave it to his son Oleg. The tribe merged into the population of [[s:kievan-rus|Kievan Rus']].

duchy-of-pomerania-stettin.t: The southern Pomeranian duchy created in 1295, centred on the Oder port of Stettin and long contested with Brandenburg.
duchy-of-pomerania-stettin.o: The partition of the [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Duchy of Pomerania]] in 1295 gave [[e:otto-i|Otto I]] the lands around Stettin (Szczecin) on the lower Oder, while his brother Bogislaw IV took Pomerania-Wolgast. Otto's descendants spent much of the 14th and 15th centuries resisting the [[s:margraviate-of-brandenburg|Margraviate of Brandenburg]]'s claims to overlordship and to the succession.
duchy-of-pomerania-stettin.r: Stettin was a Hanseatic port exporting grain, [[e:timber|timber]] and herring, and its [[e:burghers|burghers]] often acted independently of the dukes. Bogislaw X, who reunited all [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]] in 1478, reformed its administration and finances. The Treaty of Grimnitz in 1529 freed the dukes from [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg's]] feudal claims in exchange for a promise of succession, and [[e:pomerania|Pomerania]] adopted [[e:lutheranism|Lutheranism]] in 1534.
duchy-of-pomerania-stettin.e: After a new division in 1532, Stettin was ruled by a series of dukes who died without heirs. Bogislaw XIV united both duchies in 1625, but [[e:sweden|Sweden]] occupied [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]] in 1630. On his death in 1637 the Griffin line ended, and in 1648 the lands were divided between [[s:swedish-pomerania|Swedish Pomerania]] and [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]].

duchy-of-upper-and-lower-silesia.t: The small part of Silesia that Austria kept after Frederick the Great's conquest, an industrial crown land of the Habsburgs.
duchy-of-upper-and-lower-silesia.o: [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] seized most of [[s:duchy-of-silesia|Silesia]] in the War of the Austrian Succession, and under the Treaty of Breslau and the Peace of Berlin in 1742 [[e:austria|Austria]] kept only a southern strip, including the duchies of Troppau, Teschen and part of Jägerndorf. This remnant was governed as the Duchy of Upper and Lower Silesia, usually called Austrian Silesia.
duchy-of-upper-and-lower-silesia.r: Austrian [[s:duchy-of-silesia|Silesia]] was administered from Troppau (Opava), joined to [[s:margraviate-of-moravia|Moravia]] from 1782 and from 1849 a separate crown land with its own diet. Its population was German, Czech and Polish, Catholic with Lutheran minorities in Teschen. [[e:coal|Coal]] mining in the Ostrava-Karviná basin and the heavy industry around it made it one of the most industrialised parts of the monarchy.
duchy-of-upper-and-lower-silesia.e: With the collapse of [[e:austro-hungarian-empire|Austria-Hungary]] in 1918, the territory was claimed by [[s:czechoslovakia|Czechoslovakia]] and [[e:poland|Poland]]. After a brief war over Teschen in 1919, it was divided in 1920, with most going to [[e:czechoslovakia|Czechoslovakia]].

duchy-of-schleswig.t: Duchy of southern Jutland on the Danish-German border, held by Danish royal princes and Holstein counts and fought over in the 19th-century Schleswig wars.
duchy-of-schleswig.o: Southern Jutland was the frontier of the [[s:kingdom-of-denmark|Kingdom of Denmark]], guarded by the Danevirke earthworks and home to the [[e:vikings|Viking]] Age trading town of Hedeby. From the 11th century it was governed as a jarldom or duchy by members of the royal family; Canute Lavard held it from 1115, and the dukes descended from King Abel made it a hereditary fief.
duchy-of-schleswig.r: The duchy straddled Danish and German worlds: Danish speech dominated in the north, German and Frisian in the south, and the town of Schleswig on the Schlei was its capital. From 1386 the counts of [[s:county-of-holstein|Holstein]] held it, and in 1460 the Treaty of Ribe made Christian I its duke, promising Schleswig and Holstein would stay forever undivided. [[s:duchy-of-holstein-gottorp|Gottorp]] Castle became a seat of a ducal line.
duchy-of-schleswig.e: Rising Danish and German nationalism led to the First Schleswig War in 1848-1851 and the Second in 1864, after which [[e:denmark|Denmark]] ceded the duchy to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] and [[e:austria|Austria]]. Prussia annexed it in 1866-1867. A 1920 plebiscite returned northern Schleswig to Denmark, while the south remains part of [[e:germany|Germany]].

dujana-state.t: A tiny Pathan Nawabi state in Haryana, granted by the British in 1806 to a cavalry leader who had served them against the Marathas.
dujana-state.o: Abdul Samad Khan, a Pathan soldier, served Lord Lake in the Second Anglo-[[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] War, and in 1806 the British granted him Dujana and its villages as a hereditary state.
dujana-state.r: The Nawabs governed a very small farming territory under British supervision through the [[e:punjab|Punjab]] government. Little is recorded of its internal history.
dujana-state.e: Dujana acceded to [[e:india|India]] and in 1948 was merged into East [[e:punjab|Punjab]]; it lies in Jhajjar district of Haryana.

duchy-of-julich.t: A Rhineland county turned duchy between Aachen and Cologne, whose union with Cleves and Berg created a powerful state and a famous succession crisis.
duchy-of-julich.o: A count named Gerhard appears in the Jülichgau around 1003, and his family built a county around the old Roman town of Jülich west of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]]. The counts fought the archbishops of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-cologne|Cologne]] for supremacy in the lower Rhineland, sharing the victory at Worringen in 1288 with Berg and [[s:duchy-of-brabant|Brabant]].
duchy-of-julich.r: Count William V was made margrave in 1336 and duke in 1356. In 1423 Jülich united with the [[s:duchy-of-berg|Duchy of Berg]], and in 1521 with the [[s:duchy-of-cleves|Duchy of Cleves]] and the County of the Mark, forming the [[s:united-duchies-of-julich-cleves-berg|United Duchies]]. Duke William the Rich built Jülich into an Italian [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] fortress town with a citadel.
duchy-of-julich.e: When the last duke, John William, died in 1609, the Jülich succession crisis between [[e:brandenburg|Brandenburg]] and [[s:palatinate-neuburg|Palatinate-Neuburg]] nearly sparked a European war. The Treaty of Xanten in 1614 gave Jülich and Berg to Palatinate-Neuburg. [[e:french-revolutionary-occupation-of-the-netherlands|French revolutionary armies]] took Jülich in 1794, and in 1815 it became Prussian.

duchy-of-saxe-gotha.t: Ernestine Saxon duchy in Thuringia whose founder, Ernest the Pious, made it a model of Lutheran school reform and orderly government.
duchy-of-saxe-gotha.o: Saxe-Gotha was created in 1640 when the Ernestine lands of Saxe-Weimar were divided among the brothers of the ducal house, and Ernest I received Gotha. He built Friedenstein Palace as his residence. In 1672 he inherited Saxe-Altenburg, and the state became known as Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg.
duchy-of-saxe-gotha.r: Ernest the Pious introduced compulsory schooling, a famous school method and detailed church and state ordinances, rebuilding a land ruined by the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]]. On his death in 1675 his lands were divided among seven sons, creating the duchies of Coburg, Meiningen, Römhild, Eisenberg, Hildburghausen and Saalfeld. Ernest II, in the 18th century, was an [[e:age-of-enlightenment|Enlightenment]] patron of [[e:babylonian-astronomy|astronomy]] who founded the Seeberg observatory.
duchy-of-saxe-gotha.e: The line died out with Duke Frederick IV in 1825. In the redistribution of 1826 Gotha went to the Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, forming the [[s:duchy-of-saxe-coburg-and-gotha|Duchy of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha]], while Altenburg became the [[s:duchy-of-saxe-altenburg|Duchy of Saxe-Altenburg]].

duchy-of-modena-and-reggio.t: The Este duchy that became the family's main state after the loss of Ferrara, lasting until Italian unification in 1859.
duchy-of-modena-and-reggio.o: In 1452 Emperor Frederick III made Borso d'Este duke of Modena and Reggio, imperial fiefs held alongside the papal [[s:duchy-of-ferrara|Duchy of Ferrara]]. When Ferrara passed to the [[e:papacy|papacy]] in 1598, Cesare d'Este moved his court to Modena, which became the capital.
duchy-of-modena-and-reggio.r: The Este rebuilt Modena as a capital, with a ducal palace and the Biblioteca Estense, where the scholar Ludovico Antonio Muratori worked as librarian. The duchy added Mirandola, [[s:principality-of-correggio|Correggio]] and [[s:county-of-novellara|Novellara]]. After French occupation from 1796, when it joined the [[s:cispadane-republic|Cispadane Republic]], the restored duchy passed in 1814 to Francis IV of Austria-Este, who ruled harshly and executed the revolutionary Ciro Menotti in 1831.
duchy-of-modena-and-reggio.e: Francis V fled after the Austrian defeat in 1859. The duchy joined the [[s:united-provinces-of-central-italy|United Provinces of Central Italy]] and was annexed to the [[s:kingdom-of-sardinia|Kingdom of Sardinia]] in 1860.

dutch-ceylon.t: The Dutch East India Company's colony on the coasts of Sri Lanka, run for its cinnamon monopoly and leaving a lasting legal and architectural mark.
dutch-ceylon.o: Rajasinha II of the [[s:kingdom-of-kandy|Kingdom of Kandy]] invited the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] ([[e:dutch-east-india-company|VOC]]) to help expel the Portuguese. The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] took Batticaloa and Trincomalee in 1639 and Galle in 1640, then Colombo in 1656 and Jaffna in 1658, but kept the conquered coasts for themselves rather than handing them to Kandy.
dutch-ceylon.r: A governor at Colombo ruled the maritime provinces, enforcing a strict monopoly on [[e:cinnamon|cinnamon]], the colony's chief product, and also trading elephants, pearls and areca. Roman-[[e:dutch|Dutch]] law, introduced in this period, still forms the basis of Sri Lankan [[e:civil-law|civil law]]. The Dutch built forts at Galle and Jaffna, Reformed churches and canals, and a [[e:burghers|Burgher]] community of European descent emerged. Relations with Kandy alternated between trade and war.
dutch-ceylon.e: During the [[e:french-revolutionary-wars|French Revolutionary Wars]], British forces from Madras occupied the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] possessions in 1795 to 1796. They were formally ceded by the Treaty of Amiens in 1802 and became [[s:british-ceylon|British Ceylon]]. Galle Fort is now a World Heritage Site.

durrani-empire.t: The empire founded by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1747, regarded as the foundation of the modern state of Afghanistan.
durrani-empire.o: After [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah's]] assassination in 1747, Ahmad Khan Abdali, commander of his Afghan bodyguard, was chosen as king by a tribal assembly in [[e:kandahar|Kandahar]]. Taking the title Durr-i Durran, 'Pearl of Pearls', he founded the Durrani dynasty of the Sadozai clan.
durrani-empire.r: Ahmad Shah conquered [[e:herat|Herat]], [[e:kabul|Kabul]], the [[e:punjab|Punjab]], [[e:kashmir|Kashmir]] and Sindh, and in 1761 crushed the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]] at the [[e:third-battle-of-panipat|Third Battle of Panipat]]. Revenue came from Indian plunder and tribute. Pashtun tribal chiefs held great power, and the state relied on their loyalty. His son [[e:timur|Timur]] Shah moved the capital from [[e:kandahar|Kandahar]] to Kabul in 1776.
durrani-empire.e: Under [[e:timur|Timur's]] sons, rivalry between Shah Zaman, Shah Mahmud and Shah Shuja, and the power of the [[e:barakzai-dynasty|Barakzai]] ministers, broke the empire. The [[e:sikhism|Sikhs]] took the [[e:punjab|Punjab]], and by 1823 the Barakzais held [[e:kabul|Kabul]], founding the [[s:emirate-of-afghanistan|Emirate of Afghanistan]], while Sadozais kept the [[s:principality-of-herat|Principality of Herat]].

domnonee.t: Breton kingdom of northern Brittany, named after Dumnonia in Britain, whose king Judicael treated with Dagobert I as an equal.
domnonee.o: Migrants from [[s:kingdom-of-dumnonia|Dumnonia]] in south-west [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], the land of modern Devon and Cornwall, settled the northern coast of Armorica in the 5th and 6th centuries and gave it the name of their homeland. Its early rulers are known mainly from saints' lives, which may preserve legend.
domnonee.r: The kingdom stretched along the Channel coast from the Rance to the Morlaix area. Its life centred on monastic foundations such as Saint-Malo, Dol and Saint-Pol-de-Léon, linked to saints from Wales and Cornwall. The chronicle of Fredegar records that King Judicael met Dagobert I at Clichy in 636 and made peace with the [[s:franks|Franks]].
domnonee.e: In the 9th century Domnonée was absorbed into the [[s:kingdom-of-brittany|Kingdom of Brittany]] created by Nominoe and Erispoe. The bishopric of Dol and the later counties of Penthièvre and Léon preserved parts of its territory.

duchy-of-greater-poland.t: The duchy of the Piast heartland around Poznan and Gniezno, which produced Poland's first crowned king after two centuries of division.
duchy-of-greater-poland.o: Under the testament of Boleslaw III in 1138, his son Mieszko III the Old received Greater [[e:poland|Poland]], with Poznan and Gniezno, the cradle of the Piast state. For much of the next century the duchy was contested between Mieszko's descendants and was at times divided between Poznan and Kalisz.
duchy-of-greater-poland.r: Greater [[e:poland|Poland]] was a farming region, settled in the 13th century by German colonists and towns founded under Magdeburg law, such as Poznan in 1253. Its dukes, especially Wladyslaw Odonic and his sons, built up their power with the support of the church of Gniezno. Duke Przemysl II gained Pomerelia in 1294 and was crowned King of Poland in Gniezno in 1295.
duchy-of-greater-poland.e: Przemysl II was murdered in 1296, and the duchy passed to Wladyslaw I the Elbow-high, Wenceslaus II of [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] and Henry of Glogow. Wladyslaw I took it back in 1314, and in 1320 it became part of the reunited [[s:kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385|Kingdom of Poland]] (1025-1385).

duchies-of-bremen-and-verden.t: Two secularised prince-bishoprics between Elbe and Weser that passed from Sweden to Hanover, controlling the approaches to Bremen and Hamburg.
duchies-of-bremen-and-verden.o: The [[s:prince-archbishopric-of-bremen|Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen]] and the [[s:prince-bishopric-of-verden|Prince-Bishopric of Verden]] had been occupied by [[e:sweden|Sweden]] during the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]]. At the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 they were secularised and granted to the Swedish crown as the duchies of [[s:free-hanseatic-city-of-bremen|Bremen]] and [[e:verden|Verden]], with the government seated at Stade.
duchies-of-bremen-and-verden.r: The duchies kept their estates and Lutheran church while [[e:sweden|Sweden]] used them as a strategic base. The city of [[s:free-hanseatic-city-of-bremen|Bremen]] resisted Swedish claims and remained an imperial free city. [[e:denmark|Denmark]] occupied the duchies in 1712 during the [[e:great-northern-war|Great Northern War]] and sold them to the [[s:electorate-of-hanover|Electorate of Hanover]] in 1715, a transfer recognised by Sweden in 1719. Farming in the marshlands and moors was the mainstay.
duchies-of-bremen-and-verden.e: After Napoleonic occupation the lands returned to Hanover in 1813, a kingdom from 1814. In 1823 they were merged into the Stade administrative region, ending the duchies as distinct units; the area passed to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1866.

duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria.t: The Norman duchy of Robert Guiscard, which drove the Byzantines out of southern Italy and laid the groundwork for the Kingdom of Sicily.
duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria.o: Norman [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] in Byzantine Apulia elected William Iron Arm as their count at Melfi around 1042–1043. After his brothers Drogo and Humphrey, their half-brother Robert Guiscard took over in 1057, and in 1059 [[e:papacy|Pope]] [[e:nicholas-ii|Nicholas II]] invested him at Melfi as duke of Apulia, Calabria and, in prospect, [[e:sicily|Sicily]], making the papacy the duchy's overlord.
duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria.r: Guiscard captured [[s:principality-of-bari|Bari]] in 1071, ending Byzantine rule in [[e:italy|Italy]], and [[s:principality-of-salerno|Salerno]] in 1077, which became his capital. The duchy ruled Greek-speaking Calabria and [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] and [[e:latin|Latin]] Apulia, keeping Byzantine officials and Greek monasteries alongside Latin [[e:bishop|bishops]]. Its army also invaded the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]] across the Adriatic in 1081, and in 1084 sacked [[e:rome|Rome]] while rescuing [[e:papacy|Pope]] Gregory VII.
duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria.e: After Guiscard's death in 1085, his son Roger Borsa and grandson William II struggled to control rebellious barons. When William died childless in 1127, his cousin Roger II of the [[s:county-of-sicily|County of Sicily]] claimed the duchy, and in 1130 merged it into the new [[s:kingdom-of-sicily|Kingdom of Sicily]].

despotate-of-arta.t: Albanian despotate in southern Epirus, ruled by the Losha and Shpata clans from Arta until Carlo Tocco took the city in 1416.
despotate-of-arta.o: In 1358–1359 Albanian clans defeated Nikephoros II Orsini, the last Orsini despot, and divided southern Epirus. Peter Losha took Arta and was recognised as despot by Simeon Uroš, the Serbian ruler of Thessaly; Gjin Bua Shpata held the [[s:despotate-of-angelokastron-and-lepanto|Despotate of Angelokastron and Lepanto]] to the south.
despotate-of-arta.r: The despots relied on Albanian clans who had moved into Epirus, ruling a Greek town population around Arta. They fought the Serbian rulers of Ioannina, notably Thomas Preljubović, and later Esau de' Buondelmonti. After Losha's death in 1374 Gjin Bua Shpata ruled both despotates until 1399, followed by Muriq Shpata and Yaqub Shpata, who allied with the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]].
despotate-of-arta.e: Yaqub Shpata was killed in 1416, and Carlo I Tocco, ruler of Ioannina, captured Arta. The city was taken by the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in 1449.

democratic-republic-of-afghanistan.t: The communist state of Afghanistan, whose radical reforms and the Soviet invasion of 1979 ignited decades of war.
democratic-republic-of-afghanistan.o: The People's Democratic Party of [[s:islamic-emirate-of-afghanistan-2021-present|Afghanistan]] seized power in the Saur Revolution of April 1978, killing President Daoud Khan of the [[s:republic-of-afghanistan-1973-1978|Republic of Afghanistan]] (1973-1978). Nur Muhammad Taraki of the Khalq faction became head of state.
democratic-republic-of-afghanistan.r: Radical land reform, literacy and marriage decrees and the repression of clergy and opponents provoked uprisings. Hafizullah Amin killed Taraki in 1979, and in December the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] invaded, killing Amin and installing Babrak Karmal of the Parcham faction. A war against the mujahideen, backed by [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]], the [[s:united-states|United States]] and [[s:saudi-arabia|Saudi Arabia]], killed perhaps a million [[e:afghans|Afghans]] and drove some five million into exile. Mohammad Najibullah, leader from 1986, pursued 'national reconciliation' and renamed the state [[s:republic-of-afghanistan-1973-1978|Republic of Afghanistan]] in 1987.
democratic-republic-of-afghanistan.e: Soviet troops withdrew by February 1989, but the government survived until Soviet aid ended. In April 1992 mujahideen forces entered [[e:kabul|Kabul]], and the [[s:islamic-state-of-afghanistan|Islamic State of Afghanistan]] was proclaimed.

dutch-mauritius.t: The Dutch East India Company's settlement on Mauritius, which introduced sugar cane and saw the extinction of the dodo.
dutch-mauritius.o: [[e:dutch|Dutch]] sailors named Mauritius after Prince Maurice of [[s:county-of-nassau|Nassau]] in 1598, and in 1638 the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]] ([[e:dutch-east-india-company|VOC]]) founded Fort Frederik Hendrik at Grand Port to forestall French and English rivals. The first commander was Cornelis Gooyer.
dutch-mauritius.r: The small settlement exported [[e:ebony|ebony]], cut from the island's forests, and served as a supply base for ships bound for the [[e:east-indies|East Indies]]. Enslaved people were brought from Madagascar and the East Indies, and the colonists introduced [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] cane, deer and pigs. Hunting and introduced animals contributed to the extinction of the dodo, last reliably seen in 1662.
dutch-mauritius.e: The colony was abandoned in 1658, reoccupied in 1664 and finally abandoned in 1710 after cyclones, droughts and losses. [[e:france|France]] claimed the empty island in 1715 as [[s:isle-de-france|Isle de France]].

dominion-of-pakistan.t: Pakistan's first form as an independent state, a dominion of the British Commonwealth in two wings separated by a thousand miles of India.
dominion-of-pakistan.o: The demand for a separate homeland for Muslims, adopted by the All-[[e:india|India]] Muslim League in the [[e:lahore|Lahore]] Resolution of 1940, led to the partition of the [[s:british-raj|British Raj]]. On 14 August 1947 the [[e:dominion|Dominion]] of [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]] came into being, with Muhammad Ali Jinnah as Governor-General and Karachi as capital, comprising West [[e:pakistan|Pakistan]] and [[s:bangladesh|East Bengal]].
dominion-of-pakistan.r: The new state faced the upheaval of partition, with millions of refugees and massacres, and war with the [[s:dominion-of-india|Dominion of India]] over [[e:kashmir|Kashmir]] in 1947 to 1948. Jinnah died in 1948 and prime minister Liaquat Ali Khan was assassinated in 1951. The Objectives Resolution of 1949 set Islamic principles for a constitution, while the Bengali Language Movement of 1952 exposed tensions between the two wings.
dominion-of-pakistan.e: After years of constitutional deadlock and the dismissal of the Constituent Assembly in 1954, a constitution was adopted on 23 March 1956, declaring the [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Islamic Republic of Pakistan]] and ending dominion status.

duchy-of-brzesc-kujawski.t: The small Kuyavian duchy of Wladyslaw the Elbow-high, the starting point of the duke who reunited Poland in 1320.
duchy-of-brzesc-kujawski.o: When Casimir I of Kuyavia died in 1267, his sons divided the [[s:duchy-of-kuyavia|Duchy of Kuyavia]], and the southern part around Brzesc Kujawski went to the young Wladyslaw and his brother Casimir. Wladyslaw, nicknamed the Elbow-high for his small stature, was born nearby around 1260.
duchy-of-brzesc-kujawski.r: Brzesc was a modest farming land on the Vistula plain, bordered by the [[s:state-of-the-teutonic-order|State of the Teutonic Order]]. From this small base Wladyslaw I gathered further duchies, including [[s:duchy-of-sieradz|Sieradz]] and [[s:duchy-of-leczyca|Leczyca]], and after long struggles with Bohemian and Silesian rivals he was crowned King of [[e:poland|Poland]] in 1320.
duchy-of-brzesc-kujawski.e: After 1320 the duchy merged into the reunited [[s:kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385|Kingdom of Poland]] (1025-1385). In 1332 the Teutonic Knights occupied Kuyavia during their war with [[e:poland|Poland]], and it was returned to the Polish Crown by the Treaty of Kalisz in 1343.

duchy-of-lorraine.t: The duchy between France and the Empire, ruled for seven centuries by one dynasty from Nancy before passing to France in 1766.
duchy-of-lorraine.o: [[e:lorraine|Lorraine]] grew from the Duchy of Upper Lorraine, created in 959 when the [[s:duchy-of-lotharingia|Duchy of Lotharingia]] was divided. In 1048 Emperor Henry III gave it to Gerard of Alsace, whose descendants ruled until 1737. The dukes settled on Nancy as their capital and held their lands as [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:holy-roman-empire|Holy Roman Empire]].
duchy-of-lorraine.r: The duchy was bilingual, French in the west and German in the east, and surrounded by the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun. René II defeated and killed Charles the Bold before Nancy in 1477. The Guise branch led the [[e:catholic-league|Catholic League]] in [[e:france|France]], and Nancy's [[e:renaissance|Renaissance]] and baroque palaces reflected a brilliant court.
duchy-of-lorraine.e: [[e:france|France]] occupied [[e:lorraine|Lorraine]] repeatedly in the 17th century; Duke Leopold recovered it in 1697. In 1737 Francis Stephen exchanged it for [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]], and the deposed Polish king Stanisław Leszczyński ruled it for life. On his death in 1766 it was annexed to the [[s:kingdom-of-france|Kingdom of France]].

duchy-of-brabant.t: The duchy of Brussels, Leuven and Antwerp, famous for its charter of liberties, the Joyous Entry, and the economic heart of the Low Countries.
duchy-of-brabant.o: The counts of Louvain had held the title of duke of Lower [[s:duchy-of-lorraine|Lorraine]] since 1106. Around 1183 Henry I began styling himself duke of Brabant, and after the Diet of [[s:free-imperial-city-of-schwabisch-hall|Schwäbisch Hall]] in 1190 the [[s:county-of-louvain|County of Louvain]] and its neighbouring lands formed the Duchy of Brabant.
duchy-of-brabant.r: Brabant's dukes ruled with powerful towns: Brussels, [[s:county-of-louvain|Leuven]], [[e:antwerp|Antwerp]] and 's-Hertogenbosch. John I won [[s:duchy-of-limburg|Limburg]] at Worringen in 1288. The Joyous Entry of 1356 bound Duchess Joanna to respect the estates' rights, a charter sworn by every later ruler. Cloth, then Antwerp's world trade in the 16th century, made Brabant the richest part of the [[e:low-countries|Low Countries]].
duchy-of-brabant.e: Brabant passed to Philip the Good in 1430 and joined the [[s:burgundian-state|Burgundian State]], then the [[s:habsburg-netherlands|Habsburg Netherlands]]. The [[e:dutch-revolt|Dutch Revolt]] split it: the north went to the [[s:dutch-republic|Dutch Republic]] in 1648, the south stayed in the [[s:spanish-netherlands|Spanish Netherlands]] and [[s:austrian-netherlands|Austrian Netherlands]], rose in the Brabant Revolution of 1789, and was annexed by [[e:france|France]] in 1795.

duchy-of-rome.t: Byzantine district around Rome in which the popes gradually took over government, the seed of the Papal States.
duchy-of-rome.o: After the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombard]] invasion, the territory around [[e:rome|Rome]] remained in Byzantine hands, cut off from [[s:lordship-of-ravenna|Ravenna]] by Lombard Spoleto. A duke (dux) commanded its garrison under the exarch of Ravenna. From the pontificate of Gregory the Great (590–604), who organised Rome's food supply and defence, the popes became the area's real leaders.
duchy-of-rome.r: The duke led the local militia while the pope administered the vast Church estates, fed the city and negotiated with the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombards]]. A local military aristocracy grew powerful. Disputes with [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] over doctrine and taxation, especially Iconoclasm under Leo III, loosened ties to the empire. King Liutprand's gift of Sutri to the pope in 728 was its first territorial grant.
duchy-of-rome.e: When the [[e:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Lombards]] took [[s:lordship-of-ravenna|Ravenna]] in 751 and threatened [[e:rome|Rome]], [[e:papacy|Pope]] Stephen II crossed the [[e:alps|Alps]] and gained the protection of [[e:pepin-the-short|Pepin the Short]] in 754. Pepin's donation of 756 created the [[s:papal-states|Papal States]], into which the duchy was absorbed.

duchy-of-bohemia.t: The Czech duchy of the Přemyslid dynasty, home of Saint Wenceslas, which grew from Prague into a strong state and a kingdom of the Empire.
duchy-of-bohemia.o: Bořivoj I, the first historically attested Přemyslid, was baptised around 870, probably by Methodius, while under Great Moravian overlordship. After [[s:great-moravia|Great Moravia]] fell, the Přemyslids of [[e:prague|Prague]] unified the Bohemian tribes. In 895 they sought East Frankish protection, and [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] became tied to the German kingdom.
duchy-of-bohemia.r: Dukes ruled from [[e:prague|Prague]] Castle through a network of castle districts. Wenceslas, murdered by his brother Boleslaus I in 935, became the country's patron saint. Boleslaus II founded the bishopric of Prague in 973. Dukes were [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the German kings, while [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]], [[e:silver|silver]] and later colonisation shaped the economy.
duchy-of-bohemia.e: Vratislaus II received a personal royal title in 1085 and Vladislaus II in 1158. In 1198 Ottokar I secured a hereditary royal crown, confirmed by the [[e:golden-bull-of-1356|Golden Bull]] of [[e:sicily|Sicily]] in 1212, and the duchy became the [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Kingdom of Bohemia]], a leading state of the Empire.

duchy-of-saxe-merseburg.t: Albertine Saxon secondary duchy on the Saale, created by an elector's will and absorbed back into the Electorate after eighty years.
duchy-of-saxe-merseburg.o: Elector John George I of Saxony divided parts of his lands in his will among his younger sons. After his death in 1656, Christian I received Merseburg, the secularised bishopric and its district, founding the Duchy of Saxe-Merseburg, which also held parts of Lusatia.
duchy-of-saxe-merseburg.r: The dukes held their lands as secundogenitures under the [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] of the [[s:electorate-of-saxony|Electorate of Saxony]], with limited independence in foreign affairs. They rebuilt Merseburg Castle and maintained a court with music and a library. The duchy was Lutheran and agrarian. Its later dukes were known more for extravagance than for policy; Maurice William was nicknamed the Fiddle Duke.
duchy-of-saxe-merseburg.e: Heinrich, the last duke, died without heirs in 1738, and the territory reverted to the [[s:electorate-of-saxony|Electorate of Saxony]]. Merseburg passed to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1815 and is now in Saxony-Anhalt.

duchy-of-plock.t: The northern Masovian duchy around the old Piast city of Plock, a Polish vassal until its incorporation in 1495.
duchy-of-plock.o: In 1275 the [[s:duchy-of-masovia|Duchy of Masovia]] was split, and the part centred on Plock, an early Piast capital and bishopric on the Vistula, went to Boleslaw II of Masovia. For two centuries Plock was sometimes reunited with the rest of Masovia and sometimes ruled as a separate duchy.
duchy-of-plock.r: Plock was an old episcopal city with a Romanesque cathedral containing Piast tombs. Its dukes balanced between [[e:poland|Poland]], [[s:kingdom-of-bohemia|Bohemia]] and the Teutonic Order: Wenceslaus of Plock did homage to John of [[e:bohemia|Bohemia]] in 1329. From 1351 the Masovian dukes were [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the Polish Crown.
duchy-of-plock.e: The last duke of Plock, Janusz II, died in 1495, and King John I Albert incorporated the duchy into the [[s:kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385|Kingdom of Poland]] (1385-1569). The rest of Masovia followed in 1526.

demak-sultanate.t: The first Muslim sultanate of Java, founded by Raden Patah on the north coast, which replaced Majapahit as the island's leading power.
demak-sultanate.o: Demak was a port on the north coast of Central [[e:java|Java]]. In the late 15th century its ruler Raden Patah, described in Javanese tradition as a son of the last [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit]] king and a Chinese mother, threw off Majapahit's overlordship. Supported by the Wali Songo, the nine saints, he made Demak the centre of a coalition of Muslim coastal states.
demak-sultanate.r: Demak's Great Mosque, whose pillars are said to have been made by the saints themselves, became the holiest site in [[e:java|Java]]. Pati Unus led fleets against [[s:portuguese-malacca|Portuguese Malacca]] in 1513. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Trenggana expanded inland and west, taking [[e:sunda-strait|Sunda]] Kalapa from the [[s:sunda-kingdom|Sunda Kingdom]] in 1527 and conquering much of East Java.
demak-sultanate.e: Trenggana died during a campaign at Panarukan in 1546, and a succession war followed in which Arya Penangsang killed rival princes. Hadiwijaya of [[s:pajang-sultanate|Pajang]] defeated him and moved power inland, founding the Pajang Sultanate.

duchy-of-saxe-weimar.t: An Ernestine Saxon duchy centred on Weimar, forerunner of the Goethe-era duchy of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach.
duchy-of-saxe-weimar.o: The Ernestine Wettins, who lost the electorate in 1547, kept lands in Thuringia that were repeatedly divided. The Erfurt Division of 1572 gave Duke Frederick William I the lands around Weimar, while his cousins received Coburg and Eisenach.
duchy-of-saxe-weimar.r: Weimar's Lutheran dukes ruled a farming territory with the university of Jena nearby. The duchy was repeatedly divided among brothers, and in 1640 the [[s:duchy-of-saxe-gotha|Duchy of Saxe-Gotha]] split off, while Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar became a famous Protestant general in the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]]. Johann Sebastian Bach served as court organist and concertmaster at Weimar from 1708 to 1717.
duchy-of-saxe-weimar.e: When the [[s:duchy-of-saxe-eisenach|Duchy of Saxe-Eisenach]]'s line died out in 1741, Duke Ernest Augustus I united the two as the [[s:duchy-of-saxe-weimar-eisenach|Duchy of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach]]. Under Duchess Anna Amalia and Charles Augustus the united duchy became the home of Goethe and Schiller.

ditadura-nacional.t: The military dictatorship that ended Portugal's First Republic and brought António de Oliveira Salazar to power.
ditadura-nacional.o: On 28 May 1926 a military coup launched from Braga by General Manuel Gomes da Costa overthrew the [[s:first-portuguese-republic|First Portuguese Republic]]. Within weeks Gomes da Costa was pushed aside by General Óscar Carmona, who became president.
ditadura-nacional.r: The military regime dissolved parliament, introduced censorship and repressed several revolts. Unable to solve the financial crisis, it appointed the Coimbra economics professor [[e:antonio-de-oliveira-salazar|António de Oliveira Salazar]] as finance minister in 1928, with control over all spending. He balanced the budget and steadily accumulated power, becoming prime minister in 1932.
ditadura-nacional.e: A new constitution, approved by plebiscite in 1933, transformed the military dictatorship into Salazar's civilian, corporatist [[s:estado-novo-portugal|Estado Novo (Portugal)]], with Carmona remaining president.
